en: While the two venerable saints, Śrīla Rūpa and Sanātana, were being gratified,
this [work] is once again analyzed by the southern Bhaṭṭa. Om.

Having examined the first manuscript of that work— which was displaced, missing, and fragmentary— and having made a systematic arrangement, Jīvaka writes it down. //o// [1] Therein, the connection has been explained by means of the four preceding compositions.

In that regard, it has been established that Brahman—the Supreme Self, the Blessed Lord—is designated as threefold according to its manifestations: as the Absolute Reality (para-tattva) characterized by fullness, eternity, and supreme bliss; as the Relational (sambandhi); and as Brahman. And therein—
The supreme excellence of the manifestation as the Blessed One himself has been established;
and incidentally, Viṣṇu and others, as well as the four Sanas and so forth, have been shown to be his incarnations.
And it has been determined that this Blessed One is Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself;
and in the enumeration of the majesty of the Supreme Self, even those forms which are external potencies (taṭastha-śakti) consist solely of the essence of consciousness (cid-eka-rasa).

Furthermore, it has been made known that the suffering of saṃsāra belongs to those living beings (jīvas) whose knowledge of their own true nature is veiled by that very māyā— which possesses openings acquired through an aversion to the primordial reality consisting in the absence of contact with the knowledge of the beginningless supreme reality— and who have conceived a sense of self within the insentient *pradhāna* composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Likewise:
It was said by the Blessed Lord in the eleventh [canto]: "The self consists of perfect knowledge; indeed, the dispute that 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' is rooted in the perception of duality."
"Even though it is useless, it does not cease for those men whose minds have turned away from Me and from their own world.
Therefore, for that purpose, He teaches the scripture which is supremely compassionate.

In that regard, for those living beings who possess the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from experiencing the meaning of that [truth] in other births, or who have at that very moment obtained the vision and so forth of His supreme compassion, there is such a characteristic of the supreme reality (*para-tattva*).
Merely by the commencement of hearing the instruction on the subject, at that very moment and simultaneously, both its presence and its experience are known;
as it has been said: "Or what need is there for others [to describe] God?"
"In this matter, it is immediately and at that very moment taken to heart by the skillful who are desirous of hearing" (BhP 1.1.1).
Therefore, they have no need for other instructions;
however, any incidental hearing of other instructions is merely that.
Just as hearing of His pastimes is an excitant for the very rasa of those [devotees], such as Śrī Prahlāda and others,
so too, for others, that same quality, though acting as a seed, becomes something other than that due to defects such as lust and the like.
It remains obstructed by nothing but defect;
O Lord of Kuṇṭha, this mind of yours does not falter even amidst discourses on such matters.
How can I, being wretched, contemplate Your path within that which is corrupted by evil, wicked, and intense; afflicted by lust, and tormented by joy, grief, fear, and desire? [BhP 7.9.39]

Thus, according to the words of Śrī Prahlāda, who considered himself wretched, that attainment belongs only to others; for this very reason it is said in the *Brahmavaivarta*: "As long as the heart is defiled by sins, for so long indeed [is one bound]."
One should not have the notion of truth regarding the treatise, nor likewise the notion of goodness regarding the true guru.
"The great fruit of the mass of merit produced over many lifetimes arises as love and so forth simply from the company of the virtuous and the hearing of the scriptures. Thus,
although their primary intent culminates in the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), for them [there remains] the supreme reality and so forth—

When the inquiry arises as to what the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) of this instruction are, both of these must be taught through its intermediate intention (*avāntara-tātparya*).
Among those, the subject matter is [the nature of] aversion toward that [worldly existence].
Because of their mutual opposition, there is only the manifestation of that [opposing state];
and that [manifestation] is characterized by the worship of that [state], precisely because from it the knowledge of that [state] emerges.
And the purpose is the experience of that [reality];
and that experience is characterized by internal and external direct realization, from which alone the cessation of all suffering occurs for oneself.
Although these two [methods] were intended as instructions for those who have already attained realization in the previous section—

just as some poor person, having heard that there is a treasure in his house, exerts effort for its sake and obtains it— nevertheless, this instruction is given again in order to dispel any laxity regarding them.

Thus, by describing to them that very cause of suffering— consisting of aversion toward Him and so forth, which is composed of the absence of connection with His eternally established knowledge— one provides a remedy similar to medical treatment that consists in the reversal of the diagnosis of a disease.
He teaches [the necessity of] being face-to-face and so forth:
"Fear would arise from attachment to a second [entity];
for one who has strayed from the Lord, there is the opposite, which is forgetfulness."
"Therefore, O wise one, through His illusory power (māyā), one should worship Him with single-minded devotion, having become one with the Guru and the Deity who are the Lord.
And the commentary says: "Now, what is the purpose of thus worshipping the Supreme Lord for one whose fear is merely imagined by ignorance?"
Anticipating the objection that [ignorance] is removed by knowledge alone, he says "fear":
since fear arises from that [Lord] through His māyā, therefore the wise man should resort to and worship Him alone.
Surely fear would arise from attachment to a second [entity], and that [attachment] arises from the ego-identification with the body and so forth, and that...
Since its own nature does not manifest, what can Māyā do in this regard?
To this he says: "Of one who has turned away from the Lord. For one who is averse to the Lord, non-remembrance of His nature occurs through His Māyā; from that, error arises.
"I am the body. From that second attachment, fear arises.
For this is well known even in worldly illusions.
And it was said by the Blessed One:
"For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the gunas, is difficult to overcome;
but those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion."
[Thus ends Gītā 7.14.
[Page 3] One should worship with single-minded, unwavering devotion.
Furthermore, one whose self is the teacher and the deity—wherein the teacher alone is the deity, the Lord—should so worship.
The meaning is: being one for whom the Self is most dear, and who possesses such a vision; thus ends this [verse].
//11.2// The poet knows the bodiless state.
//1// [2] Furthermore— thus, it is established by itself within one's own mind.
The Lord Ananta is the self, the beloved, and the ultimate goal;
one who has attained liberation and is fixed in that goal should worship Him, wherein the causes of saṃsāra come to rest.
And the commentary says: "Then, what should be done by him?
Hari alone is to be served.
Thus, being dispassionate...
One should cultivate that [mind].
The reasons for its being worthy of cultivation are as follows: it is established by itself within one's own mind; and because it is the self, it is therefore dear.
And service to one who is dear is indeed of the nature of happiness;
this is the true meaning,
and not as if it were directed toward a non-self.
This is false; for the Blessed One possesses worshipful qualities, is infinite, and is eternal.
Since he is such as this, one should worship him.
Having a fixed meaning and a determined nature,
he is one who is satisfied by the bliss of experiencing the Blessed One.

Thus, its nature as inherently blissful has been shown. What is this [nature]? It is that wherein, when that vessel exists, there occurs the cessation—that is, the destruction—of ignorance, which is the cause of saṃsāra.
And here, by virtue of the word "ca" (and), its attainment is to be understood.

//2.2// Śrī Śuka //2// [3] In this regard, although hearing, reflection, and so forth are indeed means for attaining knowledge, they too become effective only when directed toward Him, because they serve as the cause for the experience of the form of Brahman.
Therefore, because they are useful for that lineage, the practices of Sāṅkhya and the eightfold yoga are also directed toward that very same goal.
Likewise, of those...
In some way, even devotion arises,
because action is performed as the fulfillment of His command and through such means as offering it unto Him.

Furthermore, since knowledge and other virtues are prescribed as auxiliaries to devotion by way of being causes for non-attachment to other things and so forth, nevertheless, by the statement "one should worship with devotion first," ritual action,
knowledge, and the like are not intended; rather, it refers directly to devotion characterized by hearing, chanting, and so forth.

It has been stated that one should "worship" (bhajeta). This very point is seen to be supported by reasons right from the beginning of the *Śrī Sūta Upadeśa*, as stated in twenty-two verses by the passage beginning with "sa vai... and ending with "ato vai kavayaḥ."
"That indeed is the supreme dharma for men from which arises unswerving and unimpeded devotion to Adhokṣaja, by which the self becomes perfectly serene.
(BhP 1.2.6) Indeed, that which was asked at the commencement of the Mahāpurāṇa— the singular essence of all scriptures, the absolute good— [is this very devotion].
"Speak," [he said]; to that, the reply begins with "He indeed" (sa vai) and so forth.
From that dharma, devotion toward the Transcendent One (adhokṣaja) arises, as does a delight in hearing His stories and so on.
Because, in passages such as *dharmaḥ svanuṣṭhitaḥ* (BhP 1.2.8), it is intended to be shown by way of contrast;
that indeed is the very same [result] of dharma well-performed.

In accordance with the principle that will be stated later— namely, "Perfection is the pleasing of Hari" (BhP 1.2.13)— dharma performed solely for the sake of His satisfaction is supreme and the best of all; it is not even characterized merely by renunciation (nivṛtti), because there is no difference in the state of being turned away from worldly objects.

And likewise is the statement of the venerable Nārada: "Even inaction, if devoid of devotion to Acyuta... and so forth; for how much more so [is action not auspicious] when even that action which is performed without motive is not offered to the Lord, as stated in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.12: "How then could that which is eternally inauspicious and not offered to the Lord be otherwise?"
Therefore, it will be said: "Hence, by men...
(BhP 1.2.13) and so forth; the meaning is that, consequently, devotion alone is the exclusive means to the highest good (*śreyas*).
By this, such a nature of devotion—
It is also superior by its very nature.
He describes the essential quality of that devotion: because it is blissful by its own nature, it is "uncaused," meaning it is devoid of any expectation of further rewards.

It is unimpeded because there is no other object that could grant happiness superior to it, and it cannot be obstructed by anything whatsoever. And once that devotion, characterized by delight, has arisen, through that very devotion, the yoga of devotion characterized by hearing [the scriptures] and so forth occurs.
[The path] would have been set in motion.

And consequently, in accordance with such passages as, "In whomsoever there is devotion to the Blessed One that is free from possessiveness, in him all the gods abide with all their qualities" (BhP 5.18.12), knowledge of the essential nature and other attributes of the Blessed One [would arise] toward Him and not elsewhere.
And detachment would follow that very [devotion]; thus he says:
"Devotional yoga, when practiced toward the Blessed Vāsudeva, quickly generates detachment and that knowledge which is without cause. [BhP 1.2.7]

The meaning is that the knowledge pertaining to the Upaniṣads— which is without cause and beyond the scope of dry logic and the like— produces [realization] quickly, by the mere act of hearing it slightly.
He states this by way of contrast:
If the dharma well-performed by men does not produce delight in the narrations of Viṣvaksena, it is indeed nothing but mere exhaustion;
for if, due to the absence of taking Vāsudeva as one's refuge, there is no delight— that is, no taste— for His narrations and descriptions of His pastimes.
If one were not to produce it, there would be only labor and no fruit;
since a taste for discourse is primary and supreme in all respects, that alone has been taught.

By way of illustration, a preference for other forms of worship is also taught. By the word "eva" (only/alone), the perishability of the fruits of action characterized by worldly engagement— such as heaven and the like— is indicated.

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), there is the status of being a scriptural authority supported by reasoning, as in that very context: "Just as here the world won by action perishes" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.1.6).
By the word "kevala" (mere/only), [there is the indication of] mere cessation.
The fruit of the dharma characterized by marks is not something to be accomplished;
even that which is accomplished is perishable.
In this regard as well, by that very word "hi" (for), [it refers to passages such as: "He who has supreme devotion for the Lord... [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23].

"O Lord, those who cast aside devotion— the path to the highest good— and strive only for the attainment of pure knowledge," and so forth; "having ascended with great difficulty to the supreme state, they fall back down from there, having disregarded You."

The authority of such scriptural statements as "aṅghrayaḥ" (BhP 10.2.32) and others is also indicated. From these two verses, it is understood that devotion (*bhakti*) is independent, whereas knowledge (*jñāna*) and detachment (*vairāgya*) are dependent upon it. Therefore...
Thus, it has been stated that the fruitfulness of dharma consists precisely in its being the fruit of devotion.
In this regard, others consider that the fruit of dharma is wealth (*artha*), the fruit of that is desire (*kāma*), and the fruit of that is the senses (*indriya*).
"From pleasure comes further pleasure, and from that pleasure again arises the succession of dharma and so forth; yet that [pleasure] is otherwise than [what it seems]," he says in two verses:
"For the purpose of worldly wealth does not serve the sake of dharma which leads to liberation."
For desire is not remembered as leading to the attainment of wealth that is exclusively righteous.
The gratification of the senses is not the attainment of desire; one should live with only as much as is necessary for life.
For the living being, the inquiry into reality is the goal, and not that wealth which is acquired here through ritual actions.
Regarding liberation (*apavarga*): liberation occurs according to the injunctions prescribed for each respective social class (*varṇa*).

When that [knowledge]— characterized by the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) directed toward no other cause— is applied toward the Blessed One, Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, who is the self of all, devoid of a self, indefinable, without abode, and at the time when, by means of the loosening of the knot of bondage caused by ignorance which is the cause of various states of existence...
For it is said in the prose section of the fifth book [of the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*], "Indeed, this is the association with the Great Person," that liberation is *bhakti-yoga*.
Likewise, in the *Revākhaṇḍa* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"O Janārdana, that unwavering devotion toward You is itself liberation;
for Your devotees, O Viṣṇu, O Hari, are indeed liberated.
Thus, according to the manner stated [in this verse], the meaning is "of one who accomplishes devotion."
For the sake of the goal, for the sake of the fruit;
likewise, desire for an object that is not inconsistent with such dharmas is not remembered by the knowers of reality as being for the sake of gain or for the sake of the fruit.

The fruit of desire—the enjoyment of sense objects—is not the attainment of sensory pleasure; rather, the attainment of desire is only to the extent that one may live. The meaning is that desire should be pursued only as long as such a life continues.
Furthermore, that which is well-known in this world as heaven and so forth— attained by the living being through actions performed by means of the practice of dharma— is not the true goal;
rather, it is the inquiry into reality itself.
Thus, the sense is that for that very devotion of which the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*) has been stated as an intermediate fruit, that [devotion] itself is the supreme fruit.
In response to the inquiry "What is reality?", one verse has been cited:
"Those who know reality declare that reality to be non-dual knowledge;
it is designated as Brahman, as the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and as the Blessed Lord (Bhagavān).
By the word "non-dual," its indivisibility is indicated, and with the intention of expressing that nothing else exists apart from it, that—
He accepts that it is indeed power (śakti).
In that regard, Brahman is designated as pure knowledge (jñāna) alone, which is distinct from the collection of powers, their characteristics, and their attributes.
The Supreme Self is that which is characterized by a portion of the conscious power (cit-śakti) abundant with the internal ruler-ship (antaryāmitva) and the power of māyā;
it is characterized by all powers in their complete perfection.

Regarding the term "Bhagavān," this has already been explained by the preceding three passages. And he says that this very reality, which is endowed with a threefold manifestation, is realized directly through devotion alone:
"Trusting this, the sages—endowed with knowledge and dispassion—perceive the Self within themselves through devotion acquired by hearing [the scriptures].
Through that devotion, characterized by love, which consists solely in a delight for His stories and takes the form of the supreme state," [BhP 1.2.12]... it is that very [Self].
They perceive the aforementioned reality within their own pure minds;
what need is there to mention mere knowledge? The meaning is that they even manifest it directly.
Of what nature is that Self? It is the substratum of its own essential form (svarūpa), the individual soul (jīva), and the power of illusion (māyā-śakti).
By means of that which is joined with knowledge and detachment— that is, by those two, knowledge and detachment, born of one's own self and cultivated by them; for this very reason, they [are so].
It follows that the sages perceive [the Lord] both individually and as the Supreme by their own will.
Thus, through these three words— "those who have heard," "those who have grasped," and "those who have faith"— it is shown that this very devotion belongs to those sages.
The rarity [of this] has been shown; if,
through the hearing and investigation of the meaning of all the scriptures, such as Vedānta, from the presence of a true guru, it is known as one's own necessary and supreme duty, then— again—
And the Blessed Lord, having examined Brahman in its entirety three times with his intellect, determined that which is the immutable state from which delight in the Self arises. [BhP 2.2.34]
Thus, if the capacity for reflection and the inclination toward reflection were to abandon contrary mental cultivation,
then that devotion would be attained by those who have faith through the gateway of spiritual practice (*upāsanā*);
therefore, the Śruti also adopts this for that purpose.
"The Self, indeed, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5).
Herein, "meditation" (nididhyāsana) refers to...
Worship is called vision, which is direct realization.
And this devotion, so difficult to attain, is obtained even from one's natural duty when it is applied toward pleasing Hari.
Therefore, he says that pleasing Hari alone is his supreme fruit:
[page 6]

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, for men according to their divisions of social class and stage of life, the perfection of dharma well-performed is the pleasing of Hari. "Well-performed" means acquired without flaw through great effort; [this is said] because results such as heaven are insignificant.
The sense is that such an application [of effort] is utterly improper.

If this is so, then even for dharma which gratifies Śrī Hari, its fruit is indeed devotion characterized by a taste for hearing and so forth; therefore, [the fruit] of the devotion set in motion by that [dharma] is...
And since qualities such as knowledge and dispassion follow from that, it follows that at that time one must practice devotion itself in the form of direct hearing and so forth.
To the question, "What is the point of such insistence on that? he says:

Therefore, with a single mind— free from attachment to ritual actions and the like— the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, should always be heard, glorified, meditated upon, and worshipped. (BhP 1.2.14) "With a single mind" means devoid of grasping at karma and other such worldly concerns.
In this context, "hearing" refers to the names, qualities, and so forth,
as well as their recitation. Therein, in order to explain the style that is easy to understand up to the final stage, [the text addresses] the hardships regarding the Dharma and so forth.

By means of pure reasoning alone, being indifferent [to other methods], he generates an initial inclination toward the stories of the glorious Hari and reminds him of His qualities: "Those joined with meditation upon Him [sever] the binding knot of karma."
The wise cut through this; who would not take delight in the story of Him?

The wise are those who possess discernment, are youthful, and have their minds restrained. For them, the mere meditation—simply the contemplation—of Hari is a sword; with that sword, they cut the knot of egoism within various bodies.
Who indeed would take pleasure in the talk of one who is thus bound by karma and yet cuts it asunder, and who seeks to escape from such supreme suffering? [11]
Now, even if this were so, one might suspect that those of meager fortune do not develop a taste for discourse on Him;
anticipating this, he teaches devotion— beginning with that [discourse] and culminating in steadfast devotion— through five verses while describing the means for it.

"O Brahmins, for one who is desirous of hearing and endowed with faith, a taste for the narrations of Vāsudeva arises through service to the great and by resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites" (BhP 1.2.16).
According to such passages as "On earth, the sages free from pride [reside] in the abodes of many sacred pilgrimage sites," and so forth... [BhP]

[10.87.35] Furthermore, according to the approval of its commentary that "in such places there is generally great association," one may develop a taste for the narrations of Vāsudeva through that service to the great which is obtained by chance as a result of resorting to sacred pilgrimage sites (puṇyatīrtha).

Even when wandering at a sacred site for other purposes, service characterized by seeing, touching, and conversing with great beings who are themselves wandering or residing there generally occurs spontaneously.
And by the power of that, faith arises toward his conduct;
and regarding his natural, mutual discourse concerning the Blessed One, the desire arises: "I shall hear what these two are conversing about."
And by hearing that, an inclination toward it arises;
thus, the sense is that what is heard from the great alone immediately accomplishes the task.
And so [says] Kapiladeva—
The scriptural statement: "From association with the virtuous, my conversations regarding the realization of divine power become a nectar for the heart and ears" (BhP 3.25.22), and so forth.
And therefore, [12]...

"For those who hear His own stories, Kṛṣṇa— whose hearing and chanting are meritorious— standing within the heart as the Friend of the virtuous, indeed shakes off all that is inauspicious. By means of these stories, Hari, standing within, having entered the path of meditative realization, [removes] the inauspicious latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
[Page 7] [13] And then,
when all inauspicious things have almost entirely perished through constant service to the Bhagavat,

"Devotion to the Blessed One, whose fame is supreme, becomes steadfast. By stating that such knowledge does not exist when [the world] has merely declined, but exists only when it is completely destroyed, the unimpeded nature of devotion is described.
Through service to the devotees or the scripture of the Bhāgavata, devotion becomes steadfast, continuous, and takes the form of constant meditation.
At that very time, as stated in passages such as *BhP 11.2.53*: "Even for the sake of the sovereignty of the three worlds, his memory remains unimpeded," and so forth—

He states that, by the aforementioned method, through the destruction of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the mind becomes pure essence (*sattva*), preeminent, and fit for the direct realization of the reality of the Blessed One:
"Then, the states of passion and darkness, as well as desire, greed, and so forth," [are destroyed].
When the mind is not pierced by these, it remains established and becomes serene toward the Supreme Being (*sattva*).
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "by these"—meaning by passion (*rajas*), darkness (*tamas*), and those states such as desire (*kāma*) which are produced by them.
Thus, for one whose mind is serene through the yoga of devotion to the Blessed Lord (*bhagavad-bhakti-yoga*), [the mind becomes fixed].
"The knowledge of the reality of the Blessed One arises for one who is free from attachment.
(BhP 1.2.20) Thus, by the aforementioned method, for one whose mind is serene and who is consequently free from attachment—
that is, one who has abandoned the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and the like— there arises that knowledge through the practice of *bhakti-yoga* being performed once again.
Direct realization arises as an experience, whether within the mind or externally, even without cultivation.
Regarding that direct realization— which is of the nature of its own fruit by virtue of being the singular form of supreme bliss— he states its incidental fruit:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are severed,
and one's karmas are exhausted upon seeing the Lord as the Self" (BhP 1.2.21). Here,
the "knot of the heart" refers to the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

"All doubts are severed" means that for those who prioritize hearing, reflection, and so forth, all doubts come to an end upon seeing Him alone. In that regard, first of all, through hearing, the misconceptions concerning the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) are severed.
It should be understood that through reflection (*manana*), the misconceptions regarding those [objects] are removed;
whereas through direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*),
the misconceptions and lack of conviction regarding one's own fitness for [the practice] are removed.
They perish by the mere wish of that [Brahman]; the meaning is that their appearance alone remains within them in some slight degree.
Here, demonstrating right conduct regarding the subject matter of this treatise, he concludes:
Therefore, the sages always perform devotion with supreme joy toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva,
which brings about the purification of the self— that is, the cleansing of the mind.
Not only does she possess these many qualities;

furthermore, through supreme joy, the practice of devotion—unlike the performance of ritual acts—is not of the nature of suffering at the time of its preparation or at the time of its fulfillment, but rather is of the nature of happiness itself. This is the meaning.
Therefore, it is said that they act thus constantly, both during the stage of the practitioner and during the stage of the perfected one.
//1.2// Śrī Sūta // 3-17 // [18] Thus, it is the established view that one should practice devotion to the Blessed One alone, by relinquishing effort toward ritual action, knowledge, and dispassion.
He states, in seven verses, that one must not even perform the worship of other deities, which is a specific form of ritual action;
therein, what need is there to mention others?
Even though he is indeed an incarnation of the qualities of the Śrī-Bhagavān, because— unlike Śrī-Viṣṇu— he lacks the status of being the direct Supreme Brahman himself,
and because he does not solely benefit the mode of goodness (sattva), but on the contrary increases passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas).
Regarding the point that even Brahmā and Śiva should not be worshipped by those seeking the highest good, two verses have been cited in the *Paramātma-sandarbha*:
"Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of Prakṛti; by them..."
The one Supreme Person, being joined here with this world,
assumes the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara for the sake of its maintenance and other functions;
indeed, among those names, the name Sattvatano (the embodiment of goodness) shall bring about the highest welfare for men.
"From earth comes smoke, which is harsh; from that, fire consisting of the three qualities (*trayīmaya*).
From darkness (*tamas*) arises passion (*rajas*), and from that, goodness (*sattva*), which is the vision of Brahman.
Thus, [it refers to] the one whose body is *sattva* and whose power is *sattva*.
The threefold [Veda] consists of the three Vedas; it abounds in the rituals prescribed by them.
Darkness stands in the place of wood;
passion stands in the place of smoke.
Sattva is the locus of fire;
the Veda is the locus of the action prescribed by the three Vedas.
Therefore, the action prescribed by the three Vedas is as [in] the fire.

In this very way, [the Lord] manifests directly and not in any other two [modes]; similarly, the meaning is that the Blessed One, who has become the Supreme Brahman, exists only as pure being (*sattva*).
By means of abandoning other deities, he establishes the practice of the virtuous as authoritative for devotion to the Blessed One.
Then the sages approached the Lord Adhokṣaja first;
those who follow them here are fit for the welfare of pure being.
"Atha" means "for this reason."
In the beginning, formerly;
the being, pure, whose form consists of the essence of pure being,
the Blessed One.
And his transcendence of the primary material nature (*prakṛti*) has been revealed in the *Bhagavat-sandarbha*.
Therefore, those who follow him are fit for security within this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
[19] But surely, some are seen worshipping other deities as well, such as Bhairava and others?
It is true that they have their desires fulfilled; however, even those seeking liberation do not worship others,
let alone those devoted to Him.
He says that these are the goals of human endeavor:
"Desiring liberation, those free from envy abandon the lords of beings who are terrible in form, and instead worship the peaceful portions of Nārāyaṇa. [BhP 1.2.26]
The term "lords of beings" (bhūta-patīn) is an elliptical expression for the ancestors, the lords of creatures, and others; "free from envy" means being those who do not revile other deities. [20]
[Objection: But surely even desire and greed exist in the worship of the Lord of Lakṣmī; how then do they worship others? [Reply:
Those of the nature of *rajas* and *tamas*, being of similar character, indeed worship them.
"Those desiring prosperity, power, and progeny [worship] the ancestors, the spirits, the lords of creatures, and so forth.

Regarding this, he says: because they possess a character identical to that of the ancestors and others due to their very nature being characterized by *rajas* and *tamas*, their engagement in such worship occurs precisely because of that similarity of character; this is the meaning. [21]
Therefore, it has been stated that Vāsudeva alone is to be worshipped;
and with two verses, he declares that the essential purport of all scriptures lies in him alone.
The Vedas have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal; the sacrifices have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal;
the yogas have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal; and ritual actions have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal.

Knowledge has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; austerity has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; dharma has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal; the ultimate refuge has Vāsudeva as its supreme goal. (BhP 1.2.28–29) (page 9)
And the commentary [states]: "Those for whom Vāsudeva is the supreme object of the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: "Are not the Vedas seen to be devoted to sacrifices? Anticipating this, it is stated that even they are indeed devoted to Him alone, because they serve the purpose of His worship. This is [the meaning of] *yogā*.
Regarding the Yoga-śāstras,

fearing that they too might be considered solely devoted to practices such as postures (āsana) and breath control (prāṇāyāma), it is stated that they are indeed devoted to that [liberation], because those practices are the means for attaining it.

*Jñāna* refers to the science of knowledge (*jñāna-śāstra*). Anticipating the objection that it might refer solely to that [supreme] knowledge, it is stated that knowledge itself has that as its ultimate goal. Here, *tapas* means knowledge; *dharma* means the science of dharma (*dharma-śāstra*) concerning subjects such as charity and vows.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that [the Veda] has heaven and so forth as its ultimate goal? Anticipating this, it is said that "it is understood" (*gamyate*), thus *gati* refers to the fruit consisting of heaven and so forth;
and since that too is of the nature of a portion of that bliss, it is said to have that [bliss] alone as its ultimate goal.
Or rather, by the word "Vedas" itself, that—
It has been stated that all scriptures have Vāsudeva as their ultimate goal because He is the root.
Now, one might object: "Since those scriptures are devoted to various subjects such as sacrifices, yoga, and ritual actions, they cannot have Him as their sole purpose.
Anticipating this doubt, it should be understood that even sacrifices and the like are shown to have Him as their ultimate purpose; this is the point.
In this context, it should be understood that the primary intent of yoga and the other paths is their ultimate orientation toward devotion (*bhakti*) alone, albeit in some indirect manner.
Furthermore, while the Vedas should be known as being primarily concerned with the section on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*), for some they also have a direct orientation toward devotion.
"It is seen"—
for that great-souled one who has supreme devotion for the Divine, and as for the Divine, so for the Guru, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth clearly.
[Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.23] and so forth.
Thus, having demonstrated in the thirty-second verse that the subject matter consists precisely of devotion to Him, he establishes the aforementioned harmony of all the scriptures.

"In the beginning, that very Lord, who is himself devoid of qualities (aguṇa), created this universe through his own power of illusion (ātma-māyā)—an illusion composed of the modes of nature (guṇamayi) which consists of both the real and the unreal (sad-asad-rūpā). He is all-pervading (vibhu).
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Indeed, in a reality endowed with the divine play (līlā) of creating, entering, and governing the world..."

how, then, is everything subordinate to Vāsudeva?

That by which one is anointed is *añjana*, meaning an adjunct (*upādhi*); that which removes these is *nirañjana*. That which is undesirable and of the nature of suffering— both the action performed with desire at the time of its performance and at the time of its fruition,

If it is not offered, how could it shine again?
This is because, through its outward orientation, it lacks the capacity to purify the being (sattva). Such is the point.

Thus, it is clear that knowledge is rendered useless without the association of devotion, and action is useless without being a means for its accomplishment. Furthermore: "It is contemptible for one who instructs for the sake of dharma..."
Having stated, "For one who is naturally attached [to worldly objects], there is a great transgression" (BhP 1.5.15), and so forth, he says:

If one who is unripe falls while practicing devotion, then wherever he may fall, what misfortune could have befallen him?

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: Now, however, with the intention that even disregarding steadfastness in one's own duty (*svadharma*), whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*), devotion to Hari alone should be taught, he says "having abandoned" (*tyaktvā*). [Objection:
But if, by abandoning one's own duty and worshiping, one becomes fulfilled through the ripening of devotion, then [there would be no need for duty].
There is a certain concern:
"If, however, he were to die while still unripe, or were to fall away, then there would be misfortune caused by the abandonment of his own dharma. Anticipating this, he says:

If, by some chance, one should fall from that vessel, slip away, or even die, even then there is no fear of misfortune for one who is a connoisseur of the rasa of devotion, because such a person has no further obligation to ritual action.

Did anything inauspicious ever befall this one who was a connoisseur of the rasa of devotion, even while in a low birth?
The meaning is: it never happened at all; the intention is that this was due to the presence of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of devotion.
But for those who do not share [the merit] with others, what benefit is obtained by those who merely follow their own duty?
The word "abhajatām" (of those not sharing) is a genitive case expressing a relationship.
"This is [stated] with the intention of referring only to the essential factor.

One should devote oneself to that very Truth alone;
one should not be attached to anything else as a mere secondary mark,
for from such attachment comes the downfall of the self and the cycle of worldly existence.
The illustration for one person’s perception of all things through their respective sense organs is "just as when one observes people in a dream";
for even in a dream, at times—

Having fashioned many bodies, the individual soul (jīva) perceives everything through their respective sense organs; however, for the Lord, because of His power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti), there is no bondage—this is the point.
Here, while perceiving by means of His own cognitive functions (dhī-vṛtti), He perceives everything even by means of the cognitive functions of all beings.
It has been stated thus:

because in the passage "He thought," that [creation] is heard of even prior to the creation of all mental modifications (*dhī-vṛtti*). Likewise, although dream-bodies have the Lord as their agent, they are also [said to be] created by the individual soul (*jīva*).
In response to the inquiry as to how the Lord performs the description of conceptualization through the medium of volition (*saṅkalpa*), it is stated [in the verse]:

"He who [is the one] for whom all... Since the agent—who must be construed with the phrase "should resort to the truth" (*satyaṃ bhajeta*)—has not been explicitly mentioned, this is precisely the intended meaning.
That illustration being thus established, it is like the case where the self— the dreamer,
the individual soul— is the sole observer of all the people and the objects perceived therein within the dream. It is just like that.

In this context, by the word "him" (tam), there is reference to that which is well-known from the Śrutis, namely the passages: "He thought" (sa aikṣata) [AitU 1.1.2] and "His knowledge, power, and action are innate" (svābhāvikī jñāna-bala-kriyā ca) [ŚvetU 6.8].

Because the establishment of knowledge and other qualities occurs independently of anything else, and because it is stated that "in the intermediate state there is creation" (VS 3.2.1) and "it is mere illusion, however, because its true nature is not fully manifested" (VS 3.2.3), the agency of the dreamer— established by these principles— is the fullness of the agency of the creator of the world consisting of the waking state and so forth.

It should be understood that when [the goal] is attained, the distinction is shown by the pair beginning with "truth" (satya), as well as its being the supreme human purpose (parama-puruṣārtha). //2.1// Śrī Śuka // 24–26 // [27]

He from whom Brahmā and the others are subordinate.

In the case of Viśveśvara, He is the Seer and not the seen, because He is a mass of pure consciousness (*caitanya-ghanatva*). Having explained, in sequence, the means for immediate liberation (*sadyomukti*) and gradual liberation (*kramamukti*)— namely, *jñāna-yoga* and *yoga* [of action]— and having further stated that the performance of action dedicated to the Lord (*bhagavad-arpita-karman*), which is the cause of *bhakti-yoga*, is superior even to those, he has established the superiority of *bhakti-yoga* by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*). As it is said:
"Indeed, there is no other auspicious path for one entering into this cycle of worldly existence than that through which devotion-yoga toward the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva arises.

for there is no other auspicious means, consisting of bliss and free from obstacles, than that through the performance of which devotion-yoga (bhakti-yoga) arises. This is the point.

The Blessed Lord Brahmā, having scrutinized the Absolute in its entirety three times with his intellect, resolved upon it; being established in that which is immovable, he thus found delight in the Self.
[BhP 2.2.34] The Blessed Lord Brahmā.

The meaning is: being *kūṭastha*—unwavering—and *nirvikāra*—free from modification—with a one-pointed mind (*ekāgra-citta*). By means of his wisdom, he determined and resolved;
here too, in accordance with the concluding summary, the word "ātman" denotes Hari.

And it is stated in the *Nirukta*: "Because He is the source (*ātatvāt*) and because He is the mother (*mātṛtvāt*), Hari is indeed the Supreme Self (*parama ātmā*). He states that the vision of those who know the Vedas, as well as the vision of the Vedas— which consist of the infinite majesty of Vaikuṇṭha and so forth, and whose various recensions are studied by infinite Viriñcas— is possible through that very [Lord] alone, because He, being immutable, pervades time while remaining in a single form.
Therefore, He Himself has said:
"What does He ordain? What does He declare? What does He describe and then differentiate? No one other than Me knows the heart of this [Veda] in the world" (BhP 11.21.42).
In the same way, he concludes as the answer to the question with the verse beginning "That which is to be heard" (BhP 1.19.38):
"Therefore, O King, in every way, at all times, and everywhere, the Blessed Lord Hari is to be heard, glorified, and remembered by men. (BhP 2.2.36)
By the word "and" (ca), service at the feet and so forth are also included.
Furthermore, that which was shown immediately following as the fruit of hearing and so on has been illustrated here.
Those who drink the nectar of the Lord’s own discourse, gathered within the hollows of their ears,
purify their hearts that have been defiled by sense objects.
"They go to the vicinity of his lotus-like feet" (BhP 2.2.37).

Here, by the word "purifying" (*pūnanti*), the previously mentioned path of gross concentration (*sthūla-dhāraṇa*) is set aside; for since the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) is inherently purifying, there is no need for that effort.

an unwavering devotion toward the Blessed Lord arising from association with the devotees of the Lord.

This [verse] has the sense that "the gain which brings about the supreme human goal is the only one; everything else is trivial.

The fruit [arising] from the sharpness of the faculties and so forth is distinct; however,
when there is union with the Blessed One (Bhagavat), the state of being itself is the fruit.

"They do not eat nor do they urinate; what other animals are there in the village?"—thinking even that man-like animal to be such, others say this. "They do not urinate" means they do not engage in sexual intercourse.
