"There is no path more auspicious for yogis seeking the realization of Brahman than devotion directed toward the Blessed One, the Self of all. [BhP 3.25.19]
The perfection of Brahman (*brahma-siddhi*) is the manifestation of the supreme reality. As it is said:
"In this world, the attainment of the highest good for men consists of nothing more than this:
that the mind, through intense yoga of devotion, is fixedly offered unto Me. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.25.41)

By means of bhakti-yoga, such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, the mind offered unto Me becomes steady; this is all that is required. By the words "here" (atra) and "in this" (asmin), it is implied that in anything else there is nothing more than this.
//3.25// Śrī Kapila-deva //46-47// [48] Also, in the *Śrī Kumāropadeśa*, following the instruction on knowledge:
"By devotion to the playful grace of the petals of whose lotus feet..."
The virtuous untie the knotted accumulation of karma;
likewise, even ascetics whose minds are not yet purified, though they have blocked the multitude of sense-channels, cannot do so. Therefore, worship that Vāsudeva, who is free from all conflict.
In this ocean of worldly existence, those who lack a boat desire to cross over the crocodiles of the six internal enemies with great difficulty;
therefore, you should worship the feet of the Blessed Lord Hari.
"Having made a raft, cross over the calamity of the insurmountable ocean.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "Know him"—thus knowledge is taught;
however, because that [knowledge] is difficult to accomplish, [it leads to] devotion.
He teaches by means of two [verses], beginning with "Obeisance to the lotus feet... and so forth;
for indeed, according to the Śruti [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1], "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme."
It is asked: "How is it that ascetics do not become entangled?
To this he says: "In hardship... [The word] *aplava* means that which has no boat; here, a boat (*plava*) is that which is the cause for crossing over.
For those for whom He is the Lord, there is great hardship and suffering in crossing over this world;
for they [struggle] with difficulty against the seizing grasp of the group of six sense-faculties.
They desire to cross the ocean of existence;
therefore, this [teaching] is a raft or a boat for the ocean that is difficult to cross, the ocean that is hard to traverse.
Even though both paths are equally accessible, by stating that one is difficult to traverse, it is established by itself that the other is the intended subject;
here, they merely desire to cross over, but not...
The meaning should be understood as "they cross over.
[4.22] Śrī Sanatkumāra [spoke to] Śrī Pṛthu.
[48] Therefore, that knowledge which has been taught is also intended for the purpose of accomplishing the non-futility of that instruction. [49]
He states that even when performed merely as a duty, it is done solely out of the aesthetic sentiment of devotion (bhakti-rasa):
"The venerable Sanat-kumāra, the best among men, worshipped the Supreme Person by means of that very supreme spiritual yoga which he taught."
For the virtuous one who follows the dharma of the Blessed One, striving always with faith,
devotion toward the Blessed Brahman became focused on no other object. By means of that very [devotion] acting as a gateway...
//4.23// Śrī-Maitreya //49// [50] Also in the *Śrī-Rudra-Gīta*:
"Recite this, O auspicious sons of kings; may you be purified."
Performing their own duty, with their intentions dedicated to the Blessed One.

"Worship that very Self, who abides within the self and is situated in all beings; and repeatedly chant the praises of and meditate upon Hari. (BhP 4.24.64–65) Now, worship Him alone, and not even the performance of your own duties, nor grasping at them, and so forth.
The meaning of the particle *eva* is "indeed perform. Chanting— that is, proclaiming— the Self who abides within oneself by virtue of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*),
and likewise the Supreme Self who is stationed in all other beings as well.
By the phrase "while meditating," mental and verbal activity is also prohibited elsewhere.

By the word "repeatedly" (asakṛt), it is meant that while one worship is being completed, another should not be commenced; nor should one engage in other activities such as ritual duties with excessive attachment.
The meaning is that a severance must be made.
The illustrious Rudra [was born] from Pracetas. // 50 //
(Page 17) [51] This very point will also be made clear by the venerable Nārada through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). As he said:
"That is birth, those are actions, that is lifespan, and that is mind and speech."
For by him through whom Hari, the Lord and the Soul of the Universe, is served by men.
What is the use here of three births— those pertaining to Śukra, Savitṛ, and Yajña—
or of the actions prescribed by the Three Vedas, even for a man with the lifespan of a god?
Of what use is sacred learning or austerity? Of what use are words or the fluctuations of the mind? Or of what use is subtle intellect, or strength consisting of the mastery of the senses?
Of what use is yoga or Sāṅkhya, or even renunciation and the study of sacred texts,
or what use are other auspicious things, where Hari does not bestow His very self?
For in truth, the self is the ultimate limit of all that is auspicious;
for all beings, Hari is the self, the giver of the self, and the beloved. (BhP 4.31.9–13) *Śaukram* means birth related to Śukra—the production from pure parents.
The Sāvitra [sacrifice] is performed by means of the initiation (upanayana);
the Yājñika [sacrifice] by means of the consecration (dīkṣā);
and the Indriya-rādhas [sacrifice] by means of proficiency in that [study].

Regarding this, the *Ṭīkā* states: "By the Sāṅkhya [it is meant] by the mere knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body and so forth. Then, the *Ṭīkā* on the passage beginning with "of the various goals" (*śreyasām*) asks: "But how can these various means for attaining fruits be rendered useless merely by the absence of service to Hari?"
Regarding this, it is said: the self alone is the limit, the ultimate pinnacle, of all superior fruits;
that is to say, from the perspective of practical utility and from the perspective of the absolute truth.
The meaning is that others are dear precisely because they serve the purpose of the self.
Let it be granted that the self is the limit [of affection]; what follows for Hari? To this he says: "Of all beings as well."
And he is the "giver of self," for by dispelling ignorance,
he manifests one's true nature;
and even in his divine form, he is the "bestower of self" upon Bali and others, as it were.
And He is "dear" because His nature is supreme bliss; this is the point.

Here, it should be understood that the Self of all beings—even of pure individual souls (*jīva*)—is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because He is like the sun to the individual souls who stand in the place of rays. As it has been said:

"Therefore, one's own self is most dear to all embodied beings; for its sake alone does this entire world of moving and non-moving things exist. Know this Kṛṣṇa to be the Self of all selves. [BhP 10.14.54] Thus it is said.

The intention of the Master [Śaṅkara] is that he who gives, manifests according to their respective natures, and brings under his control the two "selves"— namely, those called the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which have attained identity with Brahman— is the "Giver of the Self" (*ātmada*). Furthermore—
Just as by watering the root of a tree,
its trunk, branches, and twigs are satisfied;
and just as by the offering of vital breath, the sense faculties are nourished.
"Likewise, the worship of all worthy recipients is the worship of the Infallible One.
And the commentary states: "Furthermore, even those fruits which are caused by the propitiation of various deities through diverse ritual acts come about through the propitiation of Hari."
But by the mere propitiation of this or that deity, nothing at all is achieved;
thus he states, with an illustrative example, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā).
4.31 // Śrī Nārada [spoke] to the Pracetasas.
[52] Regarding the instruction given by Śrī Ṛṣabhadeva to his own sons, one should look ahead at the verses beginning with *ye vā mayīśe* (BhP 5.5.3) and *matto 'py anantāt* (BhP 5.5.25). [53]
At the conclusion of the dialogue between the Brahmin Rahūgaṇa and [the Buddha], this is also stated:
"O Rahūgaṇa, you too, having laid down the staff and having cultivated friendliness toward all beings, [should enter this path]."
One whose self is not attached, having taken up the sword of knowledge cooled by service to Hari, crosses to the further shore.
In this context, knowledge itself serves as the support.
Thus it was said immediately thereafter by the illustrious Rahūgaṇa himself: "Oh, the human birth is the most auspicious of all births!"
What need have you for other births,
since you possess such abundant association with these great souls who have dedicated their very selves to the glory of Dhṛṣīkeśa?
Indeed, it is no wonder that my sins have been destroyed by the dust of Your lotus feet, and that pure devotion to Adhokṣaja has arisen within me from even this momentary encounter with You.
"Non-discrimination, rooted in false reasoning, is destroyed.
[BhP 5.13.21] This is clear.
//5.13// Śrī-Brāhmaṇa [spoke] to Rahūgaṇa. //54// [54]

Likewise, at the conclusion of the instruction given by Śrī Saṅkarṣaṇa to Citraketu, the verse beginning with "by means of the elements perceived and heard" (BhP 6.16.62) should be cited first, followed by "a person should become My devotee" (BhP 6.16.63). This is also seen in the instruction for the young Asuras:
[The verse: "By means of the elements perceived and heard... etc., should be cited first, and then "a person should become My devotee" should be brought forward.
Even in the instruction for the young Asuras: [the same sequence applies].
In this world, a wise person should practice the Bhāgavata duties from childhood;
for human birth is difficult to attain, and even that is transient and yields no certain benefit [if not used for such purposes].

For just as in this world a man approaches the feet of Viṣṇu, so too should one practice the duties of a devotee (bhāgavata-dharma) even in this very human birth, since this [devotion] bestows all goals of life; for He is the beloved Self, the Lord, and the well-wishing friend of all beings.
[BhP 7.6.1–2] It is in this very human birth that one should perform the duties of a devotee, because this grants all desired ends.

Regarding birth: because of the intense immersion in great objects of sense in births such as those of the gods, and because of the absence of discrimination in births such as those of cattle, he says that having attained a human birth, one should not delay; "in youth" (*kaumāre*) means beginning from childhood.
Since even that birth is certain to be difficult to obtain again,
and since this treatise is primarily directed toward human beings, this statement is made by way of reference to them.

It should be understood that this is said by superimposing humanity upon him through the similarity of his intellect and other faculties. In this regard, he demonstrates the propriety of practicing the dharma of the Lord alone with the words "for just as...
and so forth; for here, approaching the feet of Viṣṇu is indeed appropriate and fitting for a person.

The meaning is as follows: because he is by his very nature dear to all beings—the object of their affection and the cause of their love—for that reason, the *ātman* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, there is another reason for approaching him at his feet: because...
Furthermore, this Lord is capable of acting, not acting, or acting otherwise;
and He is a friend to all, desiring to bring about their welfare. [55]
Having thus introduced this subject, he concludes it:

"Dharma, artha, and kāma—this is what is called the triple aggregate (trivarga); [it consists of] the three systems of inquiry, the triple Veda, ethics and self-restraint, and the various forms of economic activity."
I consider all this to be the truth of the Veda:
the surrender of one's own self to the Supreme Person, who is one's own true friend.
*Īkṣā* is the knowledge of the Self.

If all this collection of meanings from the Veda is a means for surrendering one's own self to that Supreme Person, who is one's own friend and inner controller, then I consider it true, because its fruit is truth.

Alternatively, "real" means that which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyākāraka*), that is to say, which is effective; otherwise, the implication is that phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth would be entirely fruitless.
// 7.6 // Śrī Prahlāda [to the Asura boys] //54-55// [56] And further:
"Among thousands of means, this one has been declared by the Blessed One."
"By which means one may easily attain devotion to the Lord, the Blessed One"—
this very means, among thousands of other methods for extracting the seeds of karma consisting of the three *guṇas* mentioned previously, was taught to me by the Blessed Śrī Nārada. By those...

The meaning is this: since, through thousands of means, from whichever specific means and in whatever manner one attains direct, immediate, and unimpeded devotion—meaning joy—toward the Lord, the Blessed One, the removal of the seeds of karma is merely a secondary fruit thereof. [57] (page 19)
And after stating the auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*) of that very means in passages such as "First, by service to the guru with devotion" (BhP 7.7.30), he says:
"In this way, by those who have conquered the six internal enemies, devotion to the Lord is performed."
"By which devotion to the Blessed Vāsudeva is attained"—
this occurs precisely through the previously mentioned methods such as service to the guru, and not by seeking it separately for its own sake.
By people who have through effort conquered the seeds of karma— characterized by desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy— devotion is indeed practiced once again.
The meaning is that even devotion toward Vāsudeva is thereby obtained.
7.7 // Prahlāda said to them:
[58] Even at the commencement of the discourse on the conduct of the castes and stages of life, when speaking of the duties common to all human beings—
it is the Blessed Lord Hari, who embodies all the Vedas, that is indeed the root of Dharma.

And that which is remembered by the knowers of it, O King, by which the self becomes serene—that is the root and authority of dharma; for the Blessed Lord is composed of all the Vedas. Thus it is remembered.
And the Smṛti is the authority for those who know that— that is, for those who know the Blessed Lord who consists of the Vedas. By these two [the Śruti and Smṛti],
it is shown that dharma which is directed away from Him is purposeless, and that the dharma of the Blessed Lord alone is necessary.
And it has been said: "Therefore—
the entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it,
the practice of the virtuous, and also the satisfaction of one's own self" (Manu 2.6).
Thus, it is also taught here as being distinguished by the statement of the *Manusmṛti*:
"In this [scripture], the supreme dharma, free from deceit, belongs to the virtuous who are devoid of envy. And this is logical.
For it has been stated: "The object to be known here is the reality that bestows auspiciousness and uproots the threefold suffering" (BhP 1.1.2).
By the phrase "by which very dharma the mind becomes serene," it is understood as being like the expression "by which the Self becomes well-pleased."
Because it was not stated as being distinguished by sound, it is understood that direct devotion characterized by hearing that [sound] and so forth is indeed superior;
and at the conclusion of the exposition of all those various dharmas, [the Lord] himself [declared this].

Having described his incidental knowledge of the reality of the Lord alone during his birth in the third birth as a Gandharva through the performance of virtuous deeds, and having described that same knowledge— arising merely from hearing and so forth born of the company of the virtuous— during his second birth in the Śūdra caste, [the text proceeds].
In attaining such a fruit as becoming an attendant of the Lord, he did not regard even his own duty (*svadharma*) as a further cause;
for in that very context, the commentary on the verse beginning "You all" (*yūyam*, BhP 7.10.48) states: "And all this..."
The common [factor] has been stated; however, for the devotee, devotion alone is the cause for the attainment of all human goals (puruṣārtha).
With this in mind, he speaks specifically regarding the Pāṇḍavas with the words "Just as... and so forth.
Therefore, even here, in relation to direct devotion—

Such is the intended meaning. Now, even though devotion (*bhakti*) is distinct from religious duty (*dharma*) in such passages as: "If one, having abandoned his own duty, worships the lotus feet of Hari, but being unripe, should then fall" (BhP 1.5.17), and so forth;

In the subsequent text beginning with "Hearing, chanting, and remembering Him, and [serving] those who have attained the state of the great" (BhP 7.11.10), the prescription of these as dharma is indeed figurative, intended both because they are necessary for all living beings and because they constitute the supreme good.

In reality, however, in the prose passage beginning with "tatrāpi" in the fifth book (*BhP* 5.9.3), the steadfastness in devotion of Śrī Jaḍabharata— which was described through such qualities as hearing and remembering the Lord's destruction of the bondage of karma— is [present] in his father.

In the prose passage beginning with "uparata" (BhP 5.9.7), by stating that those whose minds are fixed solely on the threefold knowledge (*trayī-vidyā*) and not on the supreme knowledge (*para-vidyā*), and so forth, the ignorance of His brothers— who held such contempt for Him— is revealed; thereby,
it is made known that He is distinct from mere dharma and possesses the nature of the supreme knowledge.
Therefore it is said in the Śrī-Nārasiṃha Purāṇa (page 20):
"Sanaka and the others were engaged in that dharma known as nivṛtti."
"Having spoken of one sage, Nārada, in the lineage beginning with Marīci known as the *pravṛtta*," [NārP 4.4].
By this, it is understood that he was spoken of by Brahmā;
thus, through the application of a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) involving a strained interpretation (*kaṣṭha-kalpanā*).
The inclusion of hearing and other practices within their own respective duties is solely for the purpose of directly instigating devotion even among those who are outwardly oriented;
this should be understood similarly in other instances where there are statements describing mixed forms of devotion.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the intended meaning lies precisely in devotion.
// 7.11 // Śrī Nārada to Yudhiṣṭhira //58// [59-60] Also, regarding the narrative of Jāyanteya, this is the reply to the question: "Therefore, we ask about ultimate security" [BhP 11.2.28].

I believe that for one whose mind is agitated by worldly existence, constant service to the lotus feet of Acyuta provides freedom from fear from all quarters, because it bestows the essence of the self-nature.
"And where fear ceases through the self of Viṣṇu" (BhP 11.2.33).
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "First, he speaks of absolute security with the words beginning 'I think' (*manye*);
and again, as a subsequent statement, he declares the Bhāgavata duties with the words 'those which were indeed spoken by the Blessed One' (BhP 11.2.31)."

Having spoken three verses beginning with "The means have indeed been proclaimed for the attainment of the Self" (BhP 11.2.34), and then the verse beginning with "Fear arises from attachment to a second" (BhP 11.2.36), he says here: "The wise man should worship that Lord with exclusive devotion" (BhP 11.2.37). By the word "with devotion" (*bhaktyā*), [it is shown that] this [devotion] is unmixed with knowledge and the like.
Its characteristic consists of hearing, chanting, and so forth.
By the word "ekayā" (by one), the characteristics of continuity and non-deviation are taught.

In this regard, although it was stated in the previous passage [BhP 11.2.36], beginning with "by body, speech, mind, or senses," that even worldly activity becomes a *bhāgavata-dharma* through its dedication to the Lord,
so too is its continuity established.
Even so,
the state of being characterized solely by hearing, chanting, and so forth would be contradicted; therefore,
there is non-deviation in that regard.
Immediately following that, he explains with two verses the means by which that state of being "merely that" (tanmātratva) may be attained;
therein, he first states the means for its non-deviation with the first verse:
For even though it does not exist, the duality appears to the meditator through the intellect, just as in dreams and fantasies;
the mind consists of the conceptualization and discrimination of those karmas.
The wise man should restrain it; from that, fearlessness shall arise.
"Dvaya" refers to the fivefold duality beginning with *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Although this does not exist within the pure Self (*ātman*), [it appears there].
The meaning is that it indeed exists; nevertheless, for the meditator who is engaged in meditation consisting of ignorance, it appears to his mind,
and thus even though it is pure, it is merely conceptualized— this is the meaning.
The meaning is that it is just like a dream and a mental wish;
therefore, one conceives of and discriminates actions.
One should restrain that mind;
then, through worship with unwavering devotion, there will be fearlessness—this is the intended meaning. [61]
Now, one might object: "Even so, there would still be a deviation from devotion (bhakti) through the practice of yoga in the form of the cessation of the mind.
Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that when devotion itself is practiced with such total absorption, the cessation of the mind occurs spontaneously by its very nature.
He states the means for attaining that state of pure consciousness with the second verse:
"Hearing the auspicious accounts of the births and deeds of the one who holds the discus in his hand, which [deeds] occurred in the world..."
Singing songs whose meaning is that [Supreme Being], one should wander about without shame and without attachment.
"Tad-arthakāni" means those names whose purpose is those births and those actions. These too—
Anticipating the objection that it is impossible to know them all completely, he says: one should wander about listening to and singing those songs that are well-known in the world,
remaining unattached and free from desire.

// 11.2 // Śrī-Kavi [speaks of] Videha // 59–61 // [62] Furthermore, avoiding [discussions of] karma and other such topics from the outset, he directly enjoins devotion alone: "This Veda is a discourse on the indirect; it is an instruction for the immature."
For indeed, [the Lord] prescribes actions for the sake of liberation from karma, just like a medicine [is prescribed] for [removing] poison.
But he who, being ignorant and having his senses unsubdued, does not practice what is declared in the Vedas,
indeed attains death after death through improper action and unrighteousness.

Performing only that which is enjoined by the Veda, free from attachment and offering it to the Lord, one attains the perfection of actionlessness; the scriptural mention of rewards is for the purpose of inducing interest.
"He who desires to quickly untie the knot of the heart of the Supreme Self should worship Lord Keśava according to the ritual prescribed in the Tantras," and so forth.
Regarding this, the *Ṭīkā* states: "The term 'parokṣā' (indirect) refers to that where a matter existing in one way is stated by making it appear otherwise for the sake of concealment."

That is an indirect expression (*parokṣa-vāda*). And so says the Śruti: "Though it is actually the *caturhotṛ*, they call it 'the four hotṛs' by an indirect name; for the Vedas indeed love the indirect. Indirect...
He states the very argument [of the opponent] as "for the sake of liberation through action" (*karma-mokṣāya*).

Now, one might object: "The scriptures enjoin actions for the sake of heaven and so forth, not for the sake of liberation through action. To this he replies: "Just as there is instruction for the ignorant. In this regard:

The illustration is as follows: a medicine is like a father who, while giving medicine to a child, entices him with pieces of sugar-candy, sweetmeats, and the like, making him drink it and giving him those very candies and sweets.
Yet, the purpose of obtaining that medicine is not for the sake of those candies and sweets themselves, but rather for the sake of health.
Likewise, the Veda also, enticing one with intermediate fruits, prescribes ritual actions solely for the sake of liberation from karma; this is the point.
"Ajña" (the ignorant) refers to one who lacks *jñā*—that is, the intelligence characterized by faith toward hearing the narrations of the Blessed Lord and so forth.
He whose livelihood is such;
for this very reason, the meaning is that he does not engage in that [wrong livelihood].
Likewise, one who has not conquered his senses.

The meaning is that one who desires to know Brahman may not yet be dispassionate toward enjoyments up to the highest state (pārameṣṭhya). This is because, in passages such as "one should perform ritual actions for so long" (BhP 11.2.9), both faith and dispassion—each independent of the other—are stated to constitute their respective boundaries. By means of improper action...
By way of failing to perform what is enjoined, one encounters after death a "death," that is, a torment equal to dying;
the meaning is that one undergoes repeated deaths and undergoes torments. Therefore, for those who abandon the prescribed duties, there is no deliverance whatsoever.

He says "as declared in the Vedas" to show that when an action has God as its instigating agent, through its performance according to reality— characterized by dedication to God— that [result] will occur all the more so upon His grace.
Therefore, by performing only that which is enjoined in the Veda and not that which is prohibited,
one attains the perfection of *naiṣkarmya*, which consists in being beyond the sphere of bondage through action.

[Objection: "But surely, while that action is being performed, there would be attachment to it and its fruit, and not the perfection consisting of freedom from action (naiṣkarmya); therefore, he says: 'free from attachment' (niḥsaṅgaḥ), meaning one who is without clinging, [offering] that very [action] to the Lord as the sole motive."
It is offered therein, but not with a view toward a fruit.
[Objection: But surely, since the fruit is mentioned in the scripture, the fruit must necessarily arise when the ritual action is performed.
[Reply: No; it is for the purpose of creating interest (*rocanārtha*).
These [teachings] are for the purpose of generating an inclination toward the practice, like sugar-candies and sweetmeats given when one drinks medicine;
and consequently, through that inclination toward the practice, one correctly investigates the meaning of the Vedas.
And yet—
by the passage, "O Gārgī, he who departs from this world without knowing this Imperishable is pitiable" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.10), the wretchedness of one who does not know Brahman is declared.

Having ascertained that sacrifices and other such acts are subsidiary to knowledge— based on such passages as, "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas and through celibate studentship" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22)—
he engages in actions free from desire for rewards.

Since it is established that through such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," heaven and the like are understood to be the very fruits desired, and thus they do not become undesired,
the attainment of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action) occurs by its own nature; how much more so, then, by means of the glorious dedication to the Lord?
The meaning is: "when there is grace toward that.

Thus, having stated the cause for the attainment of *naiṣkarmya* (the state of actionlessness) through delay alone, [the author now states] the cause for the fulfillment of all duties (*sarva-dharma-paryāpti*) by means of *naiṣkarmya*, according to the maxim: "Just as by watering the root of a tree... [BhP 4.31.14].

He speaks independently of a swift means even for one who desires to pierce the knot of the heart— the ego-identification with the body— of the supreme Self, the individual soul (jīva), which is otherwise to be accomplished through spiritual attainments (*siddhi*).

"He who [desires] quickly," that is, very swiftly, to cast off the knot of the heart of the other, the Self, namely the ego-identification with the body— he, indeed, [should abandon] other [means] such as ritual action (*karman*) and the like, by their very nature.

Having abandoned other views of deities, one should worship the god Keśava according to the method and procedure taught in the Tantras and, by the use of the word "and," according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas; such is the conclusion for the purpose of relinquishing the perception of other deities.
Thus, he who worships the Lord as the Self within the fire, the sun, water, the guest, and his own heart, is indeed liberated before long. "The Self" refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
//11.3// The illustrious Āvirhotra attained the disembodied state (videha). [64] And at the outset, by way of contrast:
"Those who consider themselves the best knowers of the Self generally do not worship the Blessed Lord Hari."
"What is the final goal for those who have not pacified their desires, even though they have conquered themselves?"—
this is the answer to that question:
"From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of the Puruṣa, along with the stages of life (āśramas)..."
The four castes, beginning with the Brahmins, were born separately according to their qualities.
"Those who do not worship, and instead despise, this Puruṣa who is the manifest Lord and the source of the self, fall downward, fallen from their station.
[BhP 11.5.2-3] Previously, in the *Śrī-Draviḍopadeśa*, also within the "Hymn to Śrī-Nārāyaṇa" composed by Deva—
For those who serve you, many obstacles created by the gods arise as they cross beyond their own abodes to reach your supreme state;
yet this is not so for another who offers his own portions as oblations upon the sacrificial grass.
It is said: "If you are the protector, you place your foot upon the head of obstacles.

In that regard, for those who offer their own shares in the sacrifice, no obstacles created by the gods arise; however, for those who serve you, such obstacles caused by them [the gods] do indeed occur due to envy. But as for the word "yadi" (if), it signifies certainty—that they certainly do occur.
Just as it is certain that "the Vedas are authoritative," you alone are their protector;
thus, by serving you, one places his foot upon the head of obstacles, or rather, proceeds by making you himself the very staircase.

The meaning is as follows: having heard this, [the Lord], answering the question— namely, what would be the ultimate end for those who remain within saṃsāra itself— by beginning with "He questioned the Blessed One," first states their state of being subject to transgression (pratyavāyitva) in two and a quarter verses beginning with "mukha."
He states the conclusion with the verse beginning "from the place" (sthānāt).
11.5 // Śrīcamasa [is] Videha.
[64] [65] Furthermore, since devotion alone has been declared in the manner previously stated, it would also be appropriate for him to ask about its specific distinctions.
The question "At what time? and so forth was answered in that very same way:
"In these ages—the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali—Keśava is worshipped according to various rules, with diverse colors, names, and forms" (BhP 11.5.20).
By various methods and through diverse paths.
11.5 // Videha was the recipient of Śrī [Kṛṣṇa’s] hand.
[66] Also, in the dialogue between the Blessed Lord and Uddhava:
"But you, having completely renounced all affection for your own kinsmen and relatives..."
"Having fully fixed your mind on Me, wander the earth with an equal vision," and "Uddhava is not even an atom less than Me"—
since Śrī Uddhava is thus renowned as one who has attained perfection, [the Lord] aims at him and, through him, [teaches] others.
Such is this instruction;
it should be understood similarly in other cases as well.
And therefore, by means of *jahat-lakṣaṇā* (indication through the abandonment of the primary sense), [the term] "you" [denotes] that which belongs to you—
"Follow the path with devotion" means that you should wander [in this way];
and "even-mindedness" is because, apart from me, there is nothing else to be rejected or accepted.
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude those who are outward-looking;
by this as well, the following was intended previously:
"Those who have been adorned with garlands, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and ointments used by you..."
We, your servants who eat the remnants of your food, may we conquer your illusion.
The sages whose minds are purified by the wind, the ascetics who churn the heights,
those tranquil and stainless renunciants, go to the abode known as Brahman.
But we here, O Great Yogin, wandering upon the paths of karma,
shall cross over the darkness difficult to traverse by means of your report concerning you.
"Remembering and proclaiming your deeds and words—your gait, smiles, glances, and playful jests—which were a mimicry of the ways of the world of men. (BhP 11.6.46–50) Thus [ends the section].
11.7. Śrī Bhagavān. 66. [67]

Furthermore, it is shown that the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) is difficult to accomplish by itself, whereas the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) is easily accomplished; that devotion, as a secondary consequence, generates knowledge; and that devotion is itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). As it is said: [1.12] "Even one who performs actions with devotion, having purified his intellect through it, attains thereafter the state of non-action through knowledge. [1.54] "For one whose intellect is focused on Me, whose self is conquered, and whose passion has been subdued, there is no further duty to do anywhere. [18.56] "The wise man looks upon with an equal eye a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. [18.57] "Even here, those whose minds are established in equality conquer the material nature; for the fruit of the equanimous is one. [18.66] "But for one who offers all actions to Me, regarding Me as the Supreme Goal, and who is absorbed in Me, I provide for him the yoga of discernment by which he reaches Me. [18.67] "Abandoning all duties, seek refuge in Me alone; I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. [18.68] "This is the most secret teaching; knowing this, you will be liberated from all evils; in this path, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any retrogression. [18.69] "If you hold this to be mere discursive reasoning, then you shall attain only the state of action; however, if you follow My instruction, you will attain the supreme good. [18.70] "Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you shall cross over all evil by the boat of wisdom alone. [18.71] "Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, prostrate before Me; so disciplined and absorbed in Me, you shall come to Me. [18.72] "Abandoning all other dharmas, take refuge in Me alone; I shall deliver you from all sins; do not fear. [18.73] "I am the same toward all beings; none is hateful to Me, nor dear; but those who worship Me with devotion, they abide in Me, and I too abide in them. [18.74] "Even if they be of base birth, women, vaiśyas, or śūdras, having attained My world, they do not fall again, O son of Kuntī. [18.75] "How much more so the holy brahmins and devoted royal sages! Having attained this impermanent, joyless world, engage in My yoga. [18.76] "Fix your mind on Me alone; let your intellect be absorbed in Me; thereafter you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt. [18.77] "If you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me, then practice yoga through repeated effort. [18.78] "If you are not capable even of such effortful practice, then renounce the fruits of all actions through the yoga of renunciation. [18.79] "Superior is the yoga of discernment to the yoga of renunciation; the intellect focused on Me is superior even to discernment; by means of that intellect, you shall reach Me alone. [18.80] "Abandoning this body, you shall attain Me, O son of Pṛthā; I promise you truthfully; you are dear to Me. [18.81] "Your mind may stray from Me due to the power of worldly objects, but it shall return to Me alone, O son of Kuntī, for you are devoted to Me. [18.82] "Even if you think of other things while listening to this dialogue between us, even then you shall be protected by Me, being ever-disciplined. [18.83] "This supreme secret has been told to you out of love for you; knowing this, you shall find no further duty to do anywhere. [18.84] "Reflect upon this fully and then act as you wish; by hearing this dialogue between us, even the man of small intelligence shall attain the supreme goal. [18.85] "O Parantapa, this most secret teaching has been spoken by Me; knowing this, you shall be liberated from all evils; in this path, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any retrogression. [18.86] "By Me, the Lord of Compassion, this has been told to you out of compassion; reflecting upon this fully, then act as you wish. [18.87] "Having heard this supreme and most secret teaching, Arjuna was filled with wonder and, with hair standing on end, bowed down and spoke to the Lord of Yoga. [18.88] "Arjuna said: 'The delusion born of ignorance has been destroyed by Your grace, O Keśava; I have regained my memory and am now firm; I am free from doubt. [18.89] "O Acyuta, I desire to see Your form as the Lord; if You deem me worthy, O Lord of Yoga, then show me Your eternal Self. [18.90] "The Blessed Lord said: 'Behold, O Pārtha, My forms by the hundreds and thousands, diverse in kind, divine, various in color and shape. [18.91] "Behold the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, the two Aśvins, and the Maruts; behold many wonders never seen before. [18.92] "Behold here, O Gāṇḍīva-wielder, the entire universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, centered in Me; whatever else you desire to see. [18.93] "But you cannot see Me with these eyes of yours; I give you a divine eye; behold My sovereign yoga. [18.94] "Sanjaya said: 'O King, having spoken thus, the Great Lord of Yoga, Hari, showed to Partha His supreme and most wonderful form. [18.95] "With many mouths and eyes, possessing many wondrous visions, with many divine ornaments, with many divine weapons raised, wearing celestial garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes, infinite, with faces turned in every direction. [18.96] "If the splendor of a thousand suns were to blaze forth simultaneously in the sky, that might resemble the splendor of the Great Lord. [18.97] "There Partha saw the entire universe, divided into many parts, gathered together within the body of the God of Gods. [18.98] "Then, overcome with wonder, his hair standing on end, Dhananjaya bowed his head to the Lord and spoke with joined palms. [18.99] "Arjuna said: 'O Lord, in Your body I see all the gods and hosts of various beings; I see Brahmā seated on his lotus-throne, all the Ṛṣis, and the celestial serpents. [18.100] "I see You with a crown, mace, and discus, with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes; I see You, infinite in form, on all sides, without end, beginning, or middle. [18.101] "'I see You as the supreme, unchanging Being to be known, the ultimate support of the whole universe; the eternal Puruṣa, the divine Being, the unborn, the great Lord, I see You pervading the three worlds, blazing with Your own light. [18.102] "'I see You without beginning, middle, or end, possessing infinite power, with countless arms, having the sun and moon as Your eyes, Your mouth like a blazing fire, scorching this universe with Your radiance. [18.103] "'Space is confined between Your jaws; the worlds are trembling with fear; tell me who You are, O Supreme Being; salutations to You, please be gracious; I desire to know You, the Primeval One, for I do not understand Your purpose. [18.104] "The Blessed Lord said: 'I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, fully matured; even without you, all these warriors standing here in the opposing armies shall cease to exist. [18.105] "Therefore, arise, gain glory, and vanquish your enemies; enjoying a prosperous kingdom, enjoy the wealth; by Me alone have they already been slain; be merely an instrument, O Savyasācin. [18.106] "Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and the other warriors here have already been slain by Me; do not tremble; fight; you shall conquer your enemies in battle. [18.107] "Sanjaya said: 'Hearing these words of the Lord of Yoga, Kiritin, with joined palms and trembling, bowed down
"Let him do nothing, say nothing, and think of neither the good nor the bad;
delighting in the Self through this mode of life, the sage should wander like one who is dull-witted.
Having thus described the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*) with these concluding words, he speaks in order to bring forth the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*):

"If one who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman should become proficient in the Supreme, his study indeed bears fruit; for he is like one who protects a cow that does not yield milk. In this context, by the term *para-brahman*, the Supreme Reality (*para-tattva*) alone is meant.
However, it should be understood that this is not by means of a distinction such as being a Brahmā or being a Bhagavān,
because there is equality with Him in all respects.
Thus, it has been stated that the practice of the lower Brahman (śabda-brahman) has as its purpose the practice of the higher Brahman (para-brahman).
In that regard, among all [practices]...

Thus, although it is established that the Śabda-Brahman is the subject matter specifically within these portions, namely the Upaniṣads, the realization of the Para-Brahman does not arise even through millions of investigations into it;
rather, in that [realization]...

In whichever portion the form of the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Brahman, His pastimes, and so forth are expounded, by the very practice of that, steadfastness in the form of the Blessed Lord arises. Thus it has been said:
"For one desiring to cross the ocean of worldly existence, which is exceedingly difficult to cross..."

There is no other raft for a person afflicted by the forest fire of manifold sufferings than the cultivation of the nectar of the stories of the divine pastimes of the Blessed One, the Supreme Person. (BhP 12.4.40)
O Lord, those who cast aside devotion— the path to the highest good— and strive for the sake of attaining mere intellectual knowledge,
find that only their own exhaustion remains.
"And not otherwise, like those who thresh coarse husks," and so forth.

For this very reason, he says the following two verses to show that one should not mock even Vedic speech if it is devoid of my divine play: "One who milks a cow that has already been milked, and an unchaste wife..."

My body is dependent on others, my offspring are worthless, and my wealth has been offered at Your sacred shrines; O Lord, suffering through endless sorrows, I protect only my speech, which is deficient compared to Yours. [BhP 11.11.19]
He explains the statement "words devoid of me" as meaning words that are bereft of me, the Blessed Lord, and thus empty of my pastimes and so forth.
In that [age], my purifying action— consisting of the maintenance, origination, and cessation of this world, or the birth resulting from my desired descent through divine play— does not exist.

A wise person should not uphold that barren speech in which my deeds—the purifier of the world—do not appear. For what else could be the cause of this universe’s maintenance and so forth? Having thus reflected on its supreme excellence, he speaks further regarding his playful incarnations (*līlāvatāra*).

If the birth of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and others—the desired object of the world’s love—were not to occur, then a wise and intelligent person should not uphold even that fruitless speech characterized by the Vedas. As it was said by Śrī Nārada: "For this is the fruit of a man's austerity or Vedic study," and so forth. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.5.22)
Therefore, it was sung by the Blessed Lord Himself, the purifier of the Kali age:
"Even though they have heard the nectar of Hari’s stories from the Upaniṣads,
those tears of melting hearts, trembling, and horripilation do not appear in them."
[Thus ends verse 39 of the *Padyāvalī*.
[70] Having thus stated that knowledge is accomplished through devotion alone, he concludes that path of knowledge:
"Thus, having dispelled the delusion of multiplicity within the Self through inquiry,
one should rest with the stainless mind offered to Me, who am all-pervading.
[BhP 11.11.21] "That I am bound or liberated is an explanation based on the modes of nature, not in reality," [BhP 11.11.1] thus it is said.
By means of the investigation in the manner previously described,
[one realizes] the multiplicity within the self, the pure soul— namely, [the distinction between] the state of being a deity and...
Having set aside distinctions such as being human and so forth,
and having thus fixed and maintained the mind upon Me— the omnipresent Brahman— by hearing of My pastimes and other deeds, one should attain rest. [71]
Thus, having taught devotion mixed with knowledge, he now teaches pure devotion alone— which has the quality of knowledge established as a natural consequence— through four verses, beginning with:
"If you are unable to hold the mind steady upon Brahman..."
"Perform all actions in Me without expectation"—the word "yadi" (if) is used here in the sense of certainty (*niścaye*).
As it says in the *Ṭīkā*: "If You, O Protector, set Your foot upon the head of obstacles... (*BhP* 11.11.22).
As in such passages as [11.4.10], here too it is the seeker of knowledge alone who is the subject;
and this is stated by superimposing that very status upon the illustrious Uddhava.

And therefore, by such authoritative statements as, "O Lord, casting aside devotion, which is the path to the highest good, they suffer" (BhP 10.14.4), you are certainly unable to fix the mind upon Brahman through the path of mere knowledge alone, without devotion.

Therefore, he teaches that one should take refuge in *bhakti-yoga* alone— which is attended by all virtues such as knowledge (*jñāna*) and the rest, even more so than those— by means of the verse beginning with "In me" (*mayi*), thereby indicating its status as the very ladder to that goal. [72]
Alternatively, if— due to a lack of the power of prior devotion— one who desires knowledge of Brahman should be unable to fix the mind thereon, [then...]
Therefore, it should be applied thus: "Even now, one should act in this way"; "practice" means "offer," being "disinterested," that is, free from any other desire.
Full of faith, listening to my stories which are auspicious and purify the worlds,
singing them, remembering them, and repeatedly enacting my deeds and births.
"O Uddhava, one who relies upon Me and practices virtue, pleasure, and wealth for My sake attains unwavering devotion to Me, the eternal.
And the commentary states: "By means of actions offered to Me, he describes the internal devotion of one whose being is purified."
"Thus, being full of faith"— this is the statement.

By means of dramatic representation (*abhinaya*), he himself imitates those portions among the various stages of birth, deeds, and pastimes that fall within his own desired state of devotional sentiment (*bhāva-bhakti*),
as well as those belonging to the Lord and those belonging to other devotees.
The meaning is that he acts as a gateway.
Furthermore, whatever dharma there may be, characterized by the giving of cows and so forth,
that too [is performed] for my sake, solely as an ancillary part of the great festival of my birth and other such occasions.

And whatever desire there may be, characterized by dwelling in great palaces and so forth— that too, for my sake and for the purpose of my service and so on, shall take the form of dwelling in my own abode and the like.
And as for the purpose of accumulating wealth, he should perform it solely for my sake and for the purpose of my service; thus,
taking refuge in me, he serves.

And with a mind devoid of any other support regarding worldly objects, he attains that very same devotion toward me— characterized by listening to my teachings and so forth— which is unwavering and non-deviating throughout the three periods of time,
and through the happiness thereof.

Nor should it be thought that this [devotion] will waver because of wavering in what is to be worshipped, even in cases such as *kaivalya*, due to a lack of regard for them; thus he says "eternal" (*sanātana*). [73–74]
Anticipating the doubt, "How can there be such an engagement in, or indeed the culmination of, the path of devotion?
he states the reason for it:
"By means of devotion obtained through association with the virtuous, he shall worship Me in Me."
Thus, that devotee who worships me with devotion and a longing for devotion becomes one who truly honors me.
And for that devotee, the full realization of my true nature—in both my form as Brahman and my form as the Lord—arises effortlessly; thus he says:
"He indeed finds the state directly through the instruction of the virtuous" (BhP 11.11.25).
"Directly" means solely through the attachment of devotion;
"the state" refers to the essential nature.
// 11.11 // The Illustrious Lord // 67–75 // [75] Furthermore, the preeminence of *bhakti-yoga* itself, its prior establishment,
and its being directly initiated by the Illustrious Lord.
The primacy belongs to oneself alone; others are secondary, being led by whatever whims they may have and being characterized by triviality.
As it is said, the illustrious Uddhava spoke:
"O Kṛṣṇa, those who discourse on the Veda speak of many means to the highest good;
do these possess equal importance through their diversity, or is there one that is preeminent?"
"O Lord, you have described the yoga of devotion which is independent [of other means], by which the mind, having cast off all attachment, enters into You.
And the commentary states: "Śreyāṃsi" refers to the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ*).
Is primacy due to conceptual construction, or rather is there primacy of only one [factor],
such that it serves as the cause for the arising of the notion of "primacy of one"? No.
That which is independent of anything else is "ahaituka" (causeless).
The meaning is this: regarding that *bhakti-yoga* spoken of by you, as well as those other means for attaining the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) that others proclaim—what is their fruit?
Is there primacy for all [practices] equally by virtue of their being means to the goal, or is there a relationship of primary and subordinate members?
And even if they are all primary, do they have equal results as alternatives, or is there some distinction between them? This is the inquiry. [76]

To this, the Blessed Lord replied: "At the time of dissolution, this speech known as the Veda was lost by Time; in the beginning, it was proclaimed by me to Brahmā, for within it, Dharma has my own self as its essence."
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "In that regard, devotion alone is primary because it possesses great fruit;
the others, however, [are secondary] according to their respective..."

In order to discern that these are minor fruits, primarily imagined by living beings whose notions of fruits such as heaven are like the flowers of the sky according to their own natures, he speaks of the various ways of understanding them according to nature through seven verses beginning with "by time."

"Having me as one's self" means that by which the self—the mind—is fixed upon Me alone; or else, "having me as one's self" means having my own nature as one's essence, being of the same nature as I because of the absence of [material] qualities (nirguṇatva). This refers to devotion.
The meaning is that the Dharma has been proclaimed as characterized by universal concomitance (*sarva-samanvaya*) and thus established.
This being so, he states the reason for that very [Dharma] which speaks of many kinds of excellence:
"O bull among men, those persons whose intellects are deluded by my *māyā*... [77–80]
"They speak of various doctrines according to their karma and according to their taste" (BhP 11.14.9).
This is because the nature of those people is rooted in the modes of *māyā*; thus, their intellects are deluded by My *māyā*. "Various" (*anekāntam*) means manifold.
The ultimate good is the goal of human life and its means; for it is said:
"Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor religious duty, O Uddhava, nor Vedic study, nor austerity, nor renunciation accomplishes Me as does intense devotion to Me" (BhP 11.14.20).
It does not accomplish, nor does it bring under control;
austerity is knowledge,
and renunciation is relinquishment.
For indeed, dharma endowed with truth and compassion, or knowledge accompanied by austerity,
does not properly purify a self that is devoid of devotion to Me. (BhP 11.14.22) Dharma here refers to that which is free from desire.
Knowledge is scriptural realization of Brahman;
austerity is the contemplation thereof;
but by means of the characteristics of devotion—
To the very extent that this self is polished by means of hearing and reciting my meritorious verses,
to that same extent one perceives the subtle reality.
"Just as the eye, when conjoined with ointment" (BhP 11.14.26).

And the commentary states: "But surely, from such scriptural passages as 'The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme' (TaittU 2.1.1) and 'Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death' (ŚvetU 6.15), [liberation occurs] through knowledge alone by means of the cessation of ignorance..."
It is asked: "From where is the attainment of You understood to come through the yoga of devotion?
To this it is said: "In this regard, [it is stated] 'just as... The self—that is, the mind—is cleansed and purified by hearing and reciting my meritorious verses.
And: "Knowledge is not distinct from devotion; rather, it is an intermediate function (*avāntara-vyāpāra*) of devotion"—this is the meaning.
Thus ends [verse] 11.14. Śrī Bhagavān [77–80].

Furthermore, [in the following verses 81–83], He describes the respective qualifications for the paths of action (*karma-yoga*), knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), and devotion (*bhakti-yoga*), as well as their individual causes.
Having spoken thus, [the author], through disregard for both knowledge and ritual action (jñāna-karma),
declares the primacy of devotion alone by means of five verses. Therein, in order to express disregard for the practice of knowledge, he states the cause for its qualification:
He establishes disregard for the practice of detachment:
"For the sage who worships by means of the previously described yoga of devotion,
all desires residing in the heart perish once I am situated within his heart" (BhP 11.20.29).
He shows disregard for the practice of knowledge:
"The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,
and one's karmas are exhausted when I, the Self of all, am seen" (BhP 11.20.30).
When [the Lord] is seen—that is, directly perceived—by devotion alone;
thus He said:
"Therefore, for the yogi who is endowed with devotion to Me and whose self is absorbed in Me..."
"Neither knowledge nor detachment generally constitutes the highest good here.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Thus, by way of this determination, the three types of qualified practitioners have been described.
Among them, other than devotion..."

He concludes with three verses beginning with "Therefore" that devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) alone is superior, because [other paths] are dependent on something else while this is independent, and because others depend upon it.
"One whose self is fixed on Me" (*mad-ātmanaḥ*) refers to one whose mind (*ātman*) is centered in Me.
"This is the means to the highest good"—this is the statement. Here, the intention behind the inclusion of the word "mostly" (*prāyas*) is as follows:
for those who practice through the cultivation of knowledge and dispassion, [liberation occurs]...
There is indeed no [further] purpose;
even while remaining as they are in that state, for some there arises an engagement in the path of immediate liberation, while for others there arises an engagement in the path of gradual liberation.

Thus, if there should be engagement in the path of gradual devotion according to the Śrī Gītā, beginning with the verse "Then, having become Brahman, the self becomes serene" (Gītā 18.54), let it be so.
Thus, in this way, for devotion—which is characterized by love, which is the king of all fruits, and whose own fruit is itself—there is no dependence whatsoever on knowledge and the like.
He says that even when the fruits of knowledge and the like are to be accomplished individually, there is likewise no such dependence: [84]

That which is attained through ritual actions, through austerity, and through knowledge and dispassion; that which is attained through yoga, through the duty of self-restraint, and through other means of spiritual welfare—[all such fruits are surpassed by this].
"By the yoga of devotion to Me, My devotee easily attains everything—
both heaven and liberation, or even My own abode— if he so desires.
Whatever may be achieved through other means such as pilgrimages to sacred sites and religious vows, all that is attained by the yoga of devotion to Me."
One obtains [this] through devotion to me; even there, it is attained directly, that is, without effort. What is all that? He says:
"Heaven and liberation."

Heaven is worldly happiness; liberation is the bliss of emancipation attained through the gradual purification of the being and so forth; and there is also a bliss that transcends those. Thus he says:
And my abode, Vaikuṇṭha—
if someone should desire it in any way solely as an accessory to devotion, [then that may be].
In that regard, there is a desire for heaven, as in the case of Śrī Citraketu and others;
and its status as an auxiliary to devotion has been stated: "He took delight with the women of the Vidyādharas, making Lord Hari sing."

Thus, like Śrī Śuka and others, there is a desire for liberation (*apavarga*). Through that aspiration, when Māyā has been cast far away by Śrī Kṛṣṇa— remaining for as long as it takes for a mustard seed to settle upon the tip of a cow's horn— then [liberation is attained].

The *Brahma-vaivarta* narrative states that he was born from his mother’s womb while she was alive; and in that regard, his status as an instrument of devotion is established by such *Gītā* verses as "Having become Brahman, with a serene self," and so forth.
Likewise, there is the desire for Vaikuṇṭha on the part of those who possess a specific group among the Lord's attendants (*pārṣadas*) once they have attained them. These...
Indeed, it was solely through their love and their desire to serve the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord that they obtained what was to be prayed for;
and thus they proceed, following the path of the foremost among the immortals.
11.20 // The Blessed Lord said: // 81–84 // [85] And finally:
This is the wisdom of the wise, and this is the insight of the insightful.
"That which is real, the immortal, one attains here through the mortal by means of the unreal.
And the commentary says: "Therefore, He says 'this' (eṣā) to show that the worship of Me alone is the fruit of the intellect's discrimination, of the mind's resolve, and of wisdom's skill."

He shows that very [attainment]: "May Truth and Immortality not reach me through the untruthful, unreal, mortal, and perishable human body in this very birth"— that which is so [attained] is itself the intellect (*buddhi*) and the wisdom (*manīṣā*).

Let alone the higher dharma; even the former dharma perishes.
