Thus it is also said in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "Neither the curse of Durvāsas nor even the thunderbolt of Indra is capable of slaying a person in whose heart Madhusūdana resides. [GarP 1.234.33]

// 3.22 // The illustrious Maitreya to Vidura // 124 // [125] Now, regarding the destruction of sin, he first states that it destroys even those sins not yet commenced: "Just as a fire with well-kindled flames reduces fuel to ashes,"
Likewise, O Uddhava, devotion directed toward Me destroys all sins entirely.

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "Just as a fire kindled for the purpose of cooking food on the hearth reduces pieces of wood to ashes, so too devotion directed toward Me, even if it arises through passion or other such motives, utterly consumes all sins."
The Blessed One also awakens him with the wonder of the greatness of his own devotion: "O Uddhava! Listen to this marvel."
This is stated in the Vaiśākha-māhātmya within the Pātāla-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"Just as a fire with well-kindled flames reduces fuel to ashes,"
"Devotion to the Blessed One likewise burns away sins at that very moment. (Padma Purāṇa 5.85.31).

And as in the passage, "Even if a man utters 'Hari' involuntarily, he does not deserve torment" (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 6.2.15), there is no suffix such as the gerundive (*liṅga*) or other case endings; yet, just as in the case of the *āgneyāṣṭākapāla* where the portion not entered by Pūṣan [is offered], [the result follows].
Just as in the case of "it exists" and so forth, there is an injunctive force.
Therefore, O Bhārata, the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign and the Self of all, should be heard, glorified, and remembered by one who desires fearlessness. (BhP 2.10.5)
In such passages, there is also the direct hearing of an injunction;
furthermore, the statement of a reason with the word "therefore" (iti) encompasses the fault incurred by non-performance.

Nevertheless, it has been indicated by the illustration of the entity characterized as fire—which possesses such an inherent nature—that this [devotion] does not depend upon ritual injunctions. For this very reason, one also finds such passages as: "O King, relying upon whom a man... (BhP 11.2.33).

By the phrase "with well-kindled flames," dependence on other means, the impossibility of accomplishment, and delay are refuted; that very point is made explicit by the *Padma Purāṇa* with the words "at that very moment."
// 11.14 // The Blessed Lord // 125 //
And likewise:
"Some, solely through devotion, are devoted to Vāsudeva."
"They shake off evil entirely, as the sun [dispels] the mist.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: By the word "some" (*kecit*), he shows that those for whom such devotion is primary are rare.
The phrase "devoted solely to Vāsudeva, independent of austerity and the like" is not a qualification of a specific type of eligible person (*adhikārin*).
However, this [statement] is merely a restatement (anuvāda), because others engage in it out of lack of faith, and thus it results in nothing more than that;
in this regard, even Bhāskara, by his own light alone, completely dispels the mist of his own [opinion].
It shakes off [those obstacles]; it should be understood that even those who are devoted to Vāsudeva do not [shake them off] with such effort through devotion.
Furthermore—
"O King, a sinner is not purified by austerities and the like in the same way that one whose life is dedicated to Kṛṣṇa is purified by serving His devotees.
And the commentary says: "And this is superior even to the path of knowledge; thus he says, 'he is not purified in that manner.'"
One would be purified. By the negation of that person, one is such that their life-breaths have been offered to Kṛṣṇa;
herein, as it is said, "The atonement is reflection" (BhP 6.1.10), it was previously stated that even knowledge serves as an atonement.
Therefore, the *Ṭīkā* states: "And this," and so forth.
Thus, by such statements as "one whose sins have been removed by meditation that sustains truth" (*BhP* 6.13.13), it is shown that Vṛtra was removed by meditation upon the Blessed One.

In passages such as *hatyā-pāpasyendrasya taṃ ca* (BhP 6.13.14), the prescription of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) should be understood as being for the purpose of removing the well-known reputation for sin in the common world.
Now, one might ask: even then, since he possessed love for the Lord who had manifested, how could he be... [the supreme...]?

May the killing of Vṛtra, a devotee of the Lord, pass away even through the worship of the Blessed One. It is held that even a mere great offense is to be destroyed solely by experiencing its fruit, or else destroyed by His grace.
It is said in reply: nevertheless, for Indra, who acted therein by the impulsion of the Blessed One, there is no such fault.
In this matter, worship of Him alone is prescribed as the expiation;
and since the Blessed Lord likewise taught it for the very purpose of warding off such demonic existence, there is no fault in this.
// 6.1 // Śrī Śuka // 126–127 // [128] In some places, he states through two verses that [the Name] also destroys even the sins already set in motion (*prārabdha-pāpa*):
"By hearing and chanting His name..."
O Blessed One, if even a dog, by bowing down to you or even by remembering you at any time, immediately becomes fit for the sacrificial soma-pressing, how much more so, then, upon beholding you?
Oh, alas! Even a dog-eater is more venerable than he whose tongue-tip bears your name;
such men have performed austerities, offered oblations, and bathed as noble ones.
The Brahmās spoke: "They who utter your name... [BhP 3.33.6–7].

Here, the term *śvādatva* refers specifically to the state of belonging to the particular species of dog-eaters (*śvabhakṣaka*). This is because, according to the etymology "one who eats dogs" (*śvānam atti*), the present tense usage indicates that, like a *kravyāda* (carnivore), one has acquired the habit of such an act.
However, if one intends to prescribe an expiation for occasional consumption, the past tense would be employed;
for conventional usage (rūḍhi) supersedes etymological derivation (yoga).
And that is contradicted by logic;
for this very reason, they have explained it as "śvapaca" (dog-cooker).
And here, *savana* refers to...
The Soma sacrifice is thus described.

Consequently, O Blessed One, by the mere hearing of his name or any one of its parts, there occurs the immediate destruction of the evil karma— both that which has begun and that which has already commenced— which is the cause of his low birth and which stands as an obstacle to his fitness for the *savana* rite.

It is established by the Blessed One with regard to Uddhava: "Therefore, devotion fixed on Me purifies even outcaste dog-cookers from their very birth" (BhP 11.14.20); this is for the sake of the *kaimutya* argument (the principle of "how much more so").

The word "proktam" (it is said) follows; however, what is meant here by "fitness" is merely the state of being severed from the sins of *prārabdha* karma that cause one to become an outcaste (*śvapaca*).
However, for the purpose of the *savana* rite, the infusion of another quality (*guṇāntarādhāna*) is indeed required;
just as, although Brahmin boys possess the capacity at birth, they still require the *sāvitra* and *daiksya* rites.

However, since right conduct (*sad-ācāra*) is already established by birth through the *Sāvitrī* and other rites, its application at the time of the *savana* (pressing of the Soma) is not appropriate. Therefore, with the intention that the purpose lies merely in [establishing] its venerability, the authors of the *Ṭīkā* have also stated:
"By this, venerability is indicated."
Nevertheless, since it removes the defects of birth, the fact that it destroys even *prārabdha* karma has clearly been established.
And the commentary explains this: "Aho bata! Oh, what a wonder!"
Even a dog-cooker (śvapaca) is more venerable than one upon whose tongue-tip your name resides; for that very reason, he is greater. As for why this is so, [the text] says:
"They themselves performed austerities," and so forth.
"In the chanting of Your name, austerity and other such practices are included;
therefore, they are the most meritorious"—this concludes [the passage].
Furthermore, the Blessed Lord said to Uddhava: "Devotion fixed upon Me purifies even dog-cookers."
"Also because of its possibility" (BhP 11.14.20).

Here, it is clear that by virtue of removing the defects of birth (*jāti-doṣa*), there is the removal of *prārabdha* karma. Likewise, the power to remove diseases and other causes of *prārabdha* karma is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"I bow to that Ananta, by whose remembrance and by the chanting of whose name mental anxieties and physical ailments are dissolved right then and there.
And it is said in the *Nāma-kaumudī*: "And [the power of] removing even commenced sins exists in some cases..."
"By the power of the devotee's wish" (3.33).
Śrī Devahūti [says]: [128] [129] He states that she has removed those latent impressions (vāsanā):
"By means of austerity, charity, vows, and so forth, those sins are purified;
yet that heart born of unrighteousness is not purified even by service to the feet of the Lord.
That heart of theirs, born from unrighteousness, is purified by what is called *saṃskāra*."

The meaning is that one becomes purified by service to the feet of the Lord (Īśa). And in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "The sin whose fruit has not yet begun—like a seed-corn ready to sprout—is gradually dissolved for those whose souls are devoted to Viṣṇu."
"Aprārabdha-phala" (that whose fruit has not yet begun) refers to something other than those to be described hereafter.
"Kūṭa" means tending toward becoming a seed; "bīja" means tending toward the commencement of its activity; and "prārabdha" means tending toward the manifestation of its fruit—this is the meaning.
// 6.2 // The messengers of Śrī Viṣṇu [drive away] the messengers of Yama.
[129] [130] He states the quality of removing ignorance: "You, O Infinite Blessed One, [reside] then within the inner self..."
When you have attained all powers and are established in pure bliss,
by practicing supreme devotion, you will gradually sever the deep-rooted knot of ignorance consisting of "I" and "mine."
And so it is said in the Pādma:
"Devotion to Hari, accompanied by the sciences that follow after it,
quickly burns away ignorance, just as a forest fire consumes a female serpent."
// 4.11 // Śrī Manu said to Dhruva: 130.

[131] It has been stated that he is the cause of the satisfaction of all, as in the passage beginning with "Just as by watering the root of a tree" (BhP 4.31.12). Likewise, Suruci spoke to him after raising up the boy who was prostrate at his feet:
Embracing him, she said, "Live! with a voice faltering with tears:
"To him with whom the Blessed Lord Hari is pleased by his qualities such as friendliness and the like, all beings bow down of their own accord, just as water flows toward a low place. (BhP 4.9.47)
Even Suruci, though her mother’s co-wife and a personal enemy, attained Śrīdhruva who had come through the worship of the Lord;
as it is said in the Padma Purāṇa:
"By him who has worshipped Hari, even the entire worlds are gratified;
there, all living beings, both mobile and immobile, take delight.
Thus spoke Śrī Maitreya. 4.9. 131. [132]

It has been stated that she is the cause of excellent qualities such as knowledge and dispassion, beginning with the verse: "He who possesses unconditioned devotion to the Blessed Lord" (BhP 5.18.12), and so forth; she is the cause of heaven, liberation, and the abode of the Blessed Lord.
Its being the cause of all bliss has also been stated by such passages as, "That which is not attained by rituals, nor by austerity... (BhP 11.20.32).
By its own bestowal of supreme happiness, it declares the state of being rejectable for those things—such as rituals and the like—which are achieved through infinite means beginning with knowledge.
Neither the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra,
nor sovereignty over the whole earth, nor lordship over the realms of taste;
neither the perfections of yoga nor even liberation from rebirth.
"Having offered his self to me, he desires nothing other than me.
"Sovereignty over the nectar" means lordship over Pātāla and the other regions;
"freedom from rebirth" refers to the state of liberation as Brahman.
Liberation—what need is there to say more? He does not desire even the slightest category of things to be accomplished;
rather, the meaning is that he desires Me alone—who am superior to all human goals—as the object to be attained through such devotion, and not without Me.
"One who has offered his self to Me and surrendered his very being" (11.54). Śrī Bhagavān:
Now, in order to declare that devotion is indeed beyond the material qualities (*nirguṇa*), [the Lord] begins by speaking of actions dedicated to the Blessed One.
First, he describes the quality-based nature of all actions with one verse:

"One's own duty is *sāttvika* when it is offered to Me or performed without desire for fruit; it is *rājasa* when accompanied by a longing for results; and it is *tāmasa* when it consists primarily of violence and the like. [BhP 11.25.23]
"Offered unto me" (mad-arpita) means that for which there is dedication unto me. "Fruitless" (niṣphalam) means free from desire; that in which fruit is intended is [not fruitless].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that which is performed through hypocrisy, envy, and so forth.

Now, stating that other forms of practice are included within the three *guṇas*, he declares the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of direct devotion (*sākṣād-bhakti*) in the fourth stage with the words beginning with "catuḥṣu": [134]—

"Isolation is sattvic knowledge; that which is characterized by doubt is rājasic; knowledge pertaining to material nature is tāmasic; and that which is established in Me is remembered as being beyond the modes (nirguṇa).
'Pertaining to material nature' means it is like the knowledge of children, the mute, and so forth. [BhP 11.25.23]

That which is optional and has as its object the body and so forth is *rajas*, belonging to the quality of passion (*rājasa*). "Isolation" (*kaivalya*) is the knowledge of the pure soul through its distinction from the absolute, undifferentiated Brahman;
for it is untenable that the knowledge of the mere referent of your term [Brahman] alone could constitute isolation.
Because it depends upon the knowledge of the meaning of that term;
for when the mind is endowed with purity (*sattva*), first of all, the pure and subtle individual soul (*jīva*)—
Consciousness shines forth;
therefore, because it is non-different from the single form of consciousness (cid-ekākāra), the pure and complete Brahman-consciousness is also experienced within it.
Therefore, because the quality of *sattva* alone is predominant as the cause therein, it is characterized as *sāttvika*. And so says the Śrī Gītā Upaniṣad: "From *sattva* arises [knowledge]."
Regarding the verse beginning with "jñānam" (Gītā 14.17):
as for the knowledge of the Blessed One, it is said:
"Of the gods who are of pure *sattva*, and of the sages whose souls are stainless..."

Devotion to the feet of Mukunda generally does not arise. O great sage, even among millions of liberated and perfected beings, one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa and whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely rare.
(On page 60) By such statements as these, [it is shown that] even when *sattva* and the other qualities exist, there is an absence [of their effects];
for Vṛtra, O Brahmin, was a sinful being whose very nature consisted of *rajas* and *tamas*.
"How did his mind become firmly fixed upon the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa?

(BhP 6.14.1). By stating this, it is shown that even in the absence of Him [the Lord], [the world] exists; therefore, He is not its material cause. Rather, He is its cause in the sense of being subsequent to it.
Through the description of his association with Nārada and others in a previous birth,
their minds have not yet touched the feet of the Wide-Striding One (Viṣṇu), which is for the purpose of removing all misfortune.
"...as long as one does not choose the consecration by the dust of the feet of the Great Ones who possess nothing"—
by this statement, [he describes] the association with the illustrious and great ones, who have become vessels for the fragrance of the Lord's grace.
This is the reason:
and attachment to that [wealth]—
we do not weigh even a fraction of it against heaven or against the state of no-more-rebirth.
"Of mortals who have the association of those associated with the Blessed One, what need is there to mention their blessings?
By this statement, because He is superior even to the state beyond the qualities (*nirguṇa*), He is indeed the Supreme Beyond-Qualities (*parama-nirguṇa*). He is that, and of Him...

And in passages such as, "O Brahman, He is equal toward the first-born, the beloved, and the friend" (BhP 7.1.1), His compassion toward those with attributes, such as the gods, is not real; rather, it exists only toward Śrī Prahlāda and others.

Because the great ones demonstrate this by manifesting their own state beyond the modes (*nirguṇatva*), the transcendence of the modes of association with the virtuous (*sat-saṅga*) is also made clear. Likewise, it is heard in scripture that devotion (*bhakti*) also persists even after the shaking off of attachment to the modes.
As was said by the Blessed Lord to Uddhava:
"Therefore, having obtained this body which is the source of knowledge and realization,
let the wise, having shaken off attachment to the qualities (*guṇas*), worship Me. Thus,
the statement that the knowledge of the Supreme Lord is "without qualities" (*nirguṇa*) because it is the cause of being beyond the qualities is, however, figurative (*lakṣaṇā-maya*).
This would involve an overly strained interpretation;

likewise, since the knowledge of isolation (kaivalya-jñāna) also has the absence of the guṇas as its cause, there would be no distinction [between it and other forms of knowledge], and thus the application of different illustrative examples would not occur.
Therefore, the knowledge of the Blessed One is by its very nature devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). For this very reason it is said:
"Sattvic happiness arises from the Self, whereas that which arises from sense objects is rajasic."
"Tamasic, arising from delusion and dejection, devoid of qualities, and taking refuge in Me"— in this [verse],
even the bliss of that [state] will be described as being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
[This refers to] the activity characterized by hearing and so forth.

By the statement, "Even for one who possesses devotion to form, who is desirous of hearing, and who has faith, a taste for the narrations of Vāsudeva arises through service to the great" (BhP 1.2.13), its being the sole cause [of such taste] establishes that it is indeed devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*).
Now, one might object:
"And you shall know my own glory, designated as the Supreme Brahman, revealed within your heart through my grace and by means of your inquiries" (BhP 8.24.38).
By this statement of the venerable Matsya-deva, it is shown that even the knowledge of Brahman arises from the grace of the Blessed Lord.
It is heard [in scripture]; how then can it possess qualities?
It is said: the knowledge of Brahman arises for two kinds of people;
therein, for those who worship the Blessed Lord, it arises as a secondary consequence, while for those who worship Brahman [it arises directly].
As independent entities;

however, by the worshippers of the Blessed One, it is perceived through devotion—which is of the nature of the Blessed One’s power—with a slight distinction, as in [Gītā 18.54]: "Having become Brahman, with a serene self... and so forth.

In accordance with the statement in the *Ādi-śrī-gītā*, "The sages who delight in the Self" (*BhP* 1.7.10), and following other such passages, the retinue of devotion known as the *parā* (supreme) belongs to the Blessed Lord.
However, by those who worship Brahman, it is perceived as non-different from Him, as previously stated;

for they do not consider His grace to be absolute, according to the direction of the verse: "They do not even calculate the finality of that fruit" (BhP 6.15.48), whereas others regard it as absolute.
Because this view is also respected by the most learned scholars;
likewise, because of its opposition to devotion, as stated in the words: "Those who perceive heaven, liberation, and hell as having equal value" (BhP 6.17.23).
Since liberation, like hell, is to be abandoned, it is merely a semblance of serenity; though perceived as serenity according to one's own views,
it is indeed possessed of defects because it is constructed by that very mind.
Therefore, even the knowledge of isolation (kaivalya-jñāna) is likewise;
specifically, its birth is admitted to occur through a connection with the qualities (guṇas).
But surely, both internal and external activity is for the person (puruṣa) and consists solely of the qualities (guṇas);
how then can devotion in its two forms arising from that be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa)?
It is said: neither the power of knowledge nor the power of action can be an attribute of the insentient *traiguṇya* (the three qualities), just as they are not attributes of a jar;
nor can they belong to the *jīva*, which is of the nature of consciousness.

Because its power is dependent upon Īśvara, it is secondary; thus, it follows that [the agency] belongs to the Supreme Self's consciousness alone, just as in the case of a person possessed by a deity. As it has been said:
"The body, senses, vital breath, mind, and intellect—these..."
"Those who are pierced by a portion of Him proceed in their activities.
And so says the Śruti: "The life-breath of the life-breath, the sight of the sight, the hearing of the hearing, the mind of the mind—without Him nothing whatsoever is done," and so forth.

The seers, having transcended the hearing of the ear, the mind of the mind, that which is indeed the speech of speech, and the breath of the breath, as well as the sight of the eye— [enter the immortal].
"Having departed from this world, they become immortal. (Kena Upaniṣad 1.2) This being so,
since these two [the earth and heaven] exist primarily as effects of the three qualities (guṇas), they are described as being composed of those qualities.

But by virtue of the preeminence of the Supreme Lord, they are inherently beyond the material qualities (*guṇātīta*). Thus it was said by Śrī Śuka in the chapter on the drinking of the nectar of the gods (*devāmṛtapānādhyāya*):
"That which is joined with life-breath, wealth, action, mind, and speech..."
"O men, that which is done toward the body, the self, the son, and so forth, becomes non-existent because of their separateness;
whereas that which is done by those very same persons becomes real because of their non-separateness from all.
Therefore, that which is poured at the root is what truly nourishes everything. [BhP 8.9.29]
"From separateness" means having a locus other than the Supreme Self;

"from non-separateness" means having that [Supreme Self] as its sole locus—this is the meaning. Therefore, it is indeed logical that devotion to Hari, which consists of both knowledge and action, is devoid of the [material] guṇas.

Specifically, it is accepted that through the connection with the qualities of that devotion there is an absence of rebirth; however, it is not the case that, as with the knowledge of Brahman, there is an absence of rebirth due to a connection with the qualities.
Therefore, that is devotion.
Its [the nature of devotion] will also be illustrated by qualities such as its capacity to gladden and so forth;

however, those states of devotion— both devoid of attributes (nirguṇa) and endowed with attributes (saguṇa)— which were described by the venerable Kapiladeva, are in fact merely the qualities of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of the person.
It is established that [the qualities] are cultivated within that [devotion].
Having thus intended this, and having stated the qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of devotion in its form as knowledge (*jñāna-rūpā*), he explains it in its form as action (*kriyā-rūpā*).
Even there, let us first consider the Lord’s [devotion] in the form of hearing, chanting, and so forth.

Regarding that which consists of mere dwelling according to its connection, he says: "A forest is said to be sattvic dwelling, a village is called rājasic, a gambling house is tāmasic, but My abode is beyond the guṇas. [BhP 11.15.24]

The phrase "dwelling in the forest" (vanaṃ vāsaḥ) means the act of residing associated with that [forest]; this should be understood as referring to forest-dwellers (vānaprasthas). Likewise, "village-dweller" (grāmya) refers to householders (gṛhasthas), and "dark" (tāmasa) refers to those of evil conduct. Gambling—
The term "abode" (*sadana*) is an elliptical expression;
[it refers to] "my dwelling" (*man-niketam*), meaning for those intent upon my service (*mat-sevā-parāṇām*).
And [the word] "with" (*saha*) indicates a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatva*), as in the expression "ghee is the life-force of the forest" (*vanasyāyuḥ ghṛtam*).
This is because the forest, consisting of groves of trees, is dominated by *rajas* and *tamas*.
For this very reason, it possesses the characteristic of seclusion (*viviktatva*).
Even his *sāttvika* quality is secondary because it is mixed with that pair [of *rājasa* and *tāmasa* qualities];
however, because the act of dwelling is endowed with *sattva* and because it increases that [sattva], it possesses primacy in its *sāttvika* nature. Thus, of that [act].
Thus, its status as the expressed meaning (abhidheya) is appropriate;

for this very reason, it is read [in grammatical treatises] as ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*), namely *grāmya*. Similarly, in the expression *dyūta-sadanam*, it is precisely the act of dwelling (*vāsa-kriyā*) that is intended to be expressed.
This also applies to the phrase "the abode of the person" (man-niketam).
However, by virtue of the majesty of its connection with the Blessed One, even the abode itself becomes devoid of qualities (nirguṇa);
such a state is perceived by those whose eyes are the vision of such devotion, according to the analogy of the touchstone (sparśa-maṇi).
Thus it should be understood;

just as those dwelling in heaven see all [the deities] there as having four arms, so too does the *Ṭīkā*: "But the abode of the Blessed One is directly that manifestation which is beyond attributes (*nirguṇa*)."
"Abiding"—this is the term.
Having thus described the nature of mere dwelling as being such, he states that all those activities are likewise of that same nature: [136]
"The agent who is unattached is characterized by *sattva*; he who is blinded by passion is said to be *rājasa*;
he who has lost his memory is *tāmasa*; and he who is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) takes refuge in me.
In this context, the emphasis lies solely on the action, not on the substance inherent in it.
For the body and so forth of a sattvic agent are indeed merely transformations of the three qualities (guṇas).
Having thus stated that every action is of such a nature, [the author proceeds to discuss] that which is the cause for its engagement...
Regarding faith as well, he said:
"Faith that is sattvic is spiritual; faith in ritual action is rajasic;
faith in unrighteousness is tamasic; but faith in service to Me is beyond the gunas. [BhP 11.25.27]
In this context, "unrighteousness" (adharma) refers to the duty of another (para-dharma).
The rest is as before.
Therefore, he says: "The pure Bhāgavata dharma and that which pertains to the three Vedas (traividya), which rests upon the qualities (guṇa).
Here, "pure" means *nirguṇa* (devoid of qualities), and "pertaining to the three Vedas" means that which is propounded by the three Vedas; "resting upon the qualities" refers to the latter.
And the commentary [states]: "By the word 'Veda' here, only the *karma-kāṇḍa* (the ritual section) is intended, as in such passages as [Gītā 9.21], 'Thus the dharma of the threefold [Veda]'.
Therefore, he states that devotion itself reveals the nature and power of the Blessed Lord and is self-luminous:
"For the sacrifice, for the lord of dharma, for the perfection of ritual."
Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, to Hari, the Lord of Yoga, the head of Sāṅkhya, and the Primal Nature; he who, even while laughing, uttered this noble salutation even as he was becoming a deer.

Since even for Bharata, the son of Ṛṣabha, at the time of death— even while in that deer-body— there was no possibility of that speech being produced [by another], the self-luminosity of that devotion characterized by glorification is established.
The same should be understood regarding the lordly elephant as well.

in that regard, during the stage of practice, therefore indeed the wise...

the state of having desire— which is of two kinds, pertaining to this world and pertaining to the next world— is prohibited in its entirety.
In the words of Śrī Nāga’s wife and elsewhere, it is stated: "Neither the station of Brahmā nor the abode of Mahendra," and so forth.
Therefore, [this refers to] Pṛṣadhra, the son of Vaivasvata Manu.
Furthermore, even for one who desires liberation, the designation of being "exclusively devoted" (*ekāntitva*) should be understood as merely figurative:
"Do not entice me with those boons by creating attachment to desires;
fearing such attachment and being weary of it, I, desiring liberation, have taken refuge in You. (BhP 7.10.2)

In this passage from the words of Śrī Prahlāda, "the desire for liberation" (mumukṣā) is indeed the very wish to renounce desires: "O best of givers of boons, if you will grant me excellent boons, I choose as my boon from you the non-arising of desires within my heart. [BhP 7.10.7]
Because it will be stated hereafter,
and because Śrī Nārada previously said: "All that is a child's obstacle to the yoga of devotion" (BhP 7.10.1).
In this way, it should be understood that even the performance of the sacrifice by the illustrious Ambarīṣa was solely for the purpose of gathering the world;
it was undertaken with a state of exclusive devotion directed toward Him.
It has been stated: in that regard, even the absence of desire for this world and the earning of a livelihood through devotion should be understood as being devoid of [worldly] existence.
As it says in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*: "He who does not live off Viṣṇu... [is pure].
The characteristics of a devotee:
silence, vows, sacred learning, austerity, study, the performance of one's own duty, exposition, solitary recitation, and meditative absorption— these lead to liberation.
"O Supreme Person, for those who have not conquered their senses, these matters generally become mere talk; indeed, they do not even exist for the hypocritical.
Thus, as in the words of Śrī Prahlāda.
For those who have not conquered their senses, silence and the like become mere "vārtās"—that is, means of livelihood.
However, for the hypocritical, even these do not necessarily become "vārtās," because hypocrisy has uncertain results; such is the meaning.
Therefore it has been said:
"Those who, desiring to worship the Blessed One, do not seek even the highest reward, are remembered as those skilled in their own true interest. [BhP 6.18.74]
And the commentary states, "even supreme liberation.
Therefore, it was well said: "The status of being twice-born is not sufficient," and so forth.
// 7.7 // Śrī Prahlāda [to the asura children] // 168 // [169] Then he states that this very devotion is the essence of all scriptures:
"Hearing of Viṣṇu, chanting His names, remembering Him, serving His feet,"
Worship, salutation, service, friendship, and self-surrender.
Thus, if devotion characterized by nine features were truly offered by a person to Viṣṇu, the Blessed One, I consider that to be the highest study.

These [nine features] are: hearing and chanting His names and so forth, as well as remembering them; [The remaining six are: serving Him, worshiping Him, offering prayers to Him, becoming His servant, making Him one's friend, and surrendering everything to Him.]
Attending upon the feet is service;
honoring is worship as prescribed by rule;
and saluting is prostration.

*Dāsya* is the conceit of thinking "I am His servant. *Sakhya* is the desire for His welfare through a sense of kinship. *Ātmanivedana* is the offering of one’s own body and its constituents—which stand in the place of cattle, horses, and so forth—to Him alone.
Offering for the sake of worship is like a sale; it is an entrustment of the object to another,
wherein one does not even personally undertake the concern of its maintenance or protection.
And these have been cited by the ancients:

"Parīkṣit became [the foremost] in hearing the glories of Śrī Viṣṇu, the son of Vyāsa (Śuka) in chanting them, Prahlāda in remembering Him, Lakṣmī in worshiping His feet, and Pṛthu in offering Him ritual service."
"Akrūra was for prostration; the lord of monkeys (Hanumān) for servitude; Arjuna for friendship; and Bali for the offering of his entire self—this is their supreme attainment of Kṛṣṇa.
Thus, that devotion which has the Blessed Lord as its object is characterized by these nine features.
This devotion is indeed direct in form, not indirect in the manner of offering ritual actions and the like;
and even therein, it is directed toward Śrī Viṣṇu.

If [the study] is performed in such a way— that it is dedicated to that [goal] alone and cultivated with the thought "this is for that purpose alone," and not dedicated to dharma, wealth, or other ends—
then I consider whatever has been studied by that author to be supreme.
This is the meaning. And thus says the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad:
"Devotion is his worship; that [worship] consists of fixing the mind on Him alone, by means of detachment from the conditions of this world and the next."
This very [state] is non-action (*naiṣkarmya*).
For this very reason, the combination of the nine characteristics is not necessary;
by means of a single limb alone—
Because it is heard that [the reason] does not deviate from the probandum;
however, there is sometimes a mixing with other auxiliary factors because of the diversity of faith and inclination.

Therefore, it should be understood that by means of the term "nine characteristics" (*nava-lakṣaṇa*), the performance of that alone is enjoined through a general statement regarding devotion (*bhakti*).
Furthermore, its state of possessing nine characteristics distinguishes it from others.
It has also been stated that [the others] are included within those very limbs.

// 7.5 // Śrī Prahlāda to his father // 169 // [170] Now, another method is presented to demonstrate that this devotion known as "possessing nothing" (akiñcana) abides on the highest level of all stages and is established in a specific type of qualified practitioner.

In that regard, in order to avoid turning away from the supreme reality (*para-tattva*), some degree of mere orientation toward it must be achieved by any means possible. And that [orientation] is threefold, pertaining to the manifestation of that very reality known as Brahman in its undifferentiated form (*nirviśeṣa-rūpa*).
The two are: the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-rūpa*), and the nature of devotion (*bhakti-rūpa*) which pertains to the manifestation of that very Lord in His specific forms.

And the third is the gateway to that very same pair, consisting of the form of the offering of action (*karmārpaṇa*). These three are restated here— on page 80— in order to establish the distinction of human qualifications (*puruṣa-yogyatā*),
[showing] that in this world, knowledge, action, and devotion alone are the means, and no others.
"Three yogas have been declared by me for the sake of securing the ultimate good of human beings:
knowledge, action, and devotion; there is no other means anywhere.
Here, *yogāḥ* means "means" (*upāyāḥ*).

By me, whose source is the Śāstra, the excellence consisting of the three aims of life (trivarga) and the love for liberation (mukti) has been [established]; by this, the status of devotion as a mere ritual action is excluded.
He states the causes for qualification regarding those [aims] in two verses:
For those who are disillusioned with worldly actions and have renounced them, the yoga of knowledge is prescribed here;
but for those whose minds are not disillusioned and who possess desires, the yoga of action is prescribed.
"But for that person who, by chance, has developed faith in my stories and so forth,
and who is neither despondent nor excessively attached, the yoga of devotion grants him perfection.
[BhP 11.20.7–8] Here, among these [types of practitioners], the "despondent" one is [disgusted] with the pleasures of worldly and otherworldly objects and their stability.
The meaning is: for those who have become detached from worldly and Vedic actions—which are the means to that [detachment]—and who have renounced them;
by these two words, [it refers to] those who have developed a firm desire for liberation (mumukṣu).
The intended meaning here is as follows:
the connection with what follows is that "the yoga of knowledge leads to success for these [persons];
for those possessed of desire, that—

Therefore, for those attached to those pleasures and whose minds are not disenchanted with those activities, being unable to renounce them, the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) grants success; it yields fruits corresponding to their specific intentions. As stated in passages such as, "But they indeed know and transcend the illusory power of the Divine" (*BhP 2.5.45*), this refers to those born as animals (*tiryag-janāḥ*).

By the word "api" (even), he states that in this section on devotion (*bhakti*), because there is a transgression of the restrictions based on caste (*jāti*) and so forth—unlike in the case of ritual action (*karman*) and the like—mere faith (*śraddhā*) alone is the cause; thus he says, "by chance" (*yadṛcchayā*).
By "chance," [he means] by some supreme...

Through the arising of auspiciousness born from the association with independent devotees of the Blessed One and from their grace— referring to the verse beginning with "That which was spoken for one who desires to hear and has faith" (BhP 1.2.16)—
this very verse [is presented] by himself later on.
This will be explained by two verses:
"One who has developed faith in My stories, who is weary of all activities,
and who knows that desires consist of suffering, yet is unable to renounce them."
Then, full of love, faithful, and firm in resolve, one should worship me, even while enjoying those desires, yet censuring them as they lead to suffering.
The word "how" (*katham*) is an elliptical indicator; it means that through my stories and so forth, one has developed the realization that this alone is the supreme good.

"Faith. For this very reason, he says "he knows" (*veda*) to show that while he is anxious regarding other actions, he is not so regarding those present ones which consist of the fruits of his former meritorious deeds.
Thence follows the explanation of the passage beginning with "he knows them," and so forth.
The meaning is: "starting precisely from that state characterized by being neither disgusted nor overly attached";
he should worship me with the devotion known as *ananya* (non-dual) directed toward me.

The meaning is that he would be qualified [for the practice], but not like one possessing knowledge; for when true detachment (*vairāgya*) has arisen, that [power] possesses its own inherent capacity and is independent of anything else. This will be explained immediately hereafter.
Therefore, for the yogi who is endowed with devotion to Me and whose self is absorbed in Me,
neither knowledge nor detachment is generally considered the highest good in this world.
"Whatever is attained through ritual actions, through austerity, and through knowledge and dispassion," and so forth.
Nor does this entail a dependence upon detachment from ritual action (*karma-nirveda*);
rather, that [detachment] is for the sake of establishing the supremacy of devotion (*bhakti*).
One proceeds spontaneously out of faith alone;
the term "disgusted" (*nirviṇṇa*) is merely a restatement.
Therefore, even though...
Knowledge and action also certainly depend upon faith (p.
81), because without it, correct engagement both externally and internally is impossible; nevertheless, in this context, [faith] is the cause merely as faith.
In particular, there is the acceptance of that [non-duality];
and here too, the dependence on that, as before, is solely for the sake of right practice, because without it, the devotion called "non-otherness" does not proceed in such a manner.
"Sometimes something perishes through engagement";
for this very reason, it is said: "neither disenchanted nor overly attached" (BhP 11.20.8).
Immediately following this, in the passage beginning with "or by hearing my stories" (BhP 11.24.9), the renunciation of ritual action is prescribed only when faith has arisen;
however, mere devotion is accomplished even without that [faith].
"O best of the Bhṛgus, even if chanted but once, whether with faith or even playfully, the name of Kṛṣṇa can deliver even an ordinary human being"—thus [it is said] at the beginning.
"From association with the virtuous comes knowledge of My power... [and so forth].
These stories are an elixir for the heart and ears;
by relishing them, faith, delight, and devotion will gradually arise on the path to liberation.
And because it is heard in such passages that she bestows her fruit even prior to that:
"Even Ajāmila, while dying, went to the abode of Hari by chanting His name as uttered by his son;
how much more so one who chants with faith? (BhP 6.2.49).
This is because, in such passages, one hears of the excellence of its capacity to bestow the fruit;
and that faith is indeed an auxiliary factor for the ascertainment of what is to be expressed by the treatise, since it consists in confidence therein. Therefore...
Nor does devotion enter as a constituent part of the performance [of the rite];

furthermore, even though devotion depends upon the injunction for the production of the fruit, it would not be required [as a causal factor], just as fire and so forth are not required for the act of burning and the like.
Because the very nature of hearing, chanting, and other such acts toward the Blessed One possesses such power,
how could there be any dependence upon faith and the like?

Therefore, even in cases such as those involving fools, accomplishment is seen to occur without faith— as in the statement "by faith or by playfulness" (*śraddhayā helayā vā*). However, if this "playfulness" (*helā*) is performed without prior intention and consists of a form of transgression, then it does not exist in the absence of wickedness (*daurātmya*).
It has already been stated that [the self] is sublated by devotion;
however, in the case of those who are arrogant due to the power of their knowledge and so forth, it is sublated by the opposite of that.
Just as one might grasp at a name and so forth out of envy, as in the case of a bamboo flute; in some instances,
the power of an object is seen to be obstructed,
like the power of fire in the case of wet fuel and the like.
"O dearest one, even water brought with faith by a devotee is pleasing to Me;
however, even an abundance offered by one lacking devotion does not lead to My satisfaction.
In this passage, the words "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "devotion" (*bhakti*) refer specifically to reverence (*ādara*).
He, however, is intent upon the removal of that offense characterized by disregard which obstructs the arising of the specific fruit characterized by the gratification of the Blessed One.

Therefore, faith is not a limb of devotion; rather, it is merely a qualification for the eligible person (adhikārī) with respect to the devotion known as "exclusive" (ananya), which requires one who is desirous, capable, and learned.
For this very reason, it is stated as a qualifying attribute: "But he in whom faith has arisen by chance in my stories and so forth..."
Regarding the passages "the man who...
(BhP 11.20.8) and "one who has developed faith in my stories...
(BhP 11.20.27), here the word *tataḥ* is used in the ablative case (*pañcamy-anta*) with the elision of the suffix *-lyap*, carrying the sense of "having begun from that" (*tām ārabhya*).
By the word "unlimited" (*anavadhika*), it is intended that even in the state of delighting in the self (*ātmārāmatā*), that [delight] occurs for some; thus, its sovereignty is implied.
And immediately thereafter it will be stated: "The virtuous do not [seek] anything..."
Regarding the phrase "the wise" (*dhīrāḥ*):

by this, it is made known that through the proclamation of universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*), it is further indicated that without her, neither ritual action (*karma*) nor knowledge (*jñāna*) can be perfected.

Thus, having stated that mere faith is the cause for the qualification of exclusive devotion, he instructs how one should worship: "He is full of faith" means possessing conviction; "he is pleased" means being attached once a taste has arisen.
Possessing firm resolve and being free from the failure of his determination regarding the means of practice, he, being unable to abandon them suddenly, continues to enjoy sense objects.
And he censures them.
The reason for this censure is that they result in suffering and produce sorrow and so forth in subsequent times.
In this context, sensual desires should be understood as being inherently non-virtuous.
Because, according to the scripture, it is in no way possible for one to conform to another; on the contrary:
"He who sets his mind upon the wives of others, the wealth of others, or the injury of others..."

"O King, a person does nothing; by that, Keśava is pleased"—from such statements in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa and elsewhere, it is established that the performance of action is prohibited even prior to its dedication (*karmārpaṇa*). And in this very context, regarding desireless action as well, it is said: "If one should not perform anything else" (BhP 11.20.10).
Because of the prohibition that will be stated [later],
and because by means of the injunction for the renunciation of action, there is an even closer proximity to the renunciation of evil action.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"That man who violates the boundary established by Him should not be known as a devotee of Viṣṇu; [only] Hari, who is honored by the dharma of the virtuous, is a true devotee."
For thus it is prohibited even among the Vaiṣṇavas:
"The longing for service at whose feet [removes] the impurity of the intellect accumulated over all births of ascetics..."

"In this passage, by the use of the word *sadyas* (immediately), [it refers to] those whose taste has arisen at the very moment of birth— just as a river flowing from the big toe of the foot immediately diminishes [the heat] while increasing day by day.
[BhP 4.21.31] Thus, here, through the employment of the term *sadyas*, [it denotes] those for whom devotion has been produced instantly.
When one does not desire sinful acts and desires meritorious ones,
then a man should know that Hari resides within his heart.
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇu-dharma*:
"He who, seated within the heart, by means of discipline shakes off whatever improper action has arisen in any way whatsoever" (*BhP* 11.5.38).
Here too, by the employment of the word "in any way whatsoever" (*kathañcit*), it is understood that for those who have attained devotion spontaneously...
Because its application is otherwise impossible;

for it is stated in the *Pādma* [Purāṇa], in the *Nāmāparādhabhañjana-stotra* and other works, that "for one who possesses no sinful intent through the power of the Name, purification indeed comes through the restraints (*yama*s)," and thus there is devotion to Hari.
Furthermore, even if one were to engage in that [practice] by force, it would result in the commission of an offense;
moreover, the verse "even if he be of very evil conduct" (Gītā 9.30) refers solely to the fault of disregarding Him.

But it is not intended to enjoin misconduct; for in the immediately following statement, "He quickly becomes righteous" (Gītā 9.31), no higher good is specified as resulting from the departure from misconduct.
// 11.20 // The Blessed Lord said:
// 172 // [173] But surely, in this way, the distinct arrangement of mere action, knowledge, and devotion has been stated. [Now, regarding] obligatory and occasional [rites]...
But since ritual action (karman) is necessary for all [paths], one might then ask: "In the case of such confusion, how could pure knowledge and devotion proceed?
Anticipating this objection, he precludes their eligibility for ritual action.
"One should perform ritual actions as long as one does not become weary, or until faith arises in listening to My stories and so forth" (BhP 11.20.9).
And the *Ṭīkā* explains that "ritual actions" refers to the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other such duties. Therefore—
The Śruti and Smṛti are my very commands; he who acts by transgressing them is a violator of my command and a hater of me. Even if he be my devotee, he is certainly not a Vaiṣṇava.
Even though the aforementioned fault would apply here, it does not exist because of the performance of the command;
on the contrary, it is precisely by performing those two— disenchantment and faith— that the command is fulfilled.
And as it was explained in the commentary on the verse "Having understood the virtues and the faults" (BhP 11.11.32): "By means of the firmness of devotion."
"Having completely renounced by virtue of having ceased from [further] qualification.
And this state of having ceased from qualification has been stated by Śrīkarabhājana:
"Of the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, men, and ancestors..."
O King,
he who has with his whole being gone for refuge to Mukunda, the worthy refuge, having abandoned all other duties, is neither a servant nor a debtor.

Thus, he is not their servant, but rather the servant of the Śrī Bhagavān alone; this constitutes his lack of authority. "Kartam" means "done," and in the sense of "the distinction [between what is] done," it implies that the deities and others possess independence.
This very point has been stated in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa:
"This is a god," "This sage is to be worshipped," "This is Brahmā," or "This is Bṛhaspati"—
such designations arise only so long as one does not worship Hari.
For one who has taken refuge in Him, no other ritual act need be performed as a penance for improper actions.
Because of the absence of engagement in improper actions;
and it has also been stated that even if an improper action should somehow occur, the incidental accomplishment of expiation is achieved simply by recollecting it.
By the very next verse:
"To His beloved who worships at the soles of His own feet, having abandoned all other states of being, Hari, the Supreme Lord..."
"Whatever improper action has arisen in any way, He who is seated within the heart shakes it all off"—thus [it is said].
This should be explained as: "one by whom devotion (*bhakti*), which is an inclination (*bhāva*) toward the Blessed Lord, has been abandoned in favor of another deity. In this context...
Because faith and the act of going for refuge are stated to have the renunciation of karma as their cause, they are understood to share a single meaning, and this is logical;
for faith is indeed confidence in the meaning of the scriptures.
And the treatise declares that for one who lacks such a refuge there is fear, whereas for one who has found that refuge there is fearlessness;
from this arises faith.
Taking refuge alone is the defining characteristic;
nor should there be separate worship of the Vedas and so forth, even if their purpose is merely for the sake of libation.
For instance, in passages such as "Just as by watering the root of a tree" (BhP 4.31.12), the fault of tautology would arise;
nor [is there a need for this] in the interim for one who has abandoned ritual action.

Even when devotion is obstructed by impediments, it is appropriate to feel regret for abandoning it, according to such statements as, "Having abandoned one's own duty" (BhP 1.5.17). And in the Śrī Gītā:
"Renouncing all duties, come to Me alone as your refuge."

"I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve" (Gītā 18.66)—the unity of meaning between this and the two verses beginning with "of gods, sages, beings, kinsmen, and men" (BhP 11.5.37) is observed.
Therefore, at the very commencement of devotion, the renunciation of action must be performed by its very nature.
For in the word *parityajya*, the meaning of the prefix *pari-* is indeed exactly like that; and in the *Gautamīya*:
"There is no recitation, no worship, no meditation, nor even the sequence of ritual injunctions."

He taught nothing but exclusive devotion through such passages as: "Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me" (Gītā 9.34), and "Only for those who constantly meditate upon the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa... (Gautamīya Tantra 33.57).
As it is said in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, addressing Bharata:
"O Lord of Sacrifice, Acyuta, Govinda, Mādhava, Ananta, Keśava!"
"O Kṛṣṇa, O Viṣṇu, O Hṛṣīkeśa"— this alone the king said,
O Maitreya; he uttered nothing else, even in his dreams,
because there was no opportunity for any other speech.
Thus, the abandonment of other ritual actions consisting of those very words is even more clearly accepted;
somehow (page 84).

Furthermore, because it is understood that even when an action is being performed, it is considered as already accomplished by that very name, and because that [name] is perceived everywhere, pure devotion alone is accepted as the essential factor.
As it is stated in the Padma Purāṇa: "The destination that those who have abandoned all dharmas and utter only the name of Viṣṇu reach with ease, even all the righteous do not reach. [PadmaP 6.71.99]

Therefore, even according to another view, it is appropriate that one who possesses faith has the qualification for exclusive devotion (*ananya-bhakti*) and lacks the qualification for ritual action (*karman*) and the like;
however, it must be investigated how the very existence of such faith arises.
And in that regard, taking refuge has already been taught as the defining characteristic (*liṅga*);
for within the act of taking refuge,
there are the characteristics to be described, such as "the resolve to act in accordance" and so forth.
Likewise, the absence of worldly concern, miserliness, and so forth should also be understood as a sign of faith;
for the scripture teaches that faith is characterized in just this way.
"To those people who worship me, thinking of no other, and who are constantly devoted, I provide both security and prosperity. [Gītā 9.22]

Furthermore, for a person endowed with faith, when the substances, classes, qualities, and actions related to the Blessed One are heard of in the scriptures— even regarding their worldly and practical effects— there is no lack of conviction whatsoever.
Consequently, because of the perception of these [women] as being common objects such as ordinary material things,
and due to the investigation of specific defects, there would never be a lack of engagement;
and those [defects] are of such a kind—
The powers [of this water]: it is remembered that the water from the feet of Hari pacifies untimely death, destroys all diseases, and stills all suffering.
[And so forth.
However, some who possess faith therein, due to the fault of their own transgressions, remain as if concealed, thinking that its fruit will not arise at present.

As for the fact that even those who possess faith perform acts such as bathing when they hear such [scriptural] passages as, "Whoever should remember the Lotus-Eyed One becomes pure both externally and internally," that is indeed due solely to the weight of the traditional practice of the lineage of holy masters beginning with the venerable Nārada and Vyāsa.
Otherwise, there would be an offense even in transgressing those [rules];
and they [the virtuous] thus establish a boundary for the world against miserly conduct and the like.
It should be understood that [the Buddha] established [this teaching] solely for the sake of cessation.
Furthermore, once faith has arisen— whether success or failure is achieved— one's conduct should always be one of following after it, just like someone desiring the accomplishment of gold.

And here, "attainment" (siddhi) should be understood as the very manifestation of the venerable Hari, which brings about the destruction of defects such as the internal organ and desire, and reaches the supreme limit of absolute bliss;
and in that engagement toward the accomplishment of one's own goal, there is no activity consisting of hypocrisy, the desire for status, and so forth.
Not even a trace of it occurs;
for them, great offenses such as contempt and the like do not fall at all, being preceded by knowledge.
Precisely because of this contradiction;
for this very reason, Citraketu’s offense against Śrī Mahādeva was concealed by his own conduct, as he was a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata).
It should be understood that [this occurs] precisely from the knowledge of reality;
or else, even for one who possesses faith, there may be a habitual engagement with sense objects due to the force of *prārabdha* karma and other factors.
Nevertheless, through that sublation, even at the time of connection with the object, devotion characterized by humility alone would surge forth;
as it has been said: "And while enjoying..."
In such passages as "One should censure those desires which result in suffering" (BhP 11.14.17) and "Even if my devotee is being oppressed... (BhP 11.14.18),
as well as in statements such as "Even if he be of very wicked conduct" (Gītā 9.30), she is characterized by her exclusive devotion (*ananya-bhakti*).
That faith which is "indeed that faith by which those endowed with faith sacrifice, having set aside the injunctions of the scriptures" (Gītā 17.1),
is one obtained through worldly tradition (*loka-paramparā*), and not born from the determination of the scriptures (*śāstrāvadhāraṇa*). Scriptural...

But once faith has arisen, there can be no engagement in extremely wicked conduct, because that would contradict the scriptures for pleasing Viṣṇu, such as [the passage beginning]: "The wives of others, the property of others," and so forth. (ViP 3.8.14, p. 85)
Furthermore, because of the contradiction with his devotion [to Him] expressed in passages such as "the boundary was set by Him," that misconduct does not constitute devotion to Him.
It is precisely through faith in greatness that [this occurs],
for by the word "api" (even/also), the state of being ill-behaved is indicated as something to be abandoned;
likewise, because there would be no logical connection to the subsequent statement, "he quickly becomes righteous in nature."
For, as stated in the passage beginning with "By the power of [his] name, one whose mind is sinful," there is the occurrence of transgressions;
therefore, that faith should not be introduced as a qualifying attribute for those who are qualified for scriptural devotion (*śāstrīya-bhakti*).
However, this is indeed in praise of devotion;
even such faith serves as a cause for the quality of goodness (sattva) through devotion, and not like the worship of other deities.

That this faith is of a different nature was already stated in such passages as, "Those who, casting aside the scriptural injunctions... (Gītā 17.1). As for the state of perfection of this faith, however, it is described in the *Brahma-vaivarta*:
The inquiry "What is truth and what is falsehood? proceeds;
yet even when such inquiry has been made, O King, the avoidance of the untrue is established, and then faith becomes complete and yields great fruit.
Thus, when such characteristics—characterized by the arising of faith—are present, it is prescribed [in texts] such as: "Or from hearing my stories," and so forth.
For this very reason, there is the distinction between those who are unqualified and those who are qualified.
The discourse between the venerable Lord and Nārada is established solely by the intention of what was to be said, as in:

For one who instructs others in the Dharma while being loathsome himself,

"And people do not consider his prevention [of such acts] as a fault.

"The best of physicians does not give unwholesome food even to a sick person who desires it.

Thus, having described the three types of yoga and the cause for their respective eligibility, he explains how even ritual action (*karman*) may take the form of being directly before the Blessed One:

One does not go to heaven or hell if one does not perform other [actions].

This [verse] illuminates its rarity.

Here, in the company of the wise—
When [the mind] exists, its state of being "that-only" (tan-mātratva) would indeed be the offering to the Lord;

as it was said by the venerable Hanumān: "What fool, having attained the state of servitude..."

as was stated in the previous chapter: "Peace is the intellect fixed on Me" (BhP 11.19.33), and so forth, directly—

Having stated there, "Thine [is that] which holds all powers," it follows that [the individual soul] is a portion of You specifically as qualified by Your external power (taṭastha-śakti)— which includes the power called the individual soul (jīva) among the entirety of Your powers and qualities— and not [a portion] of You as qualified by Your essential power (svarūpa-śakti) or as the mere essential nature (kevala-svarūpa).

The reason for this trust is that [the Veda] is the field where the seeds of all the Vedas are sown and the sole locus for the revival of those seeds; the meaning is that it is the source (*yoni*) of the scriptures. even if the presence of an offense exists in a person, then by that fault—
