and who are characterized by a nature of excellent goodness consisting of compassion toward all beings—
"May this meeting with you be a favor to us.

Even if one explains this as "one for whom there is a favor toward those who are virtuous," it follows that there is no favor from you toward those who are non-existent (asat) and averse to the Truth; thus, it necessarily comes down to the conclusion that the manifestation of that [favor] is appropriate only through the medium of the virtuous (*sat*). Therefore, in this way—
"Indeed, that person whom Madhusūdana beholds at the moment of birth should be known as *sāttvika*, and he shall be certain of liberation"—
this statement from the *Mokṣadharma* also refers exclusively to one whose birth follows association with the virtuous (*sat-saṅga*).
It must be understood:
the gods [approached] the Blessed One.
(180) [181] Therefore, the cause for association with the virtuous is the very freedom of conduct of the good, and nothing else. As it has been said:
Once, they approached the sacrificial session of Nimi by chance (*yadṛcchayā*).
The meaning is that those nine masters of yoga (*yogeśvara*) came by their own will (*svairatayā*), and not impelled by any other cause.
According to Amara, *yadṛcchā* means "acting according to one's own will" (*svairitā*).
Furthermore, the Supreme Lord’s role as the impeller (*prayoktṛ*) toward existing things occurs solely in accordance with their own will;
as it has been said: "of Him who consists of His own will" (BhP 10.14.2).
"And: 'I am dependent upon my devotees' (BhP 9.4.46).
Thus spoke Śrī Nārada. 11.2 // 181 // [182]
Likewise:
"Once, while wandering through these worlds, the venerable sage Aṅgiras happened upon his house by chance. (BhP 6.14.14)
Of that Citraketu;
even here, at that very time, his presence arose, though at another time it would have been so.
It should be understood that he has appeared; for this very reason, at the time of his lamentation, the venerable Aṅgiras said:
"One who is devoted to Brahman and a devotee of the Blessed Lord ought not to perish" (BhP 6.15.12).

// 6.14 // Śrī Śuka // 182 // [183] Furthermore, the compassion of the virtuous arises merely from seeing the miserable condition of others; it does not depend upon their own worship or service, as was the case with Śrī Nārada toward Nalakūvara and Maṇigrīva. Thus he said:
"As the gods treat those who worship them, so do they treat them in turn; like shadows, the virtuous, who are compassionate toward the distressed, accompany one's actions. (BhP 11.2.6).
This is clear. 11.2. The illustrious Ānakadundubhi. 183. [184]

Thus, it has been stated that the mere association with the virtuous (*sat-saṅga*) is the sole cause for being brought face-to-face with Him. He expresses this very point through a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*): "For holy places do not consist of water, nor do the gods consist of clay or stone."

"Those virtuous ones purify [others] by their very sight over a long period of time; why then do they not show such regard [for others]? To this he says: 'They purify... (10.84). Thus the Blessed Lord spoke to the assembly of sages. (184) [185]

Thus, it has been stated that the mere association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) is the sole cause for being oriented toward that [Reality]. He expresses this very point through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*):
"Pure knowledge is the one supreme reality."
But immediately beyond that is the internal Brahman, which is truth, inward-looking,
and profoundly tranquil; that which the wise call Vāsudeva, designated by the term "Bhagavat."
O Rāhūgaṇa, this [state] is not attained through austerity, nor by sacrifice, nor by the offering of oblations from the home,
nor by Vedic meters, nor even by water, fire, or the sun.
Without the consecration by the dust of the Great One’s feet. What then is the truth?
Knowledge is the truth.
It excludes conventional reality;
it is the ultimate truth.
The six qualifiers are for the purpose of excluding [the meanings of] function and cognition.
That, however, is pure and free from ignorance;
though it is one, it appears in manifold forms.
But immediately thereafter, that which is external is empty of both the outer and the inner; that, however, is the opposite: Brahman is all-pervading, whereas that [world] is limited.
That [Brahman] is the inward-facing reality.
But that [mind] takes on the form of the object;
it is tranquil and changeless, whereas that [other mind] is subject to change.
Thus, knowledge whose nature is such has been described as truth. Of what kind is it?
The word *bhagavat* is a designation for that which possesses the six qualities beginning with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*),
and that which they call knowledge (*jñāna*) is Vāsudeva.
And since that attainment does not occur without service to the great, he says: "O Rahūgaṇa,
by means of austerity, a person [attains] this knowledge."

He does not go [to that state] by means of sacrifice— that is, by Vedic ritual, by the distribution of food and so forth through the offering of oblations, or by performing services for others for the sake of those [rituals], nor by the chanting of the Vedas (*chandas*), which is the study of the Vedas, nor by water, fire, and other such objects of worship; such is this [teaching].

In this context, it should be understood that the nature of the individual soul (jīva)— as well as its knowledge characterized by subtlety and other such qualities— is refuted by [the designation of] "Brahman-hood" and so forth.
// 5.12 // The illustrious Brāhmaṇa [says] to Rahūgaṇa:
[185] [186] Thus, it has been stated that association with the virtuous (*sat-saṅga*) alone is the gateway to being in their presence; and those virtuous ones are...

In this context, only those [who are truly virtuous] are intended, and not merely those devoted to Vedic conduct, because the latter are of no use here. It is said that among them, the nature of their association with the virtuous is precisely what constitutes "being face-to-face" (sāmmukhya).
Regarding those who are great among the virtuous, he describes their twofold nature with a half-verse:
"The great are those who possess equanimity of mind, who are tranquil, free from resentment, and who are friends and virtuous."
Or those who have established their friendship and purpose with me, rather than with people who are merely concerned with the maintenance of their own bodies.
In this world, those who possess wealth and are attached to their homes, wives, and children do not find true joy; yet others remain focused on their material needs.
Those, however, who are even-minded and established in the non-dual Brahman without distinction are the great ones; the scripture now describes their character.
"Tranquil," and so forth;
he states a great distinction with the words "or those who," where the word "or" (vā) indicates an alternative position.

Because this [devotion] is the superior position, its excellence has been established by me; those for whom that very friendship and love is the goal—the supreme human end (puruṣārtha)—and who are such as they truly are, they are the "great ones" (mahāntaḥ);
this is the connection with what precedes.

Because they possess friendship for me, for that very reason they are not filled with attachment toward people who are intent on talk of worldly objects— as well as toward homes filled with wives, sons, and circles of kinsmen— even though those people are themselves preoccupied with news of the gods and the celestial realms.
However, "yāvad-arthaḥ" means those who possess as much wealth (artha) as is necessary for the purpose (artha) consistent with the worship of the Blessed Lord;
and the greatness of both [the father and son] is due to their being great knowers and great devotees.
But it is not with the intention of asserting equality between the two;
for even among the liberated and the perfected ones, he alone is the one who has Nārāyaṇa as his supreme goal. [BhP]
As stated in [6.14.5] and other passages, it should be understood that here,

in the path of knowledge (*jñāna-mārga*), there are the great ones who experience Brahman, and in the path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*), there are the great ones who have attained divine love; thus, their characteristics are common.
// 5.5 // Śrī-Ṛṣabha to his sons: 186–187. And in this regard, it should be analyzed as follows:
the great ones who have attained perfection on those respective paths are shown to be of two kinds.

And here, those who have attained perfection through knowledge (*jñāna-siddha*) are described in passages such as: "The perfected one perceives neither the body—whether situated, moving, or arisen—since he has realized his own true nature" (BhP 11.13.35). (Page 94)
In this regard, the perfected devotees are of three kinds:
those who have obtained the bodies of the Lord’s personal associates (pārṣada) and have shaken off all impurities (kaṣāya), and those whose impurities are merely dormant.
Just as Śrī Nārada and others, and Śrī Śuka and others— who were Nārada and the rest in previous births—
did when I was assuming that pure Bhāgavata body.
In passages such as: "Having completed his karma, he whose body was composed of the five elements fell into nirvāṇa" (BhP 1.6.29);

and: "Though his mind was absorbed in his own bliss and all other states were cast aside by that, his very essence was drawn away by the charming pastimes of the Unconquered One" (BhP 12.12.52), and so forth.
Alas! In this life, you ought not to look upon me here, for my impurities have not yet ripened.
I am difficult to perceive for those of false yoga.
And because this is well-known from such passages as BhP 1.6.22,
Śrī Nārada himself described his own love while he was still possessed of the "impurities" (kaṣāya) from his previous birth:
"With my limbs covered in horripilation, bursting forth due to the extreme weight of my love, I am exceedingly blissful."
"In the flood of bliss, O Sage, I was absorbed and did not perceive either [the external world or the internal self]," as stated in such passages.
Here, Śrī Bharata himself is to be cited as the example;
for his [state] consisted of the desire to protect all living beings.
It has been described that the sattvic passion (kaṣāya) has its support in the *prārabdha* [karma] and remains hidden, as does love (*prema*).
Thus, among these three types of increasing love, one should understand that each preceding one is superior to the next,
even when it persists in some cases.

If, despite the body and other factors being material, an increase is observed in love— whether through its transformation or by its very nature— then that increase should be understood as arising solely from the intensity of the love itself;
and that [increase] belongs to the object of worship.

And through the distinction between being a part and the whole in relation to the Blessed One, there is an excellence of essential nature; and through the distinctions of servitude, friendship, and so forth,
as well as the distinctions of the sprout of love, love, and so forth, there is an excellence of magnitude— this is *prīti*.
We shall demonstrate this by unfolding it in the context [of the text].
Although direct realization alone may serve as the purpose of the person, nevertheless, within that very realization, however much there is of the Blessed Lord—

The experience of the quality of loveliness (priyatva) constitutes that much excellence. For that which is by nature the locus of unconditional love, even its direct realization is tantamount to non-realization without the experience of the quality of loveliness—
just as sugar is as good as not tasted by a diseased tongue in the absence of sweetness.
For this very reason, it was said by the venerable Ṛṣabhadeva:
"As long as there is no love for me, Vāsudeva..."
"One is not liberated so long as there is connection with the body" (BhP 5.5.6).

Therefore, the gradation of the greatness of a devotee is primarily determined by the gradation of their love alone. For this very reason, it is stated as the defining characteristic of such a person: "Those who have established friendship with Me, the Lord" (BhP 5.5.3). However, where...

Excess of love, direct realization, and the absence of impurities (*kaṣāya*) and so forth also exist; that [state] is supreme and primary. It should be understood that if even one of these factors is deficient, it is inferior.
Thus, those who [are devoted] to me, the Lord...
Those who have been described by such passages as "ity ādi" (beginning with 'thus') have not yet attained bodies as associates (*pārṣada*);
likewise, even when there is detachment from sense objects, they may still possess latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
Therefore, for the sake of discerning that:
Another section is introduced:
as the King said— "Now, tell me of the Bhāgavata, what its nature is and what its duty is for men."

"Tell me, for the sake of knowing him, what he enjoys, what he speaks, and by what characteristics one who is dear to the Blessed Lord is recognized. Immediately thereafter, tell me of the devotee (bhāgavata) for the purpose of that knowledge; and among those who speak, he who—
Declare what the intrinsic nature of Dharma is; and declare its practice, how it is performed and carried out.

The inquiry into the signs of mind, body, and speech is that which asks, "Speak that which you say," and so forth. Is this not so? For previously, it was stated: "Hearing the auspicious words of the one whose hand holds the discus" (BhP 11.2.37), and so on.
(Page 95) It is true that Śrī Kavirāja did not explicitly state those respective *liṅgas* by name in the text. Nevertheless,
by restating them, he [indicates] which *liṅgas* among those make the Lord so dear and supreme.
The meaning is: "Having distinguished those signs, tell me which one is free from the distinctions such as Madhyamaka and so forth.
To that, Śrī Hari replied:
"He who perceives the nature of the Blessed One within all beings [is liberated]."
"All beings [reside] within the Blessed Self"— this is the supreme devotee (bhāgavatottama).

Therein, by means of the mental signs (mānasa-liṅga) that are to be understood through the experience of each respective [being], he characterizes the great devotee (mahā-bhāgavata) with the words "In all beings," and so forth.

"One who observes such vows, whose heart melts with intense love born from chanting his own beloved’s name" (BhP 11.2.38)— according to the manner described in these words of the venerable poet— such a person,
being under the sway of that love which manifests through physical symptoms like the melting of the heart, laughter, and weeping, [transcends] the ether, the wind, and the fire (BhP 11.2.39).

The meaning is that, in the manner thus described and so forth, one should see— that is, experience— the state of the Self as the Blessed Lord within all beings, both sentient and insentient; that is, one experiences that very experience of the Blessed Lord and so forth which is desired by the Self.
Therefore, those elements manifest within one's own mind, the self; and that Blessed One who shines therein is experienced precisely as being dependent upon it.
This is the supreme devotee of the Lord (bhāgavatottama).
It is so; this very point was stated by the illustrious queens of Vraja: "The forest creepers and trees, as if manifesting Viṣṇu within themselves, are rich with flowers and fruits" (BhP 10.35.5).
Or rather, it refers to that state of being (*bhāva*) which is love (*prema*) for the Blessed Lord within one's own self.
One perceives that very [Self] within all beings, whether sentient or insentient; the rest is as before.
Therefore, by means of devotion born from the intellect which takes the form of the devotee as its locus...
The meaning is that he pays homage to them, as was previously stated in the passage beginning with "space" and "wind. And it has been said by those very same [verses]:
"Then, having understood that song of Mukunda..."
"Whose momentum was shattered by the god of love, as marked by their whirling movements" (BhP 10.21.15), and so forth;

and "O female osprey, you lament even though you are with the illustrious queens" (BhP 10.90.7), and so forth. In these passages, the knowledge of Brahman is not being described by the Bhāgavatas, nor is that knowledge or its fruit.

This is because such a state contradicts the status of being a *bhāgavata* (devotee of the Lord), both insofar as [the devotee] is to be abandoned and because there is no distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord; furthermore,

it would utterly contradict the supreme excellence [of such devotion] according to the characteristics of exclusive devotion (*aikāntika-bhakti*) taught in passages such as *ahaituky avyavahitā* [BhP 3.29.10].

Furthermore, it must be discerned that formless cognition of the Lord is untenable precisely because it contradicts the ultimate limit of the defining characteristics found in the concluding verse: "His lotus feet are held by the girdle of the necklaces of those who have surrendered" (BhP 11.2.53). [189]

Now, by means of the specific qualification of the mental *liṅga*, he defines the Madhyama Bhāgavata: "He who practices love toward the Lord, friendship toward those dependent on Him, compassion toward the ignorant, and equanimity toward His enemies—he is the Madhyama. [BhP 11.2.46]
He loves the Supreme Lord;
the meaning is that he becomes endowed with devotion toward Him. Likewise, he maintains friendliness—that is, the disposition of a kinsman—toward His devotees who are dependent upon Him.
One should maintain compassion for the foolish— those who do not recognize devotion to Him— and for those who are indifferent,
as was said by the venerable Prahlāda:
"Then I grieve for those deluded ones whose minds are turned away from that [Self], who carry the burden of sense-objects for the sake of illusory pleasure. Thus,
there is indifference toward those who hate the Self.
The meaning is that one maintains equanimity toward their hatred by remaining undisturbed in mind;
for even toward them, there is a presence of the element of compassion due to their state of childishness,
just as in the case of the illustrious Prahlāda.
Regarding Hiraṇyakaśipu:
even when there is agitation of the mind toward those who hate the Blessed One or a devotee of the Blessed One, the meaning is that there is no attachment to them.
In this state, there is a manifestation of compassion toward the ignorant and of equanimity toward enemies;
however, it is not a manifestation of love toward all [beings] as before. Therefore—
The state of being intermediate; or, even for the superior [person], by seeing that it is dependent upon that— [page 96]— that...
The arising of the bliss of vibration occurs especially [therein];
therefore, it is not prohibited that there may be even greater devotion toward that, but rather the necessity of its presence is enjoined everywhere.
It is likewise seen even in the case of the supreme goal:

"I do not value heaven nor liberation from rebirth for even half a moment as much as the company of those who associate with the Blessed One; what need is there to mention the worldly boons of mortals? (BhP 4.24.57).
Furthermore, from the *Rudragītā*: "Therefore, you are dear to us as the Blessed Lord himself, O Bhāgavatas" (BhP 4.25.30).
Thus, one whose mind is captivated by the qualities of Hari...
The Blessed One Bādarāyaṇi,
who is eternally dear to the devotees of Viṣṇu, studied this great narrative.
And from the words of Sūta,
"Thus," as well as from such passages as "the defilers of the Bhoja lineage" (BhP 10.1.24) and so forth, even hatred toward Bādarāyaṇi and others is observed therein.
However, for those of middling capacity, there is simply no attachment to that [form].
The distinction is that even for them, because he appears as their own chosen deity in his capacity as a Teacher of that kind, the manifestation of their own desired deity is not obstructed.
And by that very vision, even Śrī Uddhava and others offer salutations to Śrī Duryodhana and others;
for their nature is pure and designated by the term "Vasudeva."

"Just as in the words of Śrī Śiva beginning with, 'When a person goes there, he is unobstructed' (BhP 4.3.21), and as stated in the *Lakṣmaṇā-haraṇa*: 'He, having saluted the son of Ambikā... (BhP 10.68.17).

First, regarding "Duryodhana and so forth": in that context where one's own internal state alone manifests everywhere, it culminates even in those who are enemies of the Blessed Lord and others. And therein—
There is no impropriety in this, for those who have even a mere speck of the dust from His lotus feet— which must be purchased at the cost of millions of their own lives—
are agitated by the sight of misconduct toward them,
according to their own nature.

They think thus: "Oh, what kind of conscious being could there be who, in this Śrī Puruṣottama— who is the source of all bliss, the object of supreme love free from all limiting conditions, adorned with the jewels of true virtues that bring grace to the entire world, and whose nectar-like conduct culminates in the welfare of all— [would act otherwise]?"
Or one should not cultivate affection for a beloved person;
for the cause of hatred toward them is even more utterly beyond the scope of our intellectual faculties.
Therefore, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings, both the faultless and the faulty are indeed deeply attached to Him.
As it was said by the venerable Śuka:
O best of the Kurus, Nārada dwelt constantly in Dvāravatī, which was protected by the arms of Govinda, being intensely eager to worship Kṛṣṇa.

"O King, who indeed, possessing sense-faculties, would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda—the source of immortality worshipped by the best of the gods—when death is imminent from every side? [BhP 11.2.1-2].
Thus, by means of the physical sign consisting of the practice of the Lord's dharma, as well as some mental sign, [he recognized him].
He defines the lowest type: "He who strives with faith for worship of Hari in the image alone,
but not toward His other devotees, is considered a common (prākṛta) devotee" (BhP 11.2.47).

In the case of the worship of an image or a statue, and even more so among other devotees, there is a lack of love for the Lord and a lack of knowledge regarding the greatness of the devotee; consequently, the qualities of a devotee characterized by universal respect do not arise.

He is a common person whose devotion has only just begun, meaning his devotion has been initiated by his very nature; furthermore, this faith is not born from a definitive understanding of the meaning of the scriptures—
for one who perceives the self in the corpse-like body composed of the three humors.
"One whose own intellect is fixed on wife and children, who regards the earth as an object of worship, and who never at any time perceives water as a sacred bathing place" (BhP 10.84.13),
and so forth— such is the scriptural teaching.
Because it arises from knowledge;
therefore, as before, it is obtained solely through the traditional succession of the world.
And for this reason, [it is] not produced by one who lacks affection or who is unlearned in the scriptures.
The practitioner endowed with faith is to be known as the primary, while the inferior is the other.

Now, the commentary: furthermore, by means of eight verses, he states the characteristics of the superior one alone because of his preeminence; this begins with the words "Having taken... and so forth. To explain:
"He who, even while perceiving objects through the senses, neither feels aversion nor rejoices,
seeing this as the illusory power (*māyā*) of Viṣṇu— he indeed is the best of devotees (*bhāgavatottama*).
One whose mind is thus permeated by Him in the manner previously described does not, for that reason, grasp at objects through the senses.
The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even having grasped" (*gṛhītvāpi*) is as follows:
this entire universe (*viśvam*) is to be abandoned because it is a manifestation of *māyā*, which is the external power (*bahir-aṅga-śakti*). This is the meaning.
Here too, there is a confusion between the bodily and the mental.
Now, by means of purely mental signs, he speaks as far as the section extends: "He who [is the cause] of the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and intellect..."
Unbewildered by the conditions of saṃsāra— namely birth, death, hunger, fear, thirst, and suffering—
he is the foremost of Bhāgavatas through his remembrance of Hari.

He who, through remembrance of Hari, remains undeluded by the worldly attributes of the body and so forth—such as birth, death, and the like—is the foremost of the Bhāgavatas; and it is said in the Śrī Gītā:
"But those people of meritorious deeds whose sin has come to an end..."
"Those who are freed from the delusion of dualities, firm in their vows, worship Me. (Gītā 7.28) [193] Likewise:
"He in whose mind there is no arising of the seeds of desire and action..."
He who has Vāsudeva as his sole abode is indeed the best of Bhāgavatas. Here, "seeds" refers to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and Vāsudeva is the refuge therein.
Likewise:
"He for whom the sense of 'I' does not cling to this body because of his birth or actions, nor because of his class, stage of life, or caste—he indeed is dear to Hari. [BhP 11.2.51]
Birth refers to a noble family;
action refers to austerity and so forth;
and castes refer to those born in the natural order, such as the consecrated king (mūrdhābhiṣikta) and others.

The meaning is that he whose sense of "I" (ahambhāva) does not cling to this body through these [qualities], but rather clings only to the body as a means for the goal of service to the Lord— he is dear to Hari and is the best of devotees;
thus the connection is with what precedes.
Because it is the subject matter of the *Prakaraṇa*, the term "beloved of Hari" refers exclusively to a *bhāgavata*;
this is due solely to being a *bhāgavata*.
Likewise—

"He for whom there is no distinction between 'self' and 'other' regarding possessions or the self, who is equal toward all beings and tranquil—he indeed is the best of devotees. (BhP 11.2.52) Regarding "possessions," which are merely objects of the sense of "mine," he perceives no such thing as "this is mine" or "that belongs to another"; and regarding the "self," he perceives no such thing as "this is myself" or "that is another. In this context—
Just as in the case of wealth, it is merely one's own partiality toward oneself that is prohibited, not the distinction between individuals.
Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhagīratha:
"O best of kings, those who consider their own suffering to be the same as the suffering of others..."
Those men who are devoted to the dharma of the Blessed One are indeed the best of Vaiṣṇavas.
Furthermore—
[they are those whose resolve is unshaken even for the sake of the sovereignty of the three worlds].

He whose mindfulness does not waver for even half a moment or a blink of an eye from the lotus feet of the Blessed One— which are sought after by those who have not conquered their own selves, such as the gods— is indeed the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas.

"By the Immovable One, the cause of the three worlds"— the meaning is that He is difficult to attain even for the gods beginning with Brahmā and Īśvara, whose very selves are centered on Hari, the Unconquered, and who seek Him out. (Page 98) [197]
Moreover, movement [of the mind] due to a longing for sense objects would occur when there is intense torment caused by desire;
however, that is not possible when one finds bliss in the service of the Blessed One. Thus he says:
"The toes of the Blessed One’s feet, which possess great strides..."

When the heat has been dispelled from the heart by the moonlight of the jewel on his fingernail, how could that [heat] prevail again for those who approach him, any more than the sun's scorching heat can prevail when the moon has risen?
And those two feet possess wide-striding strides; their branches are the toes,
and their moonlight removes all distress.
Radiance; heat refers to the feverish distress caused by desire and so forth.
Likewise:
"He whose heart does not directly emit... [198]
"Even when invoked by those who are powerless, Hari is the destroyer of the multitude of sins.
And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) says: "He states the essence of all the aforementioned characteristics: 'He emits,' etc.;
it is Hari himself..."
He whose heart does not directly abandon or release [the Lord],
yet who— though even unwilling— destroys the flood of sins by merely uttering His name; he is [such a one].
Why, then, does he not abandon it?
For one whose lotus-feet are held fast in his heart by the cord of affection and bound there is called the foremost of the bhāgavatas.
This is the statement "it exists.
Here, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is the reason for the impossibility of desire and so forth, because direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) occurs at a subsequent time.

Likewise, by the statement beginning with "even when Hari is addressed involuntarily," it is asserted that for one who possesses such affection, when He is glorified at all times through supreme absorption (parāveśa), there will be an even more complete destruction of the multitude of sins.
And it has been said: "For those who are weary of this world and desire [liberation], there is freedom from fear from any quarter" (BhP 2.1.11), and so forth.
Therefore, in both ways, even the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of evil do not exist for them.
It is implied that he desired to remain;
by this, having also pointed out the verbal indicative mark (*vācika-liṅga*), the answer to what was stated in [BhP 11.2.42] has been given.

In this section, although the verses beginning with "gṛhītvāpi" (BhP 11.2.43) describe the characteristics of the supreme bhāgavatas, it should be understood that these form both a single composite statement and individual, separate statements.
This is because all those respective characteristics are included within the supreme devotee who possesses such mastery over the Blessed One,
and because in some cases only two or three characteristics are observed.

In that regard, concerning the state of non-separation from speech, by means of each individual characteristic found within each respective statement— such as "this very one [is present] in all beings" and so forth— the Great Bhāgavata is characterized.
Through those various qualities...
By the passage beginning with "it spreads out as the cause," there is the presentation of the essence of all characteristics;
and therein, by the passage beginning with "by the remembrance of Hari," remembrance is stated as the cause.
It should be established that this final sentence is an elaboration of that very [point];
for this reason, [the text] says "each one is a supreme Bhāgavata."
Even the initial restatement is consistent;
for in the case of separate sentences where a direct connection with the Blessed One is not heard, [the restatement serves its purpose].

In this regard, it should be understood either by the force of the word *bhāgavata* itself or by the force of the context; or else, words such as "by the recollection found in preceding and subsequent verses" should be supplied. Thus, in this view, the status of being the supreme *bhāgavata* is merely relative to others.
In this regard, the sequence for the superiority of the latter is as follows: "only in worship" (arcāyām eva),
and "not by whose birth or deeds" (na yasya janma-karmābhyām).
"There is no 'self' nor 'other' for him"; "even though grasped by the senses"; "the body, the senses, and the vital breath."
There is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of this;
however, so that there may be no delusion caused by it, this sprout of newly born love should be one whose latent impression has been rendered unconscious (*mūrcchita-saṃskāra*).
Likewise, "not for the seeds of desire and action" is itself explained by the phrase "even for the sake of the splendor of the three worlds.
This indeed is the ultimate (*naiṣṭhikī*) devotion.
The recollection of the dhruva is called "meditation" (dhyāna);
even the sprout of his love has arisen such that it cannot be obscured.
Otherwise, there would be a continuous state of such recollection;
for this person is one whose defilements have been shaken off and whose sprouts of affection have been eradicated.
Hereafter, [he attains] direct realization—
Because [this love] arises from affection for the Lord and those dependent upon Him,
its threefold nature— consisting of friendliness and so forth—
is caused solely by devotion; therefore, it should not be understood as being in a state of spiritual impurity (kaṣāya).
The explanation of the phrase "toward all beings," which indicates great love from which all impurities have been shaken off, is the word "he releases" (*visṛjati*);
[this refers to] the five purificatory rites beginning with *tāpa*.
A Brahmin who performs the rites of worship and knows the fivefold purpose is remembered as a great Bhāgavata.
Thus says the statement from the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*:
"The greatness of those devoted solely to the path of worship (*arcana-mārga*) is to be understood as existing only in the midst [of the hierarchy], because their love is not yet perfected."

In this regard, the five sacraments beginning with *tāpa* (scorching) and so forth are shown in that very same place by the passage beginning: "Scorching, the sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*), as well as the name" (*Padma Purāṇa* 6.226.6).
Furthermore, the status of being the performer of the rite of new worship (*navejyā-karma*) is seen through this statement.
Worship consists of the recitation of mantras, yoga, sacrifice, salutation,
the chanting of the Name, service, and likewise the marking of one's limbs with His symbols.
"O auspicious one, the worship of Him is divided into nine types of sacrifice (*ijyā*).
This ninefold sacrificial rite is traditionally taught as the constant duty of the Brahmins.
Regarding the possession of the five goals of life: "The Blessed Lord is that supreme state; He is that substance; He is..."
The knowledge of the five principles consists of the mantra, the individual soul (jīvātman), and [the other three];
and that is explained in the Śrī-Hayashīrṣa,
which is here written in brief:
Kṛṣṇa alone is the Supreme Lord, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
his eyes are as wide as lotuses, and his hair is dark and curly.
The Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, by his divine play, is naturally and firmly embraced by the Goddess who is the very nature of consciousness and possesses a vast splendor like that of gold.
"Everlasting, omnipresent, full, all-pervading, the cause of all,

the secret of the Vedas, profound in essence, and the source of manifold powers— such is the Person (Nara)," and so forth. Therefore, I shall now describe the reality of the abode (sthāna-tattva), which is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) and imperishable.
Consisting of pure sattva, it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns and moons.

"Manifestly composed of the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss (sac-cid-ānanda), the support of all beings, and devoid of any dissolution"—thus it begins.
"O Brahman, listen to the reality of substance; I shall explain it to you in brief."
There, the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpa-pādapa) bestow all enjoyments.
The creepers become such as they are, and their existence is likewise such; so too are the fragrance, the form, the quality of taste, the substance, and whatever flowers and the like there may be.
And because of the absence of all parts to be discarded, that indeed becomes the essence in the form of nectar;
for the bark, the seed, and whatever part is solid are the portions to be discarded.
Know all that to be composed of the elements, for it is not made of non-existence;
O Brahmin, through the conjunction with taste, that which is elemental becomes flavorful.
"Therefore, O Brahmin, the *rasa* is to be realized; the *rasa* would be all-pervading and supreme.
A material substance possessing *rasa* would here take on the form of *rasa*.
Thus, in this context, the state of being the signified and the state of being the signifier belong to both the deity and its mantra.
"O Brahmin, when investigated by those who know reality, [the world] is said to be non-different [from Brahman]," and so forth.
Just as droplets arise from a wave upon the union of wind and ocean, being of the same nature as it and yet enveloped by its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
O Brahman, from that embrace of both, as well as from the Self, thousands of beings were born everywhere, in the form of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
This and other such [statements] also apply;
however, regarding the manifestations of the Blessed Lord and similar matters, one should understand that there is also some further distinction according to the respective scriptures of worship.

And this definition of the *jīva* has been formulated as being accompanied by its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), in accordance with the verse beginning, "The emergence [of the soul] is not possible" (BhP 10.87.31).
But as for that which is without limiting adjuncts:
the power of Viṣṇu is declared to be the supreme (parā), and that which is called the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the subordinate (aparā).
A third power is recognized, which consists of ignorance and karma.
Thus, according to the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "Furthermore:
'Know this other nature of Mine, which is distinct from this, to be the higher.'"
"O mighty-armed one, it is that which has become the life-force by which this world is sustained" (Gītā 7.5);
and likewise, according to the Gītā: "An eternal portion of My very self, having become the individual soul, exists in the world of living beings" (Gītā 15.7). Furthermore—
That which is the peripheral form of consciousness, having emerged from self-awareness,
is colored by the passion for the qualities (guṇas).
That is called the living being (jīva).
Thus it should be understood according to the Śrī Nārada Pañcarātra.

// 11.2 // Hari, the Lord of Yogins, [bestowed upon] Nimi // 187–198 // [199] Thus, those among the devotees of the Blessed One whose impurities and so forth were dissolved, and who were distinguished by their greatness— being distinguished as true devotees— [directed their worship] toward Hari alone in his embodied form (arcā) among those very distinctions of the true devotees.
By such passages as these, some [liberated souls] who have attained varying degrees of excellence through the relative manifestation of their respective qualities have been shown.
Now, with five verses, he describes their gradation also according to the degree of their spiritual practice (*sādhana*).
Therein, he describes the lowest type of practitioner, who possesses mixed devotion, with three verses: "Compassionate, free from malice toward all embodied beings, and patient..."
He whose essence is truth, whose nature is irreproachable, who is equanimous, and who benefits all beings.
One whose intellect is unassailed by desires, self-controlled, gentle, pure, possessing nothing, free from longing,
moderate in eating, peaceful, steadfast, and taking refuge in Me— that sage is truly wise.

He is vigilant, profound in nature, steadfast, and has conquered the sixfold group of senses; he is free from pride yet bestows honor upon others, capable, friendly, compassionate, and wise. (BhP 11.11.29–31) And the commentary states: "Compassionate" means one who cannot endure the suffering of others.
He who harbors no malice toward any embodied beings whatsoever; he who is patient and forgiving;
and he whose essence, stability, or strength is truth.
One whose nature is blameless is free from envy and the like; one who is equal toward pleasure and pain,
according to one's ability.
He is a non-doer of anything whatsoever;
his mind is unshaken by sensual desires;
he is tamed and self-restrained.
One whose senses are turned outward, who is gentle with a non-hardened mind,
who possesses nothing, and who is without grasping.
Free from desire,
devoid of ostentatious activity,
moderate in eating, and light in diet.
Peaceful, with his internal organ restrained, steadfast in his own duty, taking refuge in Me, having Me as his sole support, he is a sage,
characterized by the habit of contemplation.
Heedful means attentive;
profound-souled means free from change.

Possessed of fortitude, he is not miserable even in adversity; having conquered the six qualities, he is one by whom these six waves—sorrow and delusion, old age and death, hunger and thirst—have been overcome;
and being free from pride, he does not desire honor.
One who bestows honor upon others, who is healthy, skilled in awakening others,
friendly, and free from deceit.
The compassionate one acts solely out of compassion, and not through the greed for worldly gain; "the poet" means one who possesses perfect knowledge—this is the meaning here.
In this context, "taking refuge in me" is the predicate.

Later, in the phrase "and he, O best of beings" (*sa ca sattama*), the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that just as the previously mentioned one was the best of beings, so too is this one the best; thus, his manifestation is exactly of such a nature.
The "best" (sattama) is characterized as one whose feet are his only refuge.
Now, he describes the "middling" type, who practices unmixed, direct devotion:
"Having thus understood both virtues and faults, even those ordained by me and others..."
"He who, having abandoned all duties, worships Me—he indeed is the best of beings.
And the commentary states: "Even he who, having abandoned his own duties as enjoined by Me in the form of the Vedas, worships Me—he too is the best of beings, just as previously described."
Is it due to ignorance or from atheism? No;

for in the practice of dharma, one should abandon qualities such as the purification of the mind (*sattva-śuddhi*) and so forth that belong to the opposite side, or rather, [one should do so] through devotion (*bhakti*).
This refers to abandoning [the world] with firm resolve through the cessation of one's worldly duties;
as stated in the *Nārāyaṇa-vyūha-stava* of the *Hayaśīrṣa-pañcarātra*:
"Salutations again and again even to those who have renounced worldly duties and wealth, who have come under the influence of devotion to Viṣṇu, and who meditate upon the Supreme Self.
Here, the explanation is as follows: even if there is an absence of the connection with those various qualities within one's own self, nevertheless—

Thus, having understood the qualities such as compassion and the like, as well as their opposites as defects, according to the manner previously described, and having determined them as things to be abandoned or adopted, yet— among those very qualities— even though they were prescribed for me, all my own duties characterized as obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*), pertaining to [caste and stage of life] (*varṇāśrama*)...

Having abandoned even the prescribed duties and the knowledge that characterizes them, because they obstruct exclusive devotion to Me, one should worship Me; such a person is the most excellent (sattama).
By the use of the word "ca" (and), it is implied that the previously mentioned [duties] are also to be abandoned.

The term "sattama" (the best) indicates that even in the absence of those specific qualities, the latter is equal to the former; therefore, he who, having attained those various qualities, yet worships Me alone by abandoning [mere] knowledge of dharma, is indeed the *parama-sattama* (the supreme best).
Thus, the superiority of the individual whose devotion is directed toward no other than Me is shown over the former.
In this regard, the section from the twelfth chapter of the Śrī Gītā beginning with "One who is not hateful toward any beings" (Gītā 12.13) should also be consulted;
by the term "best of beings" (sattama), that same equanimity is indicated here as well.

It has been shown that [such a person] exists. Let it be granted for now that there is the existence of one who follows good conduct and is devoted to Him; however, even by the mere fact of being devoted to no other deity, the goodness of even a person of bad conduct is established for another noble person.
In passages such as "Even if one is of very evil conduct" (Gītā 9.30),
no such characteristic was raised during the discussion on the association with the virtuous; that is indeed because of the nature of such association for devotion.
The term "unmukha" is used with the intention that [the mind] is not applied [to worldly objects].
As it was said by the venerable Prahlāda: "By association with saintly devotees... (BhP 7.7.25).
In this context, "sādhu" refers to right conduct (*sad-ācāra*).
Thus, the gradation between devotion to the path of injunction and devotion to the Lord has been explained.

In that very context, the superiority of the latter is shown by its non-difference [from the former]. Furthermore, the threefold nature of the path of worship (arcana-mārga) is obtained from the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa.
In that context, "greatness" refers to the five formative forces beginning with suffering and so forth; "middleness" is—

"In this context— 'The branding, the sectarian mark, as well as the name, the mantra, and fifthly the sacrifice; these five indeed are the purificatory rites that are the cause of supreme single-minded devotion'—
the state of being the youngest [is mentioned]."

The defining characteristic of a Vaiṣṇava here is said to consist of bearing the conch, the discus, and other such marks, as well as the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), and indeed, the act of paying homage to Him.
Thus, at this point (page 102):
Now, he says that he who is non-dual through the mere state of pure servitude, friendship, and so forth, is the most excellent of all:
"Whether they know Me or do not know Me— whatever My extent may be and whatever My nature—
I consider those who worship Me with undivided devotion to be My most excellent devotees. (BhP 11.11.33) "Whatever" means that which is unlimited by space, time, and so forth.
And whoever— whether knowing Me or not as I am, the all-pervading Self whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss— worships Me alone with undivided devotion, O Lord of Vraja...

The meaning is that those whose object of devotion (*ālambana*) is Nandana, and who worship Him through one particular state such as servitude (*dāsya*) and so forth, never worship by any other means;
they alone, I consider to be the most devoted (*bhaktatama*). For this very reason...

In the fourth [chapter], it was requested even by the illustrious Lords of Yoga: "O Lord, there is no other dearer to You than this [world]; O Soul of the Universe, one who would perceive anything as separate from Your Self does not exist."
"Nevertheless, O affectionate one, favor those who approach You with devotion and with undivided service. Thus it is said in the Śrī Gītā.
I shall declare to you in its entirety this knowledge along with realized wisdom,
by knowing which nothing further remains here to be known.
Having said this, He spoke:
"Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind,
intellect, and ego— thus is My nature divided eightfold."
O mighty-armed one, know that this nature of Mine which has been described here is inferior; but know My other, higher nature, which is the soul (jīva), by which this entire world is sustained.
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire world.

"O Dhanañjaya, there is nothing whatsoever higher than Me; all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread. (Gītā 7.7) Thus, His status as the cause of the universe is established through His own powers known as *pradhāna* (primordial matter), *jīva* (the individual soul), and *akṣara* (the imperishable). That—
By stating that the world is non-different from Him because it consists of His power (śakti),
and by declaring that He Himself is superior to those two and is their substratum, he has taught his own innate knowledge.
And by way of this incidental discussion, there is also knowledge of the true nature of the individual soul (*jīva*). Such a person,
being a knower who contemplates my own nature and my greatness, surpasses the wise devotees, the distressed devotees, and others, and thus becomes dear to me.
Thus he spoke at the conclusion:
"O Arjuna, best of the Bharatas, four kinds of virtuous people worship Me: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom."
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is ever-disciplined, and who is devoted to the One alone, is preeminent;
for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.
"All these are indeed noble; however, the man of knowledge is My very Self—this is My view.
For he, being disciplined in mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal" (Gītā 7.16–18).
From this, the meaning is as follows:
But he who perceives living beings within you—the Self of all—knows them as non-different from you precisely because they are your power; he does not perceive them as separate or independent.
From him [comes] liberation.

Even though You have no one dearer than them, nevertheless, O Vatsala, O lover of Your servants, favor those who worship You with the attitude of being masters over their servants by means of that very same unfailing, innate devotion which is their other mode of conduct;
for, by virtue of the context, it is understood that "us" refers to the devotees who possess knowledge.

Now, in the root verse, regarding the phrase "whether knowing or not knowing," the status of knowledge and ignorance as things to be rejected or accepted is negated. In the phrase "the most devoted ones" (*bhaktatamāḥ*), [the author] specifically bypasses the word *sat* found in the preceding sentence. (Page 103)
By the specific mention of the word "devotee" (*bhakta*), it is intended here that the excellence of devotion’s essential nature (*svarūpa*) is established in this very context.
By the statement "they are my opinion," it is indicated that my particular approval lies specifically in this point.
Because such [a meaning] has not been previously stated;
for this very reason, even transcending the contextually established singular number, the plural "ye te" was employed out of reverence alone.

Therefore, what need is there to mention those whose love is established through their very being? This is the intended meaning. Their manifestation of devotional service through their being will be described hereafter.
This should be understood as the description of those following through attachment (rāgānugā). Śrī Bhagavān:
[200–201] [202] Indeed, these Vaiṣṇavas, being virtuous, are distinguished and described according to their greatness and their state of pure goodness.
Regarding the gradations within the mere sixfold division, that which has not yet been distinguished shall be analyzed later in the exposition of the specific varieties of *bhakti*.
Others, however, are Vaiṣṇavas by virtue of their own particular circles.

In that regard, with respect to those who perform ritual actions, it is as stated in the Skanda Purāṇa, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhagīratha: "Those for whom life is for the sake of dharma, and sexual union is for the sake of progeny..."
"Those men who perform [these acts] for the sake of the foremost of brāhmaṇas should be known as Vaiṣṇavas. And so forth.
In this context, the term "Vaiṣṇava" is understood to mean that whatever is performed is done solely with the understanding that it is the command of Śrī Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
He who does not deviate from the duties of his own caste, who maintains an even mind toward himself, friends, and enemies,
and who neither seizes nor harms anything, is truly exalted.
"Know him to be a devotee of Viṣṇu whose mind is thus established. (ViP 3.7.20).
But when [all actions] are offered unto Him, one's status as a Vaiṣṇava is all the more complete;
as it is said in the Pātālakhaṇḍa regarding Vaiśākha—
Regarding greatness:

"He whose life is for the sake of dharma, and whose dharma is solely for the sake of Hari, and whose days and nights are for the sake of merit—him I consider a Vaiṣṇava on this earth. (Padma Purāṇa 5.94.8) Thus it is said.
Likewise, among the followers of Śiva, in comparison with that [Vaiṣṇava standard], it is stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya*:
"Those who proceed with an equal mind toward Śiva, the Supreme Lord, and Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self—they indeed are the best of Bhāgavatas. (NārP 1.5.72) Thus it is said.
In the assemblies of the Śaivas, his status as the supreme Bhāgavata is well-known; thus it has been stated.
However, in the Vaiṣṇava Tantras, there is indeed a censure of him:
"He who [compares] the Lord Nārāyaṇa with deities such as Brahmā and Rudra..."
"One who views [all] merely with equanimity would certainly be a heretic.

Thus, although there are many such divisions among them, through the variation in their power, the variation in their compassion, and the variation in the latent impressions of devotion arising from the association with the virtuous, [there occurs] the swiftness of time and the nature [of liberation].
Devotion arises from these two excellences;
likewise, knowledge and the object of knowledge arise from association with the wise.
Although it is devotion alone that is to be expressed here as the primary subject, association with its devotees is mentioned as the cause thereof.

Even though that very [object] is to be indicated by implication (lakṣayitavya) through devotion to the expressed meaning (abhidheya), nevertheless, for the sake of its examination, a restatement (anuvāda) of each respective [point] is made.
In that regard, first of all, by means of that which arises from the connection with each respective [point]...

Through faith, a taste for various discourses, and so forth, one attains a direct vision of the Blessed One; by the very continuity of those [discourses], a taste arises for the specific manifestations of the Blessed One who are to be worshipped in each case, as well as for the specific paths of worship associated with them.
And thereafter, when there is a desire to know the specific details,
one performs the act of hearing from a venerable teacher— whether that teacher be approached as such once or repeatedly.

That [hearing] consists of the ascertainment of the meaning through the methods of the introduction and conclusion (*upakrama-upasaṃhāra*), and so forth, as well as the removal of non-belief (*asambhāvanā*) and misconception (*viparīta-bhāvanā*).
Through the excellence of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), one personally performs reflection (manana) in the form of investigating that [truth];
consequently, there arises a form of faith such as this: "When the Blessed One is manifested in everything, he thus shines eternally and everywhere."

In that regard, however, through this first-born *rucyā* (inclination), which possesses the excellence of being determined by the fulfillment of one's own desired goals and so forth, that very *śraddhā* (faith) shines forth.

In this regard, although it is possible for the culmination of excellence to occur in only one place and not everywhere, nevertheless, because some do not know what is superior to that, a faith consisting of such a notion can indeed arise even elsewhere; thus should the specific path of devotion be explained. That being so:

Once [the truth] is established, for the sake of knowledge and realized wisdom (*jñāna-vijñāna*), the various paths of meditation (*upāsanā*) characterized by profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*) are practiced; thus has the path for those whose primary focus is inquiry been shown.
However, for those whose primary focus is devotion (*ruci*), such dependence on inquiry does not arise.
However, this [process] consists precisely of a longing for the company of the saintly, the narration and hearing of their pastimes,
and the repetition of hearing and so forth, characterized by faith.

The path has been shown previously in such passages as, "For one who desires to hear and has faith" (BhP 1.2.16), and it is also to be seen in such passages as, "From association with the virtuous, there arises knowledge of My power" (BhP 3.25.22).

However, for those whose desire for devotion is characterized by love (*prīti*), the path centered on aesthetic relish (*ruci*) is indeed superior; it is not like the path centered on inquiry (*vicāra*) for those in whom such relish has not yet arisen. As was said by Prahlāda:
Neither these qualities nor the possessors of qualities— the Mahat and all others beginning with the mind, including the gods and mortals—
know You, O Wide-striding One, for they are all subject to a beginning and an end.
Having reflected thus, the wise desist from sound.

Therefore, O most worthy of honor, what need is there for the sixfold service consisting of salutation, acts of praise, worship, ritual action, mindfulness at your feet, and listening to your stories, since all these are dispelled by your very attendance?
"May people obtain devotion directed toward those who have attained the state of the supreme *paramahaṃsas*. Here, "action" (*karma*) refers to service (*paricaryā*),
and "remembrance of action" (*karma-smṛtiḥ*) refers to the recollection of the Lord's pastimes (*līlā*).
The phrase "at the feet" is connected everywhere as that which manifests devotion;
thus, in both cases, he is the guru who instructs in the method of worshipping Him.

For such a person, the former teacher of the sacred word (*śravaṇa-guru*) alone becomes [the primary one], because he has been obtained as such; even though there may have been many former teachers, it is generally among them that—
Thus, one or the other is preferred for the very same reason as before: because there will be many [candidates], only one person— the master of the glorious mantra— will be appointed.
Now, the authorities on this matter are as follows:
regarding the specific manifestation of that [Lord],
there is the inclination expressed in the passage, "One should worship the Great Person with a form that is pleasing to oneself" (BhP 11.3.48).
In the beginning, [the sacrifice] was performed by Śrīmad Āvirhotra and others;
and there is a specific inclination toward worship—my sacrifice is threefold: Vedic, Tantric, and Mixed.
"One should worship me according to the very same procedure desired for the three [deities]"— this was intended by the Blessed Lord in such passages as these.
Now, He speaks of the teacher of hearing:

Therefore, one who desires to know the supreme good should take refuge in a guru who is proficient in the Veda, which is the verbal Brahman, as well as in the Supreme Brahman, and who has taken shelter in tranquility.
(BhP 11.3.22) "In the verbal Brahman" means in the Veda through the application of inquiry into its intended meaning.
One who is proficient through direct perception (*aparokṣānubhava*) in the Supreme Brahman manifested in forms such as the Blessed Lord, and has likewise attained firm devotion (*niṣṭhā*) therein;
as was stated by Śrī Nārada at the conclusion of the *Śrī Purañjana* narrative and other texts:
"He is indeed the most beloved Self, from whom there is not even the slightest fear;
he who knows this is truly wise, and he who is wise is the Guru, Hari. Thus [it is said].
Śrī Prabuddha [taught] Nimi. 202. [203]
In this regard, there is a specific point in the *Brahma-vaivarta*:
"The speaker is proclaimed to be of two kinds: with passion (*sarāga*) and free from passion (*nīrāga*).
The passionate one is greedy and lustful; therefore, what he has said should not touch the heart."
He indeed gives instruction but does not perform an examination;
that which is taught without examination leads to the ruin of the world.
Furthermore:
Without examining the lineage, character, or conduct of another teacher,
one who seeks the hearing [of the teachings] and so forth should attend upon a master who is full of flavor and an ocean of essence.
And its quality of being full of aesthetic flavor (*sārasatva*) and so forth has been indicated in that very same [work] elsewhere:
"Even one who is possessed by desire, anger, and the like, even one who is miserly, and even one who is despondent—upon hearing him, he blossoms; such a speaker is the supreme Guru. (p. 105)
Due to the absence of such a guru, some resort to many [teachers] out of a desire to understand various methods of reasoning;
for instance:
"Indeed, knowledge from a single guru would not be well-established or fully complete."
"This Brahman is indeed proclaimed as non-dual by many sages. (BhP 11.9.31).
This is clear. 11.9. Śrī Dattātreya [said] to Yadu: 203 [204].
In that regard, for those in whom *ruci* (inclination) is predominant, there is hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth.
There, day after day, I listened with favor to the captivating narrations of Kṛṣṇa as they were being sung;
and as I listened to them with faith at every step, [my heart was transformed].

Having attained inclusion within that [devotion], consisting of knowledge, action, and their ancillaries,

The self, following that [devotion], consists of hearing, chanting, and so forth;
for in passages such as "Hearing and chanting about Viṣṇu" (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.8.38), it is specifically the hearing of Viṣṇu and the chanting of Viṣṇu that are intended.
Because they are intended [to be expressed], they are not established through superimposition; on the contrary, even in the case of those who merely imitate them, such as fools or the insane,

Just as Śrī Prahlāda observed a fast on the fourteenth day of the month of Nṛsiṃha in his previous birth, and just as the hawk that entered the mouth of a dog performed circumambulation of the Lord’s temple.

In that regard, if "sincerity" (akaitavatva) consists merely in having the capacity for attaining the state of devotion through a connection with one who is devoted to both superimposition (āropa) and attachment (saṅga), then it is sincerity; likewise, if it consists in being a subordinate factor that does not expect results for oneself or others, then it is sincerity. If being an accessory (parikaratva) implies being deceitful,

Absence of deceit (*akaitavatva*) consists in not having regard for any ulterior motive and being an auxiliary to both action (*karma*) and knowledge (*jñāna*); conversely, having regard for such a motive constitutes deceit (*sakaitavatva*). This very [quality] was previously described as "absence of deceit" (*akaitava*) and "possessionlessness" (*akiñcana*), and it is *dharma*.
In the verse "projjhita-kaitavo'tra paramaḥ" (BhP 1.1.2), one should understand that this [devotion] is the authority for its being of both kinds.

Regarding the phrase "viḍambanam" (a mockery):

thus, for this very purpose, there is a censure of both types of action—those performed with desire and those free from desire—in such passages as, "Even the state of being free from action (naiṣkarmya), if devoid of devotion to Acyuta... (BhP 1.5.12).

"One should offer that to Nārāyaṇa" (BhP 11.2.36).

"In the manner described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:

as follows: (page 112)

"Those very same things, when conceived as directed toward another, lead to the destruction of the self.

"Vāsudeva himself, meditating thus and having his impurities crushed by his own skill, while the oblations were being taken up by the Adhvaryu priests, that sacrificer meditated upon those gods who partake in the sacrifice as being within the limbs of the Supreme Person. Regarding the unseen principle (*apūrva*), there are two positions among the Mīmāṃsakas.

"Or else, a result consisting of subtle power indeed arises.

Now, if it is held that the deity is a subordinate factor (aṅga) and the ritual act is the primary element, then [dharma] would reside in the agent.

Now, since ritual action has the deity as its primary element and is for the purpose of propitiating the deity, it is logical that the *apūrva* (unseen potency) takes the form of the deity's grace; thus, it is appropriate for the *apūrva* to have the deity as its substratum, just as in the case of the *apūrva* resulting from acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).

[The question is: Why does [the sacrifice] produce an *apūrva* (unseen potency) that has Vāsudeva as its substratum, rather than having rice and other materials as its substratum? It is said in reply:

Since the primary agency belongs to the instigator by virtue of being the initiator, the *apūrva* resides only in that [instigator], and not in the sacrificer who is impelled by him.

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) would be the substrata of the *apūrva*.
He states that very point with the words "in the direct perceiver.

The reason for [his] status as the Supreme Deity is that,

In this context, it is understood that because Viṣṇu is the principal subject (*aṅgin*), his worship is also considered a fault.

Because they have that alone as their life-force.

By means of knowledge through which reality is seen, by powerful dispassion,

In this world, Prakṛti, though being burned day and night by the Puruṣa, gradually vanishes like the fire-drill wood (araṇi) when the fire has been extracted from it. That which is the cause is not the fruit; that which is the cause is not the motivator—by means of such desireless action.
