the word "excessively" (ati) [here] signifies the abandonment of results such as the infliction of pain upon living beings.
The purpose is to accept the leaves and other parts as limbs of the living being;
my abode is my image and so forth; and by means of the contemplation of Me as the inner controller within all beings.
By means of goodness,
fortitude, non-attachment, and dispassion; non-violence, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession are the restraints (yamas).
Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (niyamas).
[One should contemplate] the internal self as the Self...
The scripture of discernment;
by means of *nirahaṅkriyā*, that is, by being free from pride; [the state] of one who follows my dharma. My...
The disposition of a person who practices the Dharma is characterized by such statements as:
"My qualities, which consist merely of what has been heard, directly approach me simply through the hearing of my qualities" (BhP 3.29.11). This is the definition stated therein.
The meaning is that one attains the recollection of the fixed [Dhruva];
here, through internal hearing and so forth, there is also a state of being mixed with knowledge.
// 3.29 // Śrī Kapiladeva // 229 // [230] Now,
liberated by his own splendor from the elements consisting of what is seen and heard mixed with knowledge—
A person who is my devotee should become fully satisfied with transcendental knowledge and empirical consciousness.
By "seen" is meant the objects of this world and the next;
by "his own splendor" is meant the power of discrimination.
// 6.16 // Śrī-Saṅkarṣaṇa [meditates upon] Citraketu. [230] [231] Now, an example of one who has attained the state of absolute oneness (*kevala-svarūpa*) is cited.
Among them, there are worshippers who possess desires and those who desire absolute oneness (*kaivalya*).
It is designated as possessing various qualities by virtue of the qualities of its respective volitions (*saṅkalpa*).
Consequently, desireful [meditation] is of two kinds: *tāmasī* and *rājasī*. The former is as follows:
"He who, having intended violence, hypocrisy, or even envy, being impetuous and possessing a distorted vision, should direct his disposition toward Me— he is tāmasa.
[BhP 3.29.8] "Abhisandhāya" means having formed a resolve (saṅkalpya).

"Aggressive" means full of anger. "Having a divided vision" means that, as if toward oneself, one views everywhere—that is, wherever there is pleasure or pain—the respective deity as being devoid of compassion; this is the meaning. [232]
An example of the contrary [type] is as follows:
(p. 117) "He who, with a sense of duality, worships me in an image or the like, aiming for sense objects, fame, or even power—that worship is rājasic. [BhP 3.29.9]
"Separately"—meaning one whose state of being, or longing, is directed toward objects and the like elsewhere than in Me, and not toward Me—this demonstrates the cause of being rajasic.
Now, that which desires liberation alone is indeed sattvic; it is as follows: [233]
"Aiming for the accomplishment of ritual action, or offering it to another,
or performing sacrifice with the thought 'I am the sacrificer' and 'the sacrifice is to be performed'— such a sense of separateness is *sāttvika*.
(BhP 3.29.10) Now, that very devotion (*bhakti*) for the sake of which these various types of devotion have been described as superior is...
Because she has no desire for even the slightest [object], she is described as being free from desire, devoid of qualities, absolute, and established in her own essential nature.
She alone has been previously designated as "possessing nothing" (akiñcana), standing above all others. Regarding her, he says:
"Merely by hearing of my qualities, in me who dwells in the secret cave of all..."
The movement of the mind is uninterrupted, like the flow of the Ganges' waters into the ocean.
The characteristic of devotion-yoga (bhakti-yoga) that is beyond the material modes has indeed been declared:
it is that devotion to the Supreme Person which is uncaused and uninterrupted.
Even when offered the states of residing in the same world (sālokya), possessing the same power (sārṣṭi), proximity (sāmīpya), having the same form (sārūpya), or even oneness (ekatva),
people do not accept them without my service.
That very path is declared to be the ultimate yoga known as *bhakti-yoga*, by which one transcends the three modes of nature (*tri-guṇa*) and attains my own state of being.
This occurs merely by hearing of my qualities, and not with the intention of accomplishing some other goal therein. Prākṛta...

In Me— who rest within that cave which is beyond the range of all the sense organs composed of the *guṇas*, abiding there in secrecy and immovability— resides that movement of the mind which is uninterrupted and impossible to divert toward other objects.
Regarding the uninterruptedness [of the stream], "yathā" provides the illustrative example. The term "gati" (movement) is drawn from the preceding context because it requires that antecedent.
"Lakṣaṇa" means the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

Now, what is to be said regarding that hearing of its qualities (*guṇa-śruti*), since it cannot be designated in either of two ways—because there is no other intended object (*uddeśya*) and because it lacks the nature of a mental process?
To this he says: "It is causeless (*ahaitukī*)," [meaning] without seeking for a fruit (*phalānusandhāna*).

"Uninterrupted" means not separated; because it is established as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it is direct in form, rather than being mediated by superimposition (*āropa*) and thus characterized by an interval.
Such devotion (*bhakti*)—which is merely service through the ears and other senses—is [the means] for that [attainment].
The meaning is "its own nature.

Because the fact that the movement of the mind is without cause and so forth is established by the word *mātra* and by the word *avicchinna*, there is no need for a separate construction [of these terms].

This is because, in passages such as "the agent who is sattvic and unattached" (BhP 11.25.25) and so forth, the quality-less nature of the actions and other factors resting upon Him is established by statements such as "quality-less and taking refuge in Me" (BhP 11.25.25).

All qualities resort to me, who am devoid of qualities and independent; likewise, qualities such as equanimity and non-attachment resort to me, who am their well-wisher, beloved, and the Self. (BhP 11.13.40)

Thus, because it is heard here that even their qualities are non-material (aprākṛta), it specifically demonstrates that [the state] is indeed causeless (ahaitukī). "My people" (janā madīyāḥ) [means those who have attained liberation];
even *sālokya* and so forth, though being granted (*dīyamāna*), [are not desired by them].
"He takes": if they take [it] without serving me, then they take it solely for the purpose of serving me, and not for that [other] purpose; this is the meaning. *Sārṣṭi* means equal sovereignty.
Oneness consists in union with the Blessed One (*bhagavat-sāyujya*) and union with Brahman (*brahma-sāyujya*);
these two [result] because the self has become absorbed into that.
The sense is that because there is no purpose in continued practice, its non-occurrence is indeed necessary.
Therefore, the meaning is that [the self] itself becomes liberation (apavarga) by virtue of having an ultimate fruit.
This is because of such passages as "they do not reckon [it] as ultimate," and because that [state] is well-known as the ultimate dissolution (*atyantika-pralaya*).
If it is argued that liberation (*apavarga*) is indeed the direct realization of the Lord preceded by the transcendence of the three *guṇas*, then for that too—
He says "by which" because such a nature of reality is established by itself;
"by which" means by that which is never to be abandoned, for the sake of my existence— that is, for the sake of its manifestation.
He becomes capable and is reborn;
as it was stated in the fifth [chapter], beginning with: "In which way there is the prescription of colors and liberation" (BhP 5.19.19), and "He who [is devoted] to the Blessed One" (BhP 5.19.20).

Characterized by the yoga of devotion with no other motive, it ends with the words: "the knot of ignorance, which is the cause of various states of existence, is severed by the door of blindness" (BhP 5.19.20).
Therefore, although it is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it should be understood as being manifold indeed.
Thus it was said at the beginning of this section:
"O beautiful lady, the yoga of devotion is cultivated in many ways through various paths;
the disposition of men differs according to the path of their own inherent nature and qualities" (BhP 3.29.7).
The path [is distinguished] by its specific varieties; therefore, through the path of one's own particular yoga of devotion,

by means of the different modes of practice such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, one should cultivate the sense of self-identity, and through its various distinctions such as servitude (*dāsya*) and so forth, the [divine] qualities.
The meaning is that by the differentiation of those [qualities], such as darkness (*tamas*) and so forth, the state—that is, the intention—of persons becomes differentiated.
Regarding this, the *Muktāphala-ṭīkā* states: "This is absolute; beyond that..."
Because there is no other category [of yoga], this very one is designated by the name *bhakti-yoga*. It is so called according to its literal meaning (*anvarthena*). Regarding *bhakti*—:
This is because the word [bhakti] has its primary meaning here;
in other cases, there is attachment only to the fruit and not to Viṣṇu, since devotion is abandoned upon obtaining the fruit— such is this [distinction].
And in the Śrī-Gopāla-tāpanī Upaniṣad: "Devotion is his worship; that is the fixing of the mind upon Him alone, through the absence of any desire for rewards in this world or the next."
And this very thing is "freedom from action" (naiṣkarmya),
as stated in the Śatapatha-śruti: Yājñavalkya said, "Therefore, for the sake of his own welfare,
a person should worship Hari with love."
The meaning is: "out of love," that is, for the sake of one's own welfare through the mere desire for affection.
// 3.29 // Śrī Kapiladeva // 231-234 //
(119) [235] Thus, having established in many ways that this perception of "nothingness" (*akiñcana*) and so forth is absolute, it follows that devotion (*bhakti*) is of two kinds:
that which is based on scriptural injunction (*vaidhī*) and that which follows from passion (*rāgānugā*).
Among these, that which is "according to rule" (vaidhī) is set in motion by the procedure prescribed in the scriptures. That procedure is of two kinds;
therein, the first is the cause of engagement.
And it is the cause for the knowledge of what is to be done and what is not to be done according to that sequence;
however, the first [cause] has already been illustrated.

"Therefore, with a single mind, the Blessed Lord, the Master of the Sātvatas, should always be heard, glorified, meditated upon, and worshipped" (BhP 1.2.14), and so forth. The second [type of service] consists of worship, vows, and the like; he describes that as follows:
"He finds Me alone through the yoga of devotion with detachment;
he who would worship Me thus indeed attains the yoga of devotion.
"With detachment" means with disinterestedness (ahaituka).
To explain how the yoga of causeless devotion (*ahaituka-bhakti-yoga*) itself may come about, he says:
"The yoga of devotion" (*bhakti-yogam*). Thus:
when a person, having attained the status of the twice-born as declared by his own scripture...
"Learn from me how one should worship Me with devotion and faith," according to the method stated in such passages as BhP 11.27.8.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord. (11.27) [235] [236]

In this same way, [the rules] pertaining to Ekādaśī, Janmāṣṭamī, and so forth, are also to be understood. Now, the varieties of vaidhī-bhakti consist of taking refuge, service to the holy such as the venerable guru, hearing, chanting, and so on.
And these, even when occurring individually in groups of two, three, or more, become causes;
for it is so heard [in the scriptures]. In that regard:

First is the going for refuge. For it is one who is oppressed by the fear of cyclic existence— unremitting from the six classes of beings and so forth— and who has no other resort, that enters into refuge.
Even one who desires merely devotion, being oppressed by the aversion to the Lord caused by that [past karma],
is shown to have no other recourse in two ways.
By stating the non-existence of the internal organs as the basis, and by somehow abandoning other things that depend upon them through excessive wisdom;
as in the former case:
A mortal, terrified by the serpent of death, fled through all the worlds but did not find freedom from fear;
yet today, having reached Your lotus feet by chance, he has found it.
"He sleeps at ease; death departs from him.
As stated further on:
"Therefore, O Uddhava, casting aside both injunction and counter-injunction..."
Both worldly engagement and renunciation, as well as what is to be heard and what has already been heard.

"Go to Me alone as your sole refuge, the Self of all embodied beings, with your whole being; through Me, you shall indeed be free from fear from every quarter. And the commentary states: "The *codanā* is the Śruti, and the *praticodanā* is the Smṛti."
And in the Śrī-Gītā: "Having abandoned all duties" (Gītā 18.66), and so forth. The definition of that taking of refuge is stated in the Vaiṣṇava-tantra:
"The resolve for what is favorable and the avoidance of what is unfavorable."
"Trust that [He] will protect, as well as the choosing [of Him] for the role of protector, the surrender of oneself, and the state of supplication— this is the sixfold taking of refuge. Thus,
it is sixfold according to the distinction between the primary and secondary limbs.
In that regard, O Aṅgirasa, the act of choosing [the Lord] as one's protector is indeed the primary limb, because it is synonymous with the term "taking refuge" (*śaraṇāgati*).
The other limbs, however, are its accessories (*parikara*), consisting of *ānukūlya*...

In the face of adversity, there is the conviction that He will protect the devotees and others, or the state of mind of one who has sought refuge; "That Blessed Lord, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds, will provide for our welfare"— in this regard, our [trust is placed].
The manner beginning with "What purpose is there here for me to deliberate? (BhP 3.16.35) and so forth;
and the manner taught in the Gautamīya Tantra: "I am surrendered to the Self; whatever I am directed by some deity residing within my heart to do, that I shall do."
As it is stated in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa, in the explanation of the word "namaḥ" within the eight-syllabled mantra:
"The syllable *ma* represents egoism (*ahaṅkṛti*), while the syllable *na* is its negation."
Therefore, however, by means of the word "namas" (reverence) here, independence is negated.
At that time, he is dependent on the Blessed One and lives through his exertion;
therefore, he should abandon all application of his own power without exception.

"By the power of the Lord, however, there is nothing unattainable for him; having surrendered his worldly existence to Him, he rests and performs only His work. (Padma Purāṇa 6.226.41–46). Therefore, in the Brahma-vaivarta [Purāṇa]:

"For those from whom egoism has ceased, Keśava is not at all distant; for those possessed of egoism, however, even mountains stand between them. [BhP 3.9.9] As for wretchedness: "The Supreme Lord would not be supremely compassionate, nor would He be the most pitiable, were it not for me."
The phrase "para" and so forth refers to this manner [of seeking refuge]. Furthermore, regarding the choosing [of a protector] for the sake of protection, as stated in the *Nārasiṃha*:
"I have approached You for refuge, O God of gods, Janārdana."
Thus, whoever has come for refuge, I shall deliver them from affliction.
Such is the manner [of refuge]. That too is of three kinds, distinguished by being bodily and so forth, as stated in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"Those who have gone for refuge to Acyuta through action, mind, or speech..."
"Yama has no power over them; they are partakers of the fruit of liberation.
Thus it is explained in the *Śrī Hari-bhakti-vilāsa*:
"One who says with speech, 'I am yours,' and likewise knows [it] with the mind..."
"Taking refuge in that state, one rejoices with the body.

Thus, it should be understood that for one whose taking of refuge is complete in all its parts, the fruit is attained instantaneously and in its entirety; however, for others, it occurs according to their attainment and in due order. This very [refuge]—
He praises the taking of refuge:
"O Lord, for one who is struck by the three torments and scorched intensely upon the path of existence..."
I see no other refuge than the pair of Your feet, which are like a parasol raining down nectar—
removing all suffering for those who have come for shelter and showering the rain of Your own sweetness everywhere.
And it has been stated here:
Uddhava addressed the Blessed Lord. (11.19) [236] [237] Thus, taking refuge has been explained.
Furthermore, its priority [as the first stage] is established because its status as belonging to that [path] cannot be proven without it.

In that regard, although everything is accomplished by the very act of taking refuge, there are those who have gone for refuge but are devoid of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and yoga: "Those who have gone for refuge to Him, yet are bereft of meditation and yoga..."
Having indeed transcended death, they go to that state of Viṣṇu.
Thus it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.

Nevertheless, one who desires excellence and is capable should especially and constantly [worship] the venerable feet of the spiritual masters (*guru*) who teach the scriptures of the Blessed One, or those who teach the mantras of the Blessed One.
One should perform service.

His grace is the root for the relinquishing of those various personal compensations that are difficult to abandon during the loss of wealth, as well as for the accomplishment of the supreme grace of the Blessed One.
As previously stated, for example, in the seventh [chapter], the words of Śrī Nārada:
"One should conquer desire through lack of resolve, and anger by abandoning desire."
Greed arises from the perception of gain and loss, and fear from the contemplation of reality.

One should overcome grief and delusion through the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī), hypocrisy through the worship of the Great One (the Mahat), obstacles to yoga through silence, and violence along with desire and other such impulses through the absence of worldly striving.

Through compassion, one should abandon suffering born of living beings; through meditative absorption, that which is caused by fate; through the power of yoga, that which is born of the self; and through devotion to the quality of goodness, sleep.
"Passion and darkness are conquered by goodness, and goodness by tranquility;
indeed, a person shall conquer all this directly through devotion to the Guru. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in the Vāmana-kalpa, there is the speech of Brahmā:
"The mantra is the Guru in person; the Guru is Hari himself.
For him whose Guru is pleased, Hari himself is pleased. Thus it is said elsewhere:
"When Hari is angry, the guru is the protector; when the guru is angry, there is no one at all [to protect].
Therefore, with every effort, one should propitiate the guru alone.
For this very reason, service alone must indeed be performed constantly.

And as the Supreme Lord has stated elsewhere: "First the Guru is to be worshipped, and thereafter my own worship; by performing it thus one attains success, for otherwise it would be fruitless. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, in the Nārada-Pañcarātra it is said: "He who knows the teacher of Vaiṣṇava knowledge to be like Viṣṇu himself, and worships him with speech, mind, and body—he is a knower of the scriptures; he indeed is a Vaiṣṇava."
"Indeed, even one who speaks but a single quarter-verse [of scripture] is always worthy of worship;
how much more so one who expounds the true nature of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu! And so forth.
In the *Pādma Purāṇa*, within the hymn of Devahūti:
"If I possess the same steadfast devotion toward my guru as I have for Hari,
by that truth may Hari reveal Himself.
Therefore, he does not require anyone other than the devotees of the Lord.
As it is said in the Āgama, in the context of the fruit of *puraścaraṇa*: "Just as copper becomes gold through contact with perfected mercury (*siddharasa*)."
"By remaining in the proximity of the Guru, the disciple shall thus become identical with Viṣṇu.
This very point he states:
"Neither by sacrifice nor by progeny, nor by austerity or tranquility..."
"I would be as pleased by service to my guru as I am the self of all beings.

And the commentary says: It has been stated that there is no one to be served greater than the guru who bestows knowledge; for this very reason, he says "I am not... to declare that there is no religious duty greater than the worship of him.
Sacrifice (*ijyā*) is the duty of the householder;

procreation (*prajāti*) refers to an excellent birth, namely the initiation (*upanayana*), by which the duty of the student (*brahmacārin*) is indicated through those two; likewise, there is the duty of the forest-dweller (*vanastha*) by means of austerity (*tapas*).
"By tranquility" means by the dharma of a renunciant;
"I, the Supreme Lord, am not so pleased by that as I am by service to the guru, even though [the guru] is the self of all beings"— this is the point.
In this context, knowledge is of two kinds: that which is grounded in Brahman and that which is grounded in the Blessed Lord.
Regarding these, the former is explained in the same manner as before.
But it has been stated thus: (page 122) sacrifice (*ijyā*) is worship (*pūjā*);
procreation (*prajāti*) is the Vaiṣṇava initiation (*dīkṣā*); austerity (*tapas*) is meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
"Quiescence, Blessed One, is the ultimate."

// 10.80 // The Blessed Lord [spoke] to the brahmin Śrīdāman // 237 // [238] By the command of the venerable Guru and without contradicting service to him, it is indeed beneficial to serve other Vaiṣṇavas as well; otherwise, there would be fault.
As stated in the words of the venerable Nārada: "He who, while the Guru is present, should worship another in his presence, falls into a miserable state; his act of worship is fruitless."

One who has not taken refuge in a guru possessing the characteristics described in such passages as "He who is first well-versed in the Śābdika [Veda] and the Supreme [Brahman]" (BhP 11.3.21), and who, out of envy and so forth toward such a guru, does not grant permission for the honoring of great bhāgavatas and the like— he has from the very beginning abandoned the scriptures and is not even considered for deliberation. Both—
For indeed, a fall into calamity occurs for him;
it is with such an intention as this that it is said: "He who speaks what is devoid of logic, and he who listens with injustice..."
Both of them go to a terrible hell for inexhaustible time.
Thus it is stated in the Nārada-pañcarātra.
For this very reason, such a guru is to be worshipped from afar;
however, if he is a hater of Vaiṣṇavas, he must be abandoned altogether.
Even for a guru who is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, correction must be administered.
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*),

and because, due to his lack of devotion to Viṣṇu (*vaiṣṇava-bhāva-rāhitya*) and his state of being non-Vaiṣṇava (*avaiṣṇavatā*), he falls within the scope of statements such as "by one instructed by a non-Vaiṣṇava," and so forth.
However, if a guru possessing the aforementioned characteristics is not available,
the constant service of a single great bhāgavata is the supreme good; and he is to be regarded as equal to the venerable guru himself.
One who is well-composed and possesses a compassionate heart toward himself is to be accepted;
for whatever a person associates with becomes his own quality, like a gem. Therefore, for the prosperity of his own lineage, the wise man should resort only to those of his own kind.

Thus, according to the perspective of the *Śrī Hari-bhakti-sudhodaya*, [this applies] due to a lack of compassion for him and a lack of interest in him within one's heart. Now follows the method of service as appropriate toward everyone who merely bears the marks of a Bhāgavata.
In that regard, service to a Mahābhāgavata is of two kinds: in the form of association (*prasaṅga*) and in the form of personal attendance (*paricaryā*).
In that regard, an example in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is as follows: "Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor even dharma restrains me;
neither Vedic study, austerity, renunciation, nor sacrifices, charitable works, nor sacrificial fees [restrain me]."

Vows, sacrifices, Vedic meters, sacred fords, observances, and restraints— association with the virtuous indeed encompasses all these, for it removes attachment to everything else, and thus leads me [to the goal]. (BhP 11.12.1–2) —
As stated in the previous chapter:
"Whoever, being composed, would worship Me alone with *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial rites and works of public welfare),
attains true devotion unto Me through the service of the saintly, and thereby the remembrance of Me. By this [verse],
it is shown that when the culmination of devotion is generated through the service of the saintly, the service of the saintly is the means subsequent to all other practices.

The state of being dependent has been stated as it were. Here, by the word "iṣṭa," according to the method described in the seventh book, the Agnihotra, Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, Cāturmāsya sacrifices, animal sacrifice (paśu-yāga), Vaiśvadeva, and the offering of bali are meant [BhP 7.15.48–49].
By the word *pūrta* are meant temples, gardens, wells, tanks, ponds, water-stations, and perpetual charities (*satra*);
however, in such passages as "One should worship me with the *iṣṭa* sacrifice using oblations in the fire" (BhP 11.11.42), [the distinction is made]. (Page 123)

"Pūrtam" (meritorious works) should be understood as indicated by the Agnihotra and other such rites, and indicated by gardens, groves, pleasure-grounds, and so forth. Thus, he who would worship Me with the aforementioned kinds of *iṣṭa* and *pūrta*— for him, there shall be remembrance of Me through service to the virtuous and association with the good, accompanied by devotion.
The meaning is that one attains steadfastness in internal devotion (*antaraṅga-bhakti*).
In that regard, the inclusion of the fire-sacrifice (*agni-hotra*) and other rites within devotion [occurs] through the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) who resides in the fire.
Because fire and other elements are satisfied through the Lord’s presiding over form (*rūpa*),
and because wells, gardens, and so forth are constructed for the purpose of serving Him, there is inclusion [of these] therein.
Thus, the dependence of association with the virtuous upon all other factors has been stated;
furthermore, in that regard, its independence in yielding results according to one's desire—
To declare the state of being a donor and the supreme capacity with respect to all things, the ultimate secret was taught.
Now, O delighter of the Yadus, listen to this supreme secret as it is being heard.

"I shall speak even that which is most secret, for you are my servant, friend, and companion" (BhP 11.11.49). Because he has been described as possessing such greatness, the text states "it does not obstruct" to indicate this supreme secrecy.
Tyāga is renunciation;
dakṣiṇā is merely giving;
yajña is the worship of the gods.

The *chandāṃsi* are the secret mantras (*rahasya-mantrāḥ*). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) subdues or brings me under its control, so too neither yoga nor Sāṅkhya subdues [me]. And so forth.

Therefore, since it is understood from the context that they too exercise some degree of control [over the senses], they should be known as being solely devoted to the Blessed One and not common [to others];
for this very reason, the authors of the *Ṭīkā* state that the vows are those of Ekādaśī and so forth.

And by this much alone, it does not follow that these obligatory Vaiṣṇava vows are to be disregarded, because while one may be praised for its capacity to yield an excellence of fruit, it is impossible to thereby negate the obligatory nature of the other.
Just as those authorized to perform rituals—

O King, this Blessed One, the enjoyer of all sacrifices, is not truly worshipped with oblations poured into the mouth of fire as he is when offerings are made into the mouths of Brahmins. (BhP 7.14.17)

Just as those who have heard the previously mentioned injunction that "one should sacrifice with the Agnihotra and other rites" are unable to abandon them, so too those qualified for devotion, even after hearing [the statement], "The worship of My devotees is superior" (BhP 11.19.29),
[do not abandon] the worship of the Lord which has become obligatory following their initiation.

They are unable to renounce it in that same way. For this very reason: "The fruit which is proclaimed to result from six months of fasting is obtained in the Kali age by those who consume even a single grain of the food offering (naivedya) of Viṣṇu."
Even this does not constitute a contradiction;

for even though the Ekādaśī and other such observances are obligatory (nitya), their status as yielding great fruit is considered merely incidental (ānuṣaṅgika) in various scriptural sources. Therefore, even for the sake of preserving their obligatory nature, such a Vaiṣṇava vow must certainly be performed.

Therefore, in the previous chapter, the commentators also stated regarding the verse *ājñāyaiva guṇān doṣān* (BhP 11.11.32): "Those religious practices opposed to devotion— such as fasting on Ekādaśī when it falls on the fourteenth day, fasting on Kṛṣṇa-ekādaśī, not offering food, and performing *śrāddha* ceremonies— and so forth."
It has been stated that the meaning is "having abandoned.
And in the first [canto], in the dialogue between Śrī Bhīṣma and Yudhiṣṭhira,
regarding the verse beginning with *bhagavad-dharmān* (BhP 1.9.24), [it is said that] from pleasing Lord Hari comes the observance of the twelfth day and so forth.
The word *rūpāt* has already been explained.
Regarding the phrase "he performed vows to please Hari" (*vrātāni cere haritoṣaṇāni*), the third case ending refers to the eleventh day of the lunar fortnight (*ekādaśī*) and so forth.

Therefore, for the sake of demonstrating the conduct of the illustrious Ambarīṣa— the crest-jewel of the virtuous, whose sole vow was great devotion to the Blessed Lord— that very point is being determined. Now, let us proceed with the subject at hand.
In this context, subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) is of two kinds: primary and secondary.
Among these, through the primary kind, love is obtained.
(Page 124) "Let it be so, my dear; may the Blessed Lord Mukunda be the object of devotion for those who worship Him."
According to the principle stated in *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 5.6.18, "He never bestows liberation, nor even devotional yoga," other results are merely secondary;
here, the primary result resides in the Śrī-gopīs and others.

In the case of arrows and the like, it is secondary; in what follows, the state of being a "subjugator" (vaśīkaraṇa) is used figuratively in the sense of making [the deity] ready to bestow the fruit. He provides an illustration regarding this subjugation:
Indeed, through association with the virtuous, the Daityas, Yātudhānas,
beasts, birds, Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas [attain excellence].
Among humans, the Vidyādharas are Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and those of the lowest castes;
they are of the nature of passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) in each respective age.
Many have attained my state, such as Tvāṣṭra, Kāyādha, and others;
Vṛṣaparvan, Bali, Bāṇa, Maya, and then Vibhīṣaṇa.
Sugrīva, Hanumān, the bear, Gaja, the vulture, the merchant-trader, the hunter, the hunchback, the cowherd women in Vraja, the wives of the sacrificers, and others;
as well as the Daityas and the Asuras and Dānavas characterized by them.

in his womb occurred the association with the illustrious Nārada.

Immediately thereafter, because the awakening of devotion was observed,
Bāṇa attained union with the Blessed Lord Maheśvara; of this [Bāṇa], the arm—
After the cutting [of his wings], having realized the greatness of Viṣṇu, the attainment of the Great Bhāgavata Maheśa alone is said to be his own attainment;
he was the Dānava Maya.
In the construction of this assembly hall and other such matters, there is association with the Pāṇḍavas and association with the Blessed One;

his association with Hanumān and his association with the Blessed One [are his marks].
Sugrīva and the others, ending with Gaja, are deer.
In that regard, Ṛkṣa is Jāmbavān; his association with the Blessed One [is well known]. Gaja is Gajendra.
From this, one may infer his association with the virtuous in a previous birth,

Daśaratha, and others.

Having not cited the Gandharvas and others because they are not very well known, he cites among humans those such as the Vaiśyas; the merchant’s path refers to Tulādhāra.

In this land of Bhārata, for one whose greatness has been proclaimed in the accounts of the sage Jājali, the Gandharva, Dharma-vyādha the hunter, and the Śūdra outcaste, association with the virtuous (sat-saṅga) must be sought.
Even a hunter, a Dharma-vyādha, a Śūdra, or an outcaste [may attain liberation].

In this regard, the following story is told in the Ādivārāha Purāṇa: once, in a former Kali age, a certain Brāhmaṇa was killed by a Vaiṣṇava king named Vasu who, mistaking him for a deer in a previous birth, attained the state of a Brahma-rākṣasa toward that very king.

At the time of his departure for the worldly realm of Viṣṇu, he entered that body; and later, when the king had reached the end of his enjoyments and attained sovereignty, [the deity] emerged from his body by the power of the recitation of the hymn known as the *Brahmapārā* performed by him, assuming the name Dharma-vyādha as created by him.
Averse to excessive violence, he beheld the Lord of the Blue Mountain at the conclusion [of his penance] and praised Him;

having obtained His embrace, he attained union (*sāyujya*) with Him. Kubjā’s association with the Blessed One occurred in a previous birth, as did her association with Nārada—thus [it is told] by Māthura Hari.
This is well-known in the lineage.
Here, the cowherd women (gopīs) are common [to all], having come to Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s Vraja at that time through marriage and other such means.

There is attachment to the world of storytellers and attachment to them;
others are the Daityas and so forth, as well as the unleadable (aneḍa).

They have not studied the multitude of scriptures, nor have they served the great-souled ones;

(BhP 11.12.7) [Page 125]—by whom the multitude of scriptures has not been studied.

And for that purpose, they have not served the Great Ones; moreover, they have not observed vows nor performed austerities. As before, [the lack of] study and so forth constitutes a failure to please the Blessed One.

In this regard, some maintain that for Vṛtra and others, following their practice in previous births and so forth, whatever [attainments] occurred were accomplished through association with the virtuous; intending this, they hold that each such attainment resulted specifically from association with the virtuous.

As for what was previously stated— that divine grace occurs solely through association with a devotee (bhāgavata)— that indeed refers only to a birth in which one is already oriented toward Him;

There is no fault in saying that attachment (*saṅga*) is mentioned as a specific means (*sādhana-viśeṣa*).
Or, if in some cases attachment to the Blessed One (*bhagavat-saṅga*) were also a cause for the arising of direct presence (*sāmmukhya*), even then it would be so.

We explain: having taken the meaning of the word *sat* (the virtuous) as the means of entry, since the Blessed One at times extends compassion everywhere, and that occurs solely through association with the *sat*, there is no abandonment of our fundamental position (*abhyupagama*).

He shows this through the example of the blessed gopīs and others:
"Indeed, by pure devotion alone, the gopīs, cows, trees, deer, and others—even those of deluded intellect, serpents, and perfected beings—attained Me directly. (BhP 11.12.8)

"By *bhāva*—meaning by the affection born merely from union with Me, which is obtained through the context; here, *bhāva* is the sign of being primarily characterized by subjugation. By devotion, virtuous women bring me, their virtuous husband, under their control."

This is evident from passages such as [BhP 9.4.48] and others, as well as from [BhP 11.14.20]: "I am to be grasped by exclusive devotion alone. Furthermore, even the cows should be understood as being merely adventitious, just like the gopīs.
The *nagas* are those such as Yamalārjuna and others;

The attainment of Yamalārjuna and Kāliya is stated with reference to the eternal attainment that is necessarily concomitant with their attainment at that specific moment.
The perfected ones [attain their state] as before through two kinds of association with the virtuous;

In the verse beginning with *yathāvarundhe* (BhP 11.12.2), there is the ultimate limit of the meaning of the word *yathā*; he clarifies that very point: [242]—
That state which one might not attain—even with great effort—through yoga, Sāṅkhya, charity, vows, austerity, sacrifice, exposition, Vedic study, or renunciation;

This should be investigated.

"He purifies all the worlds like the risen thousand-rayed sun.

And because of this necessity: it should be understood that there is no fault in Indra’s engagement in the slaughter of Vṛtra by the power of his sacrifice to the Lord known as the Aśvamedha; for this was accepted by the sages who desired the pacification of the world’s affliction and the destruction of his demonic nature. (p. 137)
Now, regarding "the abandonment of the vow of dharma": even the conceit that one is equal to others in terms of dharma and so forth is negligence;
the meaning is that it constitutes an offense. And for this very reason:
"However many syllables of the Veda have been recited by the twice-born..."
That many names of Hari have been proclaimed; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, even by this extension [of attributes], the majesty of the Name alone is established;
for it has been said: "This most sweet Maṅgala is the auspiciousness of all auspicious things, the true fruit of the creeper of all the Vedas, and the very nature of Consciousness."
Likewise, in the Śrī-Viṣṇudharma: "The Ṛg-veda, the Yajur-veda, the Sāma-veda,
and the Atharva-veda have indeed been studied by him who has uttered the two syllables 'Ha-ri'."
In the Skanda Purāṇa, it is said by Pārvatī:
"O dear one, do not recite the Ṛg, Yajur, or Sāma Vedas at all;
rather, sing constantly the name of Hari, 'Govinda,' which is worthy of being sung."
In the *Śrī-Rāmāṣṭottara-śata-nāma-stotra* of the *Padma-purāṇa*: "Each single name of Viṣṇu is considered superior to all the Vedas" (*PadmaP* 6.254.27).
Now, by the words beginning with "to one who lacks faith," he shows the fault of the instructor and speaks of the instruction:

Having heard this: "one for whom 'I' and 'mine' are paramount" means one who is indifferent toward that [object] because their sole intent is directed toward egoism (*ahaṃtā*) and possessiveness (*mamatā*).
"Whose single name has entered the path of recollection in his speech."

In such passages, by the term *pāṣaṇḍa* (heretic), which has its cause in [attachment to] the body, wealth, and so forth, the ten offenses (*aparādha*) are indicated, because they consist of heresy; likewise,
there is another offense for those of that same kind.
It is stated in the *Pādma-vaiśākha-māhātmya*:
"And those men who go about disregarding the glorification of the Blessed One, they go to a terrible hell because of that sinful deed. [PadmaP 5.96.63] Thus it is said.
And regarding these offenses, it is stated in that very same place that there is no other atonement:
"For those joined with offenses against the Name, the names themselves remove the evil;
when applied without interruption, they alone are effective for the goal."
In this regard, for offenses such as those beginning with *steya* (theft), the continuous chanting of the Name and so forth is appropriate solely for the sake of pleasing Him;
as seen in the account of Ambarīṣa’s conduct and elsewhere, that alone—
This is because one perceives offenses as being forgivable.
And it has been stated in the *Nāmakaumudī*: "For a great offense, only the experience [of its fruit] is the remover, or else [the offender's] favor [toward the victim]."
Therefore, since there is no other alternative, it has been well said: "for those who are becoming disenchanted... (BhP 2.1.11).
Thus spoke Śrī Śuka. 2.1. 265 [266].

Thus it was said by the illustrious Nārada in the *Bṛhan-nāradīya*: "Since even the Manus and the lords of sages are unable to reach the limit of the glories of His name, how can one of impaired intellect worship Him?"
Now follows the glorification of Śrī-rūpa:
"In order to attract the eyes of women," and so forth—[as stated in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 11.30.3]:
"That Śrī, when being praised by poets, generates delight in their words."
The perfection of the splendor of that form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, when being glorified, generates passion only for His praises within the words of poets who celebrate Him;
thus it has been said by Śrī...
"May existence, along with its evils, be averted from us in the hells by the four-fold refuge," as stated in BhP 3.15.49 and elsewhere;
and "If even our words were like *tulasī* to Your feet... (11.30).
Thus spoke King Parīkṣit to Śrī Śuka. (266) [267]
Now, the glorification of virtues:
for this [glorification] is indeed the fruit of a person's austerity, sacred learning, well-performed sacrifice, and eloquent hymns, as well as of their intellect and generosity.
The meaning established by the poets as unerring is this: the description of the qualities of the One of Supreme Fame.
"Śruta" refers to the study of the Vedas. [BhP 1.5.22] (p138)
*Sviṣṭam* refers to sacrifice and the like;
*sūktam* refers to victory through mantras and the like;
*buddhiḥ* refers to non-scriptural cognition.
A gift has been given;
for those who remain steadfast while these things are offered to the Blessed One, the result is the constant fruit of the unswerving goal.
What is that? It is the chanting of the qualities of the One of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka).

Even though delight—which consists of the supreme human goal—is accomplished through the description of His qualities, it is stated that the description of those qualities, on the contrary, possesses the quality of never falling away due to its eternal and constant joy.
Therefore, by means of its non-falling away, it indicates that delight itself is its fruit.

// 1.5 // Śrī Nārada [said] to Śrī Vyāsa: [267] Now follows the glorification of the divine play (līlā)—[268]— The Lord Nārada said to the venerable Vyāsa: "Now, the glorification of the divine play."
For one who constantly listens with faith and recounts his own deeds,
the Blessed One enters the heart in no very long time—
that is, in a very short time.
It enters and vibrates.
// 2.8 // O illustrious Parīkṣit!
Those words are false and unreal, for they are not discourses on the unreal; that which is not spoken of as the Blessed Lord Adhokṣaja is indeed the truth, and that alone is auspiciousness.
"That very merit arises from the qualities of the Blessed One" (BhP 12.12.49), and so forth;
"that which is sung as the glory of the One of Excellent Renown" (BhP 12.12.50)—
[these refer to] the unreal and the untrue.
Those [discourses] in which there is talk of the wicked, of the Blessed One, and of others besides His devotees;
whereas that in which the fame of the Lord of Excellent Renown (Uttamaśloka) is sung is indeed what [should be heard].
"The singing of his pastimes alone is the truth," and so forth.
How is there truthfulness and auspiciousness?

And: "In that regard, [the word 'yat'] means that from which there arises the manifestation of the Lord's qualities within the heart of the singer; that is to say, it bestows delight in Him. As stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O protector of the earth, wherever the Vaiṣṇava narrative exists..."
In each and every place Hari goes, just as a cow is affectionate toward her calf.

In the Viṣṇudharma and the Skanda Purāṇa, it is stated in the words of the Blessed One: "I shall never abandon that man who constantly recites my stories, who delights in hearing my stories, and whose mind is filled with love for my stories."
And here, by the phrase "it is sung," it follows that if one possesses a beautiful voice (*sukaṇṭhatā*), one must indeed perform singing, and that is praiseworthy;
the same applies to names and so forth. And it has been said:
Singing songs and names that have that as their meaning, one should wander without shame and without attachment;
such is the vow for one who glorifies the name of his own Beloved.
"One whose affection has arisen and whose mind is melted intensely," as it is said in BhP 12.2.37;
and elsewhere:
"Those which are the cause of the activity of the universe's dissolution and origination here..."
"Lord Hari performed deeds whose objects were not shared by others;
for he who sings of them, O dear one, or hears them, or even rejoices in them, devotion toward the Blessed One—the path to liberation—will surely arise. [BhP 10.69.29]

The meaning is that in the absence of the power to sing, or when one encounters someone superior to oneself, one listens to it; and in the absence of such power, one even approves of it. This is stated by Śrī Viṣṇu in the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-dharma*:
"If your heart is drawn toward the Gandharvas by passion,
then, fixing your mind upon me, you should sing my sacred stories.
Thus it is said in the *Kārttika-māhātmya* of the *Pādma-purāṇa*, in the words of the Blessed Lord.
I do not dwell in Vaikuṇṭha, nor in the hearts of yogis;
O Nārada, I abide wherever my devotees sing my praises.
"Men perform worship and other services for them with perfumes, incense, and so forth;

yet through that, I attain supreme joy, which I do not attain from my own worship. And they are the supreme benefactors of all living beings indeed, how much more so of their own kin? As it has been said:
In the *Nārasiṃha-purāṇa*, it is said by Śrī Prahlāda (p.
139): "O Nṛsiṃha, those virtuous ones who, filled with joy, loudly chant Your name, are the unconditional kinsmen of all living beings."
And here, "saṅkīrtana" is said to be chanting performed by many people together;
however, it should be understood that this is even superior to the former because it nourishes a particular kind of wonder.
And regarding the recitation of the names,
as it was taught by the Blessed Lord Himself during His descent to purify the Kali-yuga:
"One who is humbler than even a blade of grass, yet more patient than even a tree..."
Hari should always be glorified by one who is free from pride and who bestows honor upon others.
[Thus ends Padyāvalī 32. // 12.12 // Śrī Sūta said:
// 269 // [270] And this devotion known as *kīrtana* (chanting) consists of the Lord’s [qualities] through substances, types, qualities, and actions for the sake of the wretched...
The renown of the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and other texts is that she consists of compassion whose sole object is the people;
and her wretchedness in the Kali age is as described in the Brahmavaivarta:

"Therefore, in the Kali age, practices such as austerity, yoga, knowledge, and sacrifice do not reach completion with all their constituent parts, even when performed by embodied beings who are highly skilled. For this very reason, having appeared in the world— which is by its very nature exceedingly wretched during the Kali age— he [the Lord] brings them [to perfection] without effort.

Bestowing the entire fruit of all great sādhanas performed during those respective ages, she fulfills one's purpose; for this very reason, through her alone, the Lord is especially pleased in the Kali age. And so it is said: "In this world, the chanting of the glories of Śrī Hari is the supreme austerity."
In the Kali age, one should especially perform these acts for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu.
Thus, according to the statements in the *Skanda Purāṇa* regarding the greatness of the Cāturmāsya vow,
it is said:
"That which is attained by meditating on Viṣṇu in the Kṛta age is attained by worshipping Him with sacrifices in the Tretā age."

"In the Dvāpara age, through service; in the Kali age, by chanting the glories of Hari. (BhP 12.3.52) Whatever may be attained through those respective means in the Kṛta and other ages, all that occurs in the Kali age simply by chanting the glories of Hari. And elsewhere: (ViP 6.2.17)—

"What one attains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, or by worshipping in the Dvāpara, that one attains in the Kali age simply by chanting the name of Keśava. Thus spoke Śrī Śuka. (270) [271]
Therefore:
"The noble ones, who recognize virtue and partake of its essence, honor this Kali age, wherein all one's own goals are attained through mere chanting alone. (BhP 11.5.36)
Those who know the qualities— meaning those who recognize his quality in the form of the propagation of his glories—
and for that very reason, who partake of the essence by grasping only the essence rather than seizing upon his faults, honor the Kali age as being nothing but virtue.

The meaning is that he demonstrates this by means of that very *saṅkīrtana* (chanting) as it is practiced, independently of any other means (*sādhana*). Everything that is to be accomplished through thousands of means such as meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth in the Kṛta and other ages—[he shows] the majesty of *kīrtana* alone:
[272] He states the greatness of *kīrtana* alone:
For there is no gain higher than this for embodied beings wandering here,
from which one may find supreme peace and the cycle of worldly existence ceases—
namely, from this *kīrtana*.
Because from that chanting [comes] supreme peace— that is, tranquility (śama),
which according to the words of the Blessed One is the intellect (buddhi) established in Me— a state unattainable even through meditation and other such means.
O Blessed One, one attains the most excellent culmination;

as a consequence, cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is destroyed. For this very reason, O Blessed One, even those such as Kṛta and others have established the culmination of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) in such a manner.
They have not reached their ultimate end; for,

according to the Skanda Purāṇa and other texts, it is said that "O King, in the Kali age, the highly fortunate ones constantly perform kīrtana, whereas in the Kṛta and other ages, people desired birth in the Kali age."
And as for the greatness of chanting (kīrtana), which is the cause of such a final consummation:

since it was not revealed at that time by the Blessed One— who is characterized by an extraordinary compassion for the wretched— on the occasion when those respective capacities were available, therefore...
Thinking that those beings, though capable of meditation and other practices, would not achieve much by merely moving their tongues and lips, they did not place their faith in that; then,
having heard that in the Kali age people would have supreme devotion to the Blessed One, for that purpose, [they established it] specifically in the Kali age.

He says that they desire nothing other than their own birth [in the Kali age]: "O King, in the Kali age, people desire to be born; indeed, in the Kali age, there will be those who are solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa. (BhP 11.5.35)
"Being devoted to that" (tat-parāyaṇatva) here means possessing an excellence of love for Him.
This very state is indicated by the phrase "the supreme peace" (paramāṃ śāntim) through its effect; it belongs even to the liberated and perfected ones (siddha), and [is directed toward] Nārāyaṇa—
Just as in the verse, "The one who is the supreme refuge, whose self is perfectly tranquil, is very difficult to find" (BhP 6.14.5),

here too it should not be said that there is an excellence of quality in chanting due to association with the Kali age, because the restriction of time and place is prohibited for devotion in general.
"Having specifically observed the names, one should always and everywhere proclaim the names of Viṣṇu, whose weapon is the discus, within the *Viṣṇudharma*.
And likewise in the *Skānda*:
"It does not depend upon place, time, state, self, purity, and so forth; rather, this very name is independent and grants whatever is desired.
And in the Viṣṇudharma:

"For him, the Kṛta age exists in the Kali age; for him, the Kali age exists in the Kṛta age—[this is true] of him in whose mind Govinda resides and in whose heart Acyuta dwells. Furthermore, it is not merely because of the capacity for other means in the Kali age that a great fruit arises even from a small [practice].
But it should not be thought that this is because of its greater weight;

for one who has fixed his mind upon it does not go to hell, even heaven is an obstacle when compared to its contemplation, and for those who have established their self and mind within it, even the world of Brahmā is insignificant.
"The Imperishable One, who bestows liberation upon those men of pure intellect whose minds are established in Him— what wonder is it that sin goes to its destruction when that Acyuta is glorified?

Thus, by the very fact that even mere remembrance (smaraṇa)— which extends up to meditative absorption (samādhi)— is superior, the excellence of glorification (kīrtana) is established all the more by way of contrast (kaumutyena).
This is shown in the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa; therefore it is said: "For those who are becoming disenchanted with this... (BhP 2.1.11), and so forth. And likewise:
The remembrance of Viṣṇu, which destroys sin,
is accomplished with great effort;
yet [the remembrance of Śiva] is achieved by the mere movement of the lips.
But chanting [the Lord's names] is even better than that.
Thus it is said in the *Vaiṣṇava-cintāmaṇi*:
"O Bhārata, the names of Hari always abide in the mouth of that person by whom Vāsudeva was worshipped in previous hundreds of births."
Thus it is stated elsewhere;
and in the *Nāmāparādhabhajanastotra*, it is said: "Even one who has committed every offense," and so forth. Therefore, in every age, the power of the glorious *kīrtana* is indeed equal.
And in the Kali age, since that [devotion] is accepted by the Blessed Lord out of compassion, it is established that its praise is intended precisely for that reason.
Therefore, although it has been stated that devotion to others should be practiced in the Kali age, it must be done only in conjunction with that [devotion to Kṛṣṇa].
"For the wise indeed worship with sacrifices consisting primarily of the chanting of names" (BhP 11.5.29).
And here, the independent chanting of the Name alone is declared to be supremely praiseworthy.
"Hari's name, Hari's name, Hari's name alone;
in the Kali age there is no other way, indeed there is none, indeed there is none. Thus it is stated in such passages.
Therefore, it is well said: "The noble ones celebrate the Kali age," and so forth—this being the triad [of verses].
//11.5// Śrī-Karabhājana [attained] Nimi // 271-273 // [274] Thus,
it has been shown that in the Kali age, the attainment of being solely devoted to the Supreme Lord is achieved precisely through the power of the widespread practice of chanting His names.
In this regard, he confirms by way of contrast that those who are offenders by entering into heretical sects will indeed become turned away from that [path]:
"O King, in the Kali age, [one does not worship] the Supreme Guru of the worlds..."
With their minds divided by heretics, mortals will for the most part worship the Blessed One Acyuta, whose lotus feet are bowed to by the lords of the three worlds.
Whatever name a man may utter while dying, or while falling or stumbling, helpless and afflicted by illness— he, having his karmic bolts shattered, attains the supreme goal.
People in the Kali age will not attain that which they shall worship;
this is clear.
// 12.3 // Śrī Śuka said: // 274 // [275] Thus, *kīrtana* has been explained.
In this *kīrtana*, one’s own wretchedness and one’s own desired object—
The recitation of the *Vijñapti* and the *Stava* should also be included therein.
Likewise, the chanting of the names and so forth found in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavatam* should be understood, as before, to be superior to the chanting of the names and so forth belonging to others.
"But in the Kali age, that [scripture] is highly praised:
'When Kṛṣṇa has departed to His own abode along with dharma, knowledge, and the rest,
this sun of the Purāṇas has now risen for those whose vision is lost in the Kali age' (BhP 1.3.42)."

Now, if one whose inner heart has been purified by taking refuge and other such practices should perform remembrance (*smaraṇa*) without abandoning the chanting of the Name— since it has been stated [in BhP 2.1.11]: "For those who are weary of this world and desire it, there is fearlessness from all sides"— then he should do so.
And that mental synthesis is precisely what becomes manifold through its connection with names and so forth;
therein lies the commonality of recollection.
"This much alone is the yoga taught by my disciples, Sanaka and the others, so that the mind, withdrawn from all directions, is truly absorbed in Me.
The meaning is: "in whatever manner it is absorbed in Me, this much is the extent of it."
And likewise, in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the speech of Brahmā: "Having churned all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again," and so forth.
// 11.13 // The Blessed Lord // 275 // [276] In that regard, as for the remembrance of the Name: the supreme name of Hari is to be chanted, meditated upon, and sung continuously.
And it should be praised in many ways by one who desires manifold states of liberation.
This should be understood according to the *Jābāli-saṃhitā* and other such texts;
however, the remembrance of the Name depends upon the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*).
In the root text, however, it is not explicitly stated that [the former] is inferior to that [latter] because of its glorification;
rather, it speaks of the remembrance of the form:
"Non-forgetfulness of the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa."
It destroys inauspicious things and extends well-being;
it brings about the purification of the being, devotion to the Supreme Self, and knowledge conjoined with higher realization and dispassion.
(Verse 12.12) Devotion characterized by love for Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, is the primary fruit; all others, however, are incidental.
Moreover:
"Does the Teacher of the World not grant even his own self to one who remembers his lotus feet; how much more so the objects of wealth and desire, which are not so highly prized? [BhP 10.80.11]

"He remembers for one who remembers" means that, manifesting visibly, he brings himself under the control of the rememberer. The plural number in "objects of desire" (*arthakāmān*) includes liberation (*mokṣa*) as well; this is the indication (*liṅga*).
According to the principle of concomitance (*samavāya-nyāya*):
because its majesty is such, for that very reason this has also been stated in the *Garuḍa-purāṇa*.
"When even a single moment has passed devoid of meditation, it is right to cry out loudly, like one who has been plundered by bandits.
Thus [spoke] the wife of the brahmin Śrīdāman to him. 10.80. 277 [278].
Now, as before, one should contemplate the recollection of the service to the retinue of qualities and the divine pastimes, which are easily attainable through the method of gradual steps.
This recollection is fivefold; namely: whatever [is appropriate].
Investigation is recollection.
Drawing the mind from all [objects] and maintaining it in a general form is concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
Dhyāna is the specific contemplation of form and so forth;
that which is uninterrupted like a stream of nectar is *dhruvānusmṛti*.
"Samādhi is the manifestation of the object of meditation alone.
Regarding that, "recollection" means by whatever means possible.
The imperishable Nārāyaṇa, when remembered, will undoubtedly be gracious even toward one who is burdened with sins.
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhannāradīya-purāṇa* and other texts:
"Meditation (*dhāraṇā*)— the mind of one who meditates upon objects becomes attached to those very objects."
"The mind of one who remembers Me is dissolved into Me alone" (BhP 11.14.27), and so forth.
As for meditation (*dhyāna*):
meditation upon the pair of the Lord’s feet is declared to be free from the dualities of worldly existence.
Even for the wicked, that which is beneficial is ordained through association.
Thus it is stated in the *Nārasiṃha Purāṇa* and other texts.
Therein, "free from duality" (*nirdvandvam*) means transcending the succession of sufferings consisting of cold, heat, and so forth;
this is what has been proclaimed in the scripture.
It has been ordained; and even for the sinner, by mere association, that which is most excellent and supremely beneficial has been ordained in that very place—this is the meaning.
And constant remembrance [of Me] occurs through the mere recollection of My qualities, as stated in BhP 3.29.10 and elsewhere.

And in passages such as "His memory remains unimpeded even for the sake of the prosperity of the three worlds" (BhP 11.2.51), this very point has been demonstrated by the venerable Śrī Rāmānuja in the first Sūtra. He states the meditative concentration (samādhi):
He did not perceive the arrival of those two, the lords who are the very soul of the universe;
his mental faculties being obstructed, he was unaware of himself and of the entire world.
(BhP 12.10.9) "Of those two" refers to Rudra and his wife.
Because they are portions of the Blessed One and His powers, both the world and the Self are His instigators;
the reason for this is that his mental fluctuations are restrained and his mind is permeated by the Blessed One.
Because of the previously stated passage, "He attained supreme devotion toward the Blessed Lord" (BhP 12.10.6), this state is indeed distinct from that samādhi on Brahman known as *asamprajñāta*.
Furthermore, when that [Lord] is endowed with pastimes and the like, the manifestation of Him alone is *samādhi*. As it is said:
"For the sake of liberation from all bonds, contemplate through *samādhi* the activities of the Wide-striding One" (*BhP* 1.5.13). (p. 143)
This is clear.
Such is the nature [of devotion] for servants and other devotees;
previously, however, it was generally peaceful (śānta).

"Of the devotees... whose minds are absorbed in their own bliss, who have cast aside all other states of being, yet whose very essence is drawn away by the charming pastimes of the Unconquered One"—from such statements as these.
Śrī Nārada [spoke thus] to Vyāsa. 279–280.
Now, if there is both desire and capability, then service at his feet must be performed without abandoning that [meditation].
And this service is performed by some for the sake of accomplishing remembrance (*smaraṇa*);
likewise, it is stated in the *Viṣṇurahasya*:
The Supreme Lord’s statement:
"O divine sage, neither yogis who are perfectly devoted to meditation nor those devoted to the yoga of action please me as much as devotion does."
"Through the sequence of ritual action, yoga also proceeds for the meditator.
Here, "yoga" refers to *samādhi*.
In the phrase "service to the feet," the word "feet" (*pāda*) is used solely out of devotion. Therefore...
Respectful service is enjoined;
and "service" (sevā) refers to attendance and so forth that is appropriate to the time, place, and other circumstances. For example:
The longing to serve whose feet instantly destroys the impurity of the intellect accumulated over countless lifetimes, as it grows ever stronger day by day.
Just as the river flowing from his big toe [quenches the thirst of travelers],
so too is this [stream of grace] sufficient for the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ascetics tormented by the cycle of worldly existence;
it belongs to his very foot.
He states "mahimā" (greatness) by means of an illustration, beginning with "yathā" (just as).
[4.21] Pṛthu [worshipped] Śrī-Viṣṇu.
[280] [281] Likewise—
O All-pervading Lord, O Hari, having propitiated You, the bestower of liberation, what person would desire any other boon than service to Your feet, which is the most sought-after by the destitute?
"Let the noble one choose as his boon the bondage of the self.
[BhP 10.51.55] They are "possessing nothing," meaning they are devoid of desires even for liberation;
the reason for this is: "Having propitiated you, who?"

The meaning is that one should choose—that is, take refuge in—you who are the giver of liberation (apavargada) and who manifest as the giver of liberation. The indeclinable *varam* means "slightly dear";
thus, one should choose even one's own bondage as something slightly dear.
And immediately after this, in the passage beginning with "Having bestowed blessings upon him... (BhP 10.51.56) and including the word "Nirañjana" (the Stainless One),
the nature of that Puruṣottama— who is already established as the object of service by virtue of being the feet of worship— is described as *saccidānanda* (existence, consciousness, and bliss).
This is indeed what was intended.

Mucukunda [addressed] the Blessed Lord: "In this service of the feet—[consisting of] seeing, touching, circumambulating, following after, and [serving] the form of the Blessed Lord—" [10.51] [282] [283] Here, regarding the service of the feet, [the text mentions] the sight of the glorious form, its touch, circumambulation, following behind, and the Blessed Lord...
Visits for bathing at his holy sites, such as Mandira-Gaṅgā, Puruṣottama, Dvārakā, Mathurā, and others, are also to be included [within this category],
because they are essentially part of that [devotional service].
