I dwell with that very self as my sole delight. [BhP 11.8.40]
"Amunā" means together with the delight that is pregnant with the true nature of reality;
first, I dwell by means of the self—that is, by the mind alone.
For this path, in which aesthetic inclination (*ruci*) is paramount, the mind is the primary factor.
Because, for one who has not yet attained the form of the Beloved, such worship is generally appropriate through the mind alone;
by this [it is shown] that the venerable...
Even in the case of images and the like, such arrogance is avoided;
the same should be understood to apply to states such as being a father and so forth.

// 11.8 // Śrī-Piṅgalā // 311 // [312-314] Thus has been shown the one consisting of the conceit of being a beloved wife; this is found in the *Brahmavaivarta* Purāṇa, in the section on the arts of love (*kāmakalā*).
Furthermore, attachment and devotion consisting of the conceit of being a servant and so forth should be understood as occurring elsewhere.
Thus, in the passage beginning with *tasmā amūs tanu-bhṛtām* (BhP 7.9.24), the words of Śrī Prahlāda are: "Lead me to the side of Your own servants."

As it is said in the Śrī-Nārada-Pañcarātra: "O Lord of the World, when will You, endowed with splendor, speak with a deep voice to me, whose hand is occupied with a fly-whisk, saying, 'Do this'? Thus it is said.
As it is told in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Sanatkumāra-prokta Saṃhitā*, within the narrative of King Prābhākara:
"Though he was childless, he did not desire a son, reflecting upon his duties [and] upon Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, the Soul of All, the Eternal."
Having formally adopted as his son that which is to be known through all the Upaniṣads,
King Svarāja proceeded to consecrate him according to the prescribed rites.
He did not directly petition Janārdana for a son, [for] the boon of the Lord had already been granted:
"I shall become your son," and so forth.
Therefore, it is said in the *Śrī-Nārāyaṇa-vyūha-stava*:
"Salutations again and again to those who, ever-diligent, meditate upon Dharma as they would their husband, son, friend, brother, or father, and with the same affection as toward a mother.

Here, the phrase "as [toward] a husband, etc. is to be understood as a qualification of the object of meditation (the dhyeya), while "as toward a father" is a qualification of the meditator (the dhyātṛ). Likewise...

By the suffix *vat* in the expression "like a mother" (*mātṛvat*), it is not at all accepted that there is a cultivation of non-difference from that well-known mother; rather, it is simply the cultivation of being conformed to her.

In this same way, it should be understood regarding the state of being a father and so forth; otherwise, just as there would be a fault in the worship of the Blessed One through the practice of identifying with Him (*ahaṅgrahopāsanā*), there would likewise be a fault in those cases.
Thus, by the phrase "meditating," the previously mentioned primacy of the mind is indeed accepted. Furthermore—
By this statement, the principle of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument) regarding those things established by various forms of attachment is implied.

Now, one might object: according to the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā sūtra, "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (1.1.2), it is heard that in the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā system, the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is produced solely through an injunction (*vidhi*).

Likewise, in the *Yāmala*, a fault is heard regarding the performance without the procedure prescribed in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and *Pañcarātra*, and so forth; that is, a fault is heard for performing without the restrictive sequence mentioned in any one of those sources such as the *Śruti*. Thus:

"The Śruti and Smṛti are my very commands; he who acts by transgressing them is a violator of my command and a hater of me. Even if he be my devotee, he is certainly not a Vaiṣṇava. Here, the transgression of the mandatory rites and prohibitions declared in the Śruti and other scriptures constitutes the loss of Vaiṣṇava-hood.
An objection is heard:
"How, then, can there be accomplishment by that [devotion] independently of scriptural injunction? It is replied:
Because the power of the object—namely, the name, qualities, and so forth, of the illustrious Blessed One—is established, devotion does not depend on ritual duty (*dharma*) as [other means might].
[The result] is dependent upon an injunction (*codanā*).
Therefore, it is heard in many places that the attainment of the fruit occurs even without knowledge and so forth;
however, the injunction applies specifically to those cases where there is no spontaneous inclination [toward action].
Likewise, the sequential method (krama-vidhi) has that as its object;
for in that very state characterized by various distractions, there is an absence of interest due to devotion consisting of passion (rāga).
He does not understand the proper method;

for even when performing the practice in some manner— whether by running or closing his eyes, according to the maxim beginning with "even though there is [a path]," and so forth— if success were achieved through such performance, then the true path would be...
It is fashioned as a boundary for the sake of gradual entry and for the sake of mental attachment;

otherwise, due to the absence of such a taste that would cause a continuous inclination toward devotion and because of the failure to accept the boundary, one is struck down by internal and other portents. But it is not...
Even though it possesses spontaneous activity, it establishes a boundary;
for, by the very inclination of that [activity], there arises through the Lord’s grace an adherence to specific stages characterized by delightful passion.
This has been stated by Him Himself in such passages as, "Whether knowing Me or not knowing Me" (BhP 11.11.33), and so forth;
for even the ill-intentioned devotion of those whose nature is characterized by passion becomes identical [to pure devotion] through mere imitation.
Attainment is heard of, as in the case of Pūtanā through her imitation of a nurse;
thus it has been said: "The good..."
"If even Pūtanā, along with her kin, [was liberated] as if by mere dress" (BhP 10.14.35)—
how much more so for those who possess delight in Him through the practice of such constant and perfect devotion? As it has been said:
Pūtanā, the demoness who slays the children of the world and subsists on blood,
attained the state of the righteous even by giving her breast to Hari with the intent to kill him.
"How much more so for one who, with faith and devotion, offers what is most dear to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self; indeed, those who are attached to Him are like His own mothers.
Thus it is said: "For those who are single-mindedly devoted to Me, there are no qualities arising from virtue or vice" (BhP 10.20.4).

Thus, exclusive devotion (ekāntitva) is indeed the culmination of bhakti. It arises either through personal inclination alone or through respect for the injunctions of the scriptures. Since such inclination is rare, that which constitutes exclusivity even in the absence of the latter [scriptural injunction]—that is [the subject].
The meaning is that for one who possesses such absolute pride, it is mere hypocrisy;
therefore, its censure follows immediately thereafter through such passages as those found in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas.
However, even if there is a personal preference for such acts, it is not proper to censure them, as in the case of Pūtanā and others. Thus it is said in the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
"A great deed may be performed out of one's own independent will, and not merely because it is enjoined by the Vedas."
"Those who lack even the pleasure [derived from] the Blessed One are indeed considered heretics.
Here, "pleasure" refers to such a liking (*ruci*).
Thus, in this context, there is a censure of precisely the disregard for the Teacher, and not [of the Teacher] himself.
Regarding the phrase "running with eyes closed due to ignorance" and so forth,
this is also stated in the *Gautamīya-tantra* on page 165:
For those who constantly contemplate the lotus feet of Kṛṣṇa, there is neither recitation, nor worship, nor meditation, nor even the sequence of ritual injunctions.

However, for one in whom such a taste has not yet arisen, even that practice which follows from passion (*rāgānugā*) must be performed as conjoined with the scriptural injunction (*vaidhī*), merely out of respect for the excellence of the virtuous.
Likewise, for one who is established [in the path] for the sake of maintaining the world (*loka-saṃgraha*), [the practice] in whom such a taste has arisen...
And according to one's inclination; furthermore, in this case of mixing, the *vaidhī* [meditation] should be performed by unifying [the object] with the flow of passion (*rāgānugaya*) as appropriate.
Some meditate on the eighteen-syllable mantra as being composed of all those things—such as the time of milking the cow and the playing of the flute—drawn forth by it.

And just as I consider that certain such forms of worship were directly instructed for me— specifically for the people of Vraja— by the venerable feet of my guru for the sake of accomplishing my particular desired goal;
They contemplate that he is indeed serving the Lord, the son of the King of Vraja, in person; thus,
even while performing his own necessary duties— which are merely those enjoined by the Vedas and Smṛtis, such as "The Vedas and Smṛtis are my very commands"— he remains focused on Him.
The transgression of prohibitions is of two kinds,
for they are either those declared in the Dharmaśāstras or those declared in the Bhaktiśāstras.

Whether through faith in devotion to the Blessed One or through misconduct, there is no falling away from the state of being a Vaiṣṇava in the case of proximity to the non-performance or performance of the two [obligatory duties], because of such statements as: "Of gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, and men... (BhP 11.5.37).
Moreover, because of such statements as "even if one is of very wicked conduct" (Gītā 9.30),
for one who possesses such a taste, [the Lord is dear] precisely because of that very taste, despite being [otherwise] disliked.
There is not even a desire for the bliss of non-rebirth, much less for that which is the object of supreme loathing;
therefore, there is no spontaneous inclination toward it.
If, however, through negligence or the like, some improper action (*vikarma*) should occasionally occur, [it must be remedied].
It perishes in an instant.
And it has been said: "Seated within the heart, he shakes off all improper action (vikarma), however it may have arisen" (BhP 11.5.38).
Now, regarding those two mentioned in the Vaiṣṇava scriptures: they have as their sole purpose the pleasing of Viṣṇu alone.
And since it is heard that they are of such a nature, one who possesses a natural inclination and taste for them [will be drawn to them] spontaneously.
There would be both engagement and non-engagement,
because the arising of joy has its sole life-force in that satisfaction; for this very reason,
there is no distinction therein between what is done and what is not done by a particular perfected devotee whose nature is characterized by the passion being followed within himself.
And investigation would have to be required;
however, the distinction is simply this: when that [recollection] has been produced, there occurs a non-grasping of the qualifier.

In this regard, since even the expectation of the sequence and rules prescribed in the scriptures occurs through the very inclination of passion (*rāga-ruci*), it falls within the category of *rāgānugā* (practice following passion).
And those who are devoted to the *anugā* consisting of passion that shines forth in Śrī Gokula and other such places [are likewise included].

They, however, perform the practice of Vaiṣṇava worldly duties (*laukika-dharma*) precisely according to the intention of Śrī Kṛṣṇa— which consists of the desire for His own welfare, the absence of obstacles to association with Him, and so forth. Therefore,
because it is *ruci* (inclination) alone that initiates the true dharma (*sad-dharma*) within the path of *rāgānugā*, the *śruti* and *smṛti* are indeed My commands.
Thus, this statement does not have as its object the path of devotion to Him;
rather, its object is exclusively the paths of worship established by external scriptures, such as those of Buddha, Ṛṣabha, Dattātreya, and others.
Thus it has been said:
"O Lord, if one whose soul is opposed to the Vedic dharma should worship you,
he goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all that has been summoned."
Thus, even though the *rāgānugā* [form of worship] is not enjoined by scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), it does not lie outside the Veda;
for it is well-known within the Veda and the Vedas, as it is practiced according to one's inclination in various contexts.
However, the description of Buddhas and others within the Vedas is outside the Vedic tradition and is indeed contradictory, as it is said:
"Then, when the Kali age had begun, [these were created] for the delusion of the enemies of the gods."
"Buddha, the son of Añjana, will appear among the Kīkaṭas"—and so forth.
Therefore, devotion following from attachment (*rāgānugā*) is indeed valid;
likewise, that which arises from scriptural injunction (*vaidhī*) is also superior.
For it has been shown that the statement regarding the boundary (*maryādā*) is indeed for the purpose of [indicating] immersion (*āveśa*).
Furthermore, that immersion occurs through a mental state characterized by a particular inclination (*ruci*), and not otherwise. (Page 166)
By the impulsion of ritual injunction; for that [mind] has the nature of being spontaneous, and let there be,
for now, a state of conformity toward it.

Even through that which is most strictly prohibited, by way of an adverse disposition, entry [into the state] may occur instantaneously; by the power of that entry, the defects of the adverse state shall be eliminated,
and there shall be the cessation of all misfortune.
An illustration is also seen regarding the power of the path of devotion (*bhāva-mārga*):
in that regard, if there is a favorable disposition, then even the attainment of the goal is accomplished solely through supreme single-minded devotion (*paramaikāntika*).
Now, the section concerning the superior power of the general path of devotion (*bhakti-mārga*) is introduced.
Śrī Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Oh, how truly wonderful this is, which is difficult even for those who are exclusively devoted (*ekāntin*) to attain!"

"O Sage, we all desire to know this: how it was that the attainment of Vāsudeva, the supreme reality, occurred for the enemy Caidya, since such attainment is not possible even for those who are single-mindedly devoted and possess supreme knowledge."
"By reviling the Blessed One, Vena was cast into darkness by the twice-born.
"In darkness" means in hell;
after experiencing many hells and other such states, there follows the birth as Pṛthu.
"Because of hearing about the emergence of his power,
he— this sinful son of Damaghoṣa, starting from his sweet speech, as well as the impatient Dantavakra and the evil-minded one toward Govinda— is now [hostile]," and so forth. [BhP 7.1.17]
Clearly.
Yudhiṣṭhira [spoke to] Nārada.
(312–314) [315–320] Thereupon, the illustrious Nārada spoke this reply: "Oh, Blessed One! By the fall into hell of one who reviles the Lord..."
What is your intention in saying that it "must be cultivated"? Is it because it causes affliction to the Blessed One,
or because— even in its absence— it is heard as a censure of what is prohibited, like the drinking of liquor and so forth?
In that regard, first of all,
for deluded people, censure and the like proceed solely with reference to the ordinary qualities such as *tamas* and so forth.

Consequently, for that [Supreme Being] whose locus extends up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is no engagement at all with the censure and so forth produced by that nature regarding His transcendental qualities,
form, and the like; nor is He, like the individual soul (*jīva*), subject to the reality that extends up to primordial nature.
Once [the state] has arisen, there is the conceit of being the Blessed One;
consequently, for him, there is indeed no suffering whatsoever. This very point is stated in three and a half verses:

O King, this body is fashioned by the lack of discrimination between the primary material cause (pradhāna) and the Supreme (para) for the sake of censure, praise, honor, and insult. Censure (*nindana*) is the proclamation of faults.
"Insult" means contempt.
For the sake of discerning censure, praise, and so forth,
the body is imagined for living beings through the non-discrimination between the Pradhāna and the Puruṣa.

It was thus composed. And therefore: "O King, through pride in that [self], there arises violence, as well as harshness of punishment; and here among living beings, the inequality of 'mine' and 'I' [prevails]."
This egoism is bound to that [body]; by its destruction, there is the destruction of living beings.
Likewise, for the Self of all, there is no egoism apart from absolute liberation (kaivalya).
For how can violence be attributed to one who effects the self-restraint of another?
In this worldly realm of material nature, just as there is the sense of "mine" and "I" among living beings due to identification with that physical body...
An inequality arises;
for instance, through the harshness of punishment and verbal abuse committed by him, which serve as the causes, violence also occurs.
The meaning is that just as the killing of a living being occurs through the destruction of that body with which one identifies, so too it does not occur for one who has no such identification.
For what reason could violence be attributed to this Supreme Lord? The meaning is that it cannot be for any reason at all.
Furthermore, the reason for the absence of such conceit is his absolute isolation (*kaivalya*).

Because of the purity established through the principle of *kaimutya* (the "how much more so" argument) in the passage: "Those who dwell in the city of Vaikuṇṭha are devoid of body, senses, and life-breath" (BhP 7.1.35);
such is the pure *saccidānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss), which is inaccessible to censure and the like.
The meaning is "because it begins with *vigraha*," etc.;
and its being inaccessible to that [intellect] is expressed by the words "I am not manifest" (*nāhaṃ prakāśaḥ*).

"Enveloped by the yoga-māyā of all" (Gītā 7.25); from the Śrī Bhagavad Gītā [it follows that He is distinct]. The reason for such distinction is that He is the Self of all; the reason for that is His being the Supreme.
For one who is free from attachment to the power of *prakṛti*,
there is another reason why violence is not an object [of action]: because the Subduer possesses supreme, wondrous, and infinite power, he is the instructor of all beings.

Thus, since there is no partiality in the Blessed One caused by censure or the like, therefore, even that which is merely a semblance of Him— such as "by whatever means, even once, [an image of His limb]" (BhP 10.12.39)— is likewise [efficacious].

Because for one who meditates upon Him, through that very absorption—even for one who meditates with enmity—there is the destruction of even the sins committed through censure and the like by means of that absorption itself; thus, attaining union (*sāyujya*) and other states is appropriate. With this intention, he says "Therefore" and so forth. For instance:

Therefore, one should engage [the mind] through the persistence of enmity, or through freedom from enmity, or through fear, or through affection, or through desire; in no way should one look upon it as separate.
Regarding the word "yuñjyāt" (one should engage), since it is impossible to enjoin affection, desire, and so forth, it refers merely to their possibility.

The term *liṅ* [indicates]: if one should apply oneself to, or meditate upon, even one of the factors such as the persistence of enmity (*vairānubandha*) and so forth, then one does not perceive the Blessed One as separate; the meaning is that one becomes possessed by that [state]. "Persistence of enmity" (*vairānubandha*) refers to enmity—...
The non-interruption of existence;
"without enmity" (nirvaira) refers merely to the absence of enmity, which is called equanimity (audāsīnya).
By this, the state of being devoid of desire and so forth is also implied.
The meaning is the absence of states such as enmity; or, by means of that absence of states such as enmity, one should apply oneself [to meditation];
one should meditate with the mere thought that it is prescribed.

The meaning is that one should practice *bhakti-yoga* characterized by meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). "Affection" (*sneha*) refers to a particular kind of natural love between two people, characterized by an intense passion beyond ordinary desire.
For the practitioner, however, it is simply that very inclination toward Him.

Thus, since it is established that for all of them the fruit is indeed that possession (āveśa) by Him, in order to quickly achieve such possession through those paths consisting of devotion (bhāva), there is no equality between devotion consisting of ritual injunction (vidhi-bhakti) and even the most censured enmity (vaira).
Thus he said:
"It is my firm conviction that a mortal does not attain such absorption through the yoga of devotion as he does through the persistence of enmity. [BhP 7.1.27]

The phrase "by a continuity of enmity" is also an elliptical indication of fear. For instance, through the rapid attainment of identification with that [object] or absorption in it— [an absorption] performed by means of *bhakti-yoga* consisting merely of the thought that one is acting according to scriptural injunction— it does not [occur].
Likewise: let alone the matter of the Blessed One—who possesses the power of such objects and who manifests within them—or even the appearance of the Blessed One’s form;
[let alone that], even in the case of the ordinary person, there is merely the state of being that [Blessed One].

The great fruit of becoming absorbed in what is to be cultivated is observed; he demonstrates this very point with an illustration: "A worm confined within a wall by a silk-worm caterpillar, while remembering that [caterpillar], attains its very nature through the union of intense longing and fear."
Thus, when the Lord Kṛṣṇa appeared as a human through His illusory power (māyā), those whose sins were purified by enmity attained Him by constant meditation upon Him.
"Saṃrambha" means hatred and "bhaya" means fear; "yoga" refers to absorption in those two states, and by that [absorption], they attained Him.
"Tat-svarūpatām" means its own nature, its own form or configuration; "that which possesses that" is the meaning of "tat-sārūpyam" (similarity to that). "Evam" has the sense of "even so."
Since he is the Supreme Brahman in human form, appearing as an ordinary man only through *māyā*,
surely there is no sin in hating him even if one were to harm an insect.

Anticipating the objection that this might be the case there, he says: "By the very contemplation [of the enemy] through enmity, one whose sins are purified by that very [contemplation] becomes possessed of Him; the sense is that the absorption in His meditation possesses such power."
Nor should it be said that perfection is attained only through the dharma of the Lord as prescribed in the scriptures, and not through desire and so forth as prescribed therein; for [it is said]:
"Whether out of desire, hatred, fear, or affection, just as the mind is fixed on the Lord through devotion... (page 168).
"Having entered into that and abandoned their sin, many have attained His state.

(BhP 7.1.29) The meaning is that just as people attain His state by entering the mind into the Lord through prescribed devotion (*bhakti*), so too have many attained it through desire and other such [unprescribed] means.
Among those [defilements] such as desire and so forth, having abandoned that evil which consists of hatred and fear—
one should understand that fear also produces evil because it is permeated by hatred.
In this regard, some consider even desire to be a sin;
concerning this, it is investigated whether, in the case of the Blessed One, desire alone brings about sin, or rather desire when conjoined with the state of being a husband.
Alternatively,

if it is argued that he alone is "endowed with the state of being a paramour," then is he not likewise [an object of aversion] because he has fallen into the category of those characterized by hatred and so forth?
Or [it may be] by way of its very own nature.

Or else, it is by way of transgression—namely, through the drinking from the lower lip and so forth toward the Lord who is supremely pure, or through the imposition of [attributes such as] being a lustful man and so forth—or by hearing of sin. It is not by the first [of these].

This was stated previously: "And that Caidya attained perfection, even though he was an enemy of Hṛṣīkeśa; how much more so those who are dear to Adhokṣaja? (BhP 10.29.13). In this passage, hatred and the like are disparaged, whereas devotion to Him is praised.

And therefore, because desire (*kāma*) consists of pleasure (*prīti*), just like affection (*sneha*), there is no fault in its being like that [affection], as in the case of "beloved ones" (*priyāḥ*).
For desire is indeed of such a nature.
He whose sole form is love;
as in the verse beginning, "O Beloved, fearing the roughness of your well-formed lotus-feet, we place them gently upon our breasts," he disregards even his own pleasure.
For it is observed that the intention [of the Lord] is directed solely toward what is favorable to them; however, the disposition of Sairindhrī consists primarily of a desire for sexual pleasure,
and because she lacks that exclusive intention found in the Śrī Gopīs, she is censured only in comparison to them, but not by her very nature.

In passages such as *sānaṅga-tapta-kucayoḥ* (BhP 10.48.6), they praise Him by way of their own effects, stating that "they wipe away their pains with His infinite feet" and "having embraced their beloved, who is the embodiment of bliss. Even there, in the verse *sahoṣyatām iha preṣṭha* (BhP 10.48.8), there is [an expression of] love—
And she was manifested;
for this very reason: "Having thus attained that Lord, the Master of Kaivalya, who is so difficult to reach..."

"Alas! Having propitiated Viṣṇu, the Lord of all lords, who is otherwise so difficult to please, this unfortunate woman has asked for this by offering her body's unguents. "That person of evil intellect, being devoid of true essence, chooses that which is grasped only by the mind after having worshipped Him. *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* 10.48.8–11.
And they apply the text in this way:
*kaivalya* means exclusivity;
he who is the Lord to be served by means of that [exclusivity]—him [one should serve].
Formerly, although she possessed such misfortune characterized by the three-fold crookedness and other defects—
oh, what a wonder!— now, by means of this portion of the Lord's dharma characterized by the application of bodily unguents, this [body] has become... [beautiful].
"O dearest one, stay here with me for a few days and enjoy yourself"—it was by such words as these that he begged for the fortune of his love. Therefore:
"What merit has been performed by this mendicant Avadhūta?"
"Deprived of fortune, censured in this world, and base"—
this statement is just like the words of the city-dwellers addressed to the brāhmaṇa Śrīdāman;
for is she not indeed a lustful woman?
Why is she praised?
To this he says: "difficult to propitiate.
[She is difficult to propitiate] because she is not that which is grasped by the mind as something ordinary.
In this very way, that person of evil intellect chooses and desires an object;
however, she [the goddess] desires only the Blessed One— thus the sense is that she is indeed one of supreme intelligence.
Thus,
having avoided [the charge] that such desire is included within the category of hatred and the like, its nature as a bringer of evil has been refuted.
Now, even the worldly practice therein— consisting of the attribution of lustfulness and so forth, as well as acts such as drinking from the lower lip— is likewise [refuted].
It is not a cause for transgression, because,
according to the maxim "but as in the world, sport is the sole motive," sport is established there by its very nature.

And herein, it is understood that through His [pastimes] such as Śrī, Bhū, and Līlā, His enjoyment of independent pastimes is realized precisely because such pastimes are eternally established in Śrī-Vaikunṭha and other realms.

Likewise, because the beloved women [of the Lord] also possess forms that are the very nature and potency (*svarūpa-śakti*) of Him, they are of supremely pure form; and since there is no difference between them and Him, even the drinking from His lips and so forth would not be appropriate [from a worldly perspective]. Nevertheless, according to the previous reasoning, these acts are indeed desired by Him. Nor is it the case that...
A fault should not be imputed by ordinary people;
for it is only by attaining that appropriate state and such a nature— consisting of the form of His own essential power— that He attains it through His own will alone.
Furthermore, that desire does not bring about evil simply by hearing of it,
precisely because of not hearing of it; and since she was already united with him as her husband, there is certainly no fault in this.
On the contrary, praise is heard:
"What can be described as the austerity of those who, with love, served the Teacher of the World with the thought that He was their husband, by massaging His feet and other such acts? (BhP 10.9.27).
The state of that [devotion] is also heard of among munis of great majesty;
as in the words of the Kurma Purāṇa cited by the venerable Mādhvācārya:

"The high-souled daughters of Agni, through their ascetic penance, chose womanhood [for themselves] and Lord Vāsudeva— the unborn, all-pervading source of the universe— as their husband. For this very reason, He is saluted with the words "husband, son, friend, brother," and so forth.

Furthermore, this [conduct] does not bring about sin by way of being a paramour, because it was answered by those very women themselves with the words: "O dear one, [it is not so], for there is compliance toward the husband, children, and friends" (BhP 10.29.19), and so forth;
thus it applies to both the gopīs and their husbands.
And by such words of Śrī Śuka as:
"O gods, even with a lifespan equal to yours, I am not able to describe the virtuous deeds of you who are united with the faultless. [BhP 10.32.22]

Thus, here by the phrase "of those who are faultlessly united," both the venerable Lord himself and others such as these are seen to possess that same state. For example, there is a statement from the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the Padma Purāṇa:
In former times, all the great sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest,
upon seeing Rāma, who was Hari himself, desired to eat his beautifully formed body there.
"They all attained womanhood and were born in Gokula;
having obtained Hari through desire, they were thereafter liberated from the ocean of worldly existence" (Padma Purāṇa 6.245.164).
Therefore, because they arose even among men in the form of women and because their object was the Blessed Lord, they were not *prākṛta* (ordinary).

For it is heard in scripture that "this common passion aroused by the god of love is, in truth, the destroyer of Manmatha himself," and because he is worshipped as the very embodiment of desire (*kāma*) in the Āgamas and other texts.
It should be understood that this very Kāma was manifested by the Blessed Lord Himself as something truly extraordinary;
for even among His supreme devotees, such as Śrī Uddhava and others, praise for Him is heard in passages such as: "These cowherd women on earth are the foremost among embodied beings" (BhP 10.47.51).
What more need be said? That state [of being the Lord] is well-known even for the Vedas in the *Bṛhad-vāmana-purāṇa*;
for therein, even the Śrutis are described as eternal—(page)
170) It is well known that those who desired the state of perfected gopīs became members of his retinue in that very form. This very fact is indicated by what was said by them themselves:

Even his enemies attained that which sages, yoked in firm yoga of breath, mind, and senses, worship within their hearts— merely by remembering Him; for women fixed their minds upon His staff-like arms, which were like the coils of the lord of serpents.
"We too are equal to them, seeing with an equal eye, having drunk the nectar of their lotus feet" (BhP 10.87.23).
This meaning is perfectly clear:
that the reality called Brahman, which is attained through the study of the scriptures and effort—

The sages mostly worship that [Lord], yet even His enemies have attained Him merely by remembering Him, without having to perform such worship. Likewise, O Śrī Nandanandana, those women— the beautiful-browed gopīs—
whose minds are truly fixed upon Your two staff-like arms, which are equal to the body of the king of elephants, are indeed possessed of true devotion.
The nectar of Your very lotus feet attained the sweetness of love born from the particularity of contact with Her; we,
the Vedas, though possessing equal vision and being true, attained equality with them by attaining the state of such gopīs, yet we have gone only as far as the nectar of the dust of those feet.
The meaning is as follows:
the transformation of case endings occurs by virtue of the sense;
"aṅghri" is a term used out of respect.
Here, by the phrase "even his enemies went [to him] through remembrance," the fact that the path of devotion (bhāva-mārga) accomplishes its goal instantaneously is demonstrated.
By the phrase "those of equal vision" (sama-dṛśaḥ), it is indicated that among those paths, the path of attachment (rāgānugā) alone is the most effective means for that end.
Otherwise, the Śrutis, which are experts in all means and ends, would apply elsewhere. Likewise,
in this pair of pairs consisting of remembrance (smaraṇa) and the other [perception], it is shown that the first in each respective pair is primary and the second is secondary.
Since the word "api" (also/even) occurs in both instances and is read together with the subsequent passage, they must have the same meaning;
therefore, those referred to as "women" should be understood as the eternal Śrī-Gopikās.
Likewise, it is well known in the *Bṛhad-vāmana* that "they were seen by the Vedas" in the eternal abode of Śrī Kṛṣṇa; thus,
the sin mentioned in the passage beginning with "out of lust or out of hatred" has been correctly explained.
Regarding the phrase "having abandoned" (*hitvā*), among those [categories], there is the passage beginning with "the evil of hatred and fear" (*dveṣa-bhayayor yad-aghama*).
Then, in order to illustrate the statement "many have gone to that state," he says:
"The cowherd women out of desire, Kaṃsa out of fear, and King Caidya and others out of hatred."
"O Lord, you are the Vṛṣṇis because of our relationship; you are we because of your affection and devotion.
This statement is made by relying on the previous state of those specific gopīs who follow the path of the *sādhaka*.
The word "we" refers to how, when I was employed by Śrī Nārada, he said: "In me, that pure *bhāgavatī*..."

Since the status of being an attendant (*pārṣada*) has been established through the manner described in the verse beginning with *tanum* (BhP 1.6.28), the statement "we ourselves" is made by relying on their former state;
therein lies ritualistic devotion (*vaidhī bhakti*). Now—

For one who has attained such passion, the qualities arising from virtues and defects do not apply— according to the maxim, "for those with exclusive devotion to Me" (BhP 11.20.36)— and thus his state shines forth as consisting solely of passion, independent of scriptural injunctions. For this very reason,
the phrase "they have gone to that goal" indicates that even their attainment of the fruit is already in the past.
In this regard,
even contemporary women and men may attain that same state of being through merely hearing of His qualities and other attributes, just as it is said:
"He who, upon being heard of alone, forcibly draws away the minds of women."
"Or rather, he who is wide-striding and widely-praised—how much more so for those who behold him? (BhP 10.90.17).

Alternatively, even for Caidya, who was a follower of the attendants (*pārṣada*), his status as a means of accomplishment is indicated simply by the observation of the disappearance of the appearance of adventitious afflictions.

"The affection that arises from relationship is passion; because of that, you Vṛṣṇis and [I]..."—this constitutes one [instance]. In this illustrative sentence, because it clearly demonstrates the same meaning as what was stated previously in "because of that continuity of enmity" and so forth, and in "from desire" and so forth, it serves as an example of that very point.
The phrase "of the five" is used in accordance with what will be stated [later]; thus,
it is connected to both cases.
And because both types of affection exist, the mention of their relationship is for the purpose of making known the specific nature of passion alone;
here too, as in the case of the cowherd women, the particular Vṛṣṇis are the objects of the practitioners' pursuit.

Furthermore, the specific qualities related to the Pāṇḍavas are indicated as the means of accomplishment by relying upon their previous state; therefore, even in the case of affection born of relationship, it should be understood as being merely a matter of personal inclination toward them. By means of devotion thus established, in order to indicate the path of realization (*bhāva-mārga*) through its very attainment:
Because he had been attacked. Anticipating the objection, "If perfection can be achieved even through hatred, then why was Vena cast into hell?", he says:
"Not even one among the five would be Vena toward a person. (BhP 7.1.31)
With reference to the Blessed One as the object, none of the five types of animosity, such as enmity and so forth, would exist;
for him, there is only incidental censure directed toward him.
The enmity was of a limited duration and not a persistent state of hostility;
therefore, the sense is that because there was an absence of intense meditation [on hatred], it was only the evil [of the initial act] that bore fruit there.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that even those whose nature is equal to that of asuras should not commit the rash act of pursuing enmity for the sake of their own liberation.

Therefore, even the over-extension of the rule regarding the passage beginning with "Those indeed who have been spoken of by the Blessed One" (BhP 11.2.32) is precluded, because they are not considered "spoken of" since that was not his intended meaning.
For this reason:
"Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa" (BhP 7.1.31).
Here too, as before, the phrase "one should fix" (*niveśayet*) expresses mere approval (*sammati-mātra*) rather than an injunction (*vidhi*).
By whatever [means], even among those...
The meaning is: by means of a single most effective method.

That which is accomplished only after a long time through the path of ritualistic devotion (*vaidhi-bhakti*) is accomplished there without delay merely through a specific state of being (*bhāva-viśeṣa*).
And this is true even regarding hatred and the like.

Therefore, when he is of such a nature—the very essence of supreme and excellent qualities—let alone talk of hostility, which is the province of base people; for what inferior person could possibly maintain indifference toward him?
"Even by relying on affection, one should not act [in such a way]; thus, that very state of being most appropriate is accepted within the *rāgānugā* [path] alone.
(7.1) Śrī Nārada [spoke] to Yudhiṣṭhira. (312–323) [324]

Thus, although the path of devotion (bhāva-mārga) in its general form is indeed powerful, he states by way of a *kaimutya* argument that it is specifically the path following from passion (*rāgānugā*) that is the subject to be explained:
"Him whom kings such as Śiśupāla and Pauṇḍraka [assailed] with enmity..."

Śālva and others, meditating on Him through His gait, graceful movements, glances, and so forth, attained a likeness to Him while lying down, sitting, and in other postures—those whose minds were thus captivated; what then need be said of those whose hearts are devoted? [BhP 11.5.48]
Those whose cognitions of forms possess those various shapes—
thus it is said in the *Garuḍa*:
"The ignorant ones, reviling the best of gods..."
"Since even evildoers such as Śiśupāla and Suyodhana attained liberation, their sins being shaken off by mere remembrance,
what doubt can there be regarding those people who possess supreme devotion? Thus it is said.

In the verse, "Just as by the persistence of enmity" (BhP 7.1.26), one should not apply the idea that the persistence of enmity is superior to everything else. And as for the statement: "Having overcome the offense against a brāhmaṇa through the application of fury toward Me..."
"You two shall return to my presence again in a very short time," thus spoke Vaikuṇṭha to Jaya and Vijaya.
That too was merely an appearance of an offense on their part.
He manifests the semblance of exertion and application solely for the sake of enjoyment, because the attainment of those two is established by their very nature;
he elaborates that [manifestation] merely for the purpose of the sport of battle.
In this regard, some consider even hatred and the like to be forms of devotion (*bhakti*);
that is incorrect, because devotion consists of service and so forth.
For words are established only in accordance [with their conventional usage], whereas in the case of enmity, they are not so established because they are contrary to that [usage].

And in the *Pādmottara-khaṇḍa*, the distinction between devotion, hatred, and so forth is understood: "The Lord of Men (Janārdana) is seen by yogins through devotion; he is never seen through lack of devotion. He cannot be seen through anger or through envy. [PadmaP 6.238.83] Thus it is said.
And in this regard,
in such passages as "Surely I consider the Asuras to be Bhāgavatas" (BhP 3.2.24), the status of even those [Asuras] as Bhāgavatas is indicated in the speech of the venerable Uddhava.
Not so;
for since the word "I think" (manye) indicates a poetic fancy (utprekṣā), it is established that he himself does not possess the status of a Bhāgavata therein. That...
Therefore, it is entirely appropriate that he— possessing such grief and longing, and endowed with the mere fortune of a vision— should have composed this poetic fancy (utprekṣā);
for alas, we ourselves are merely those whose faces are turned outward.
For those who, at the time of death, do not even have the possibility of beholding the moon-like face [of the Buddha],
and from whom the asuras...
There were also devotees who,
at that time, attained the good fortune of beholding the moon-like face of Him.
Therefore, devotion can never exist in hatred and the like. Thus, the path of *rāgānugā* has been established. Śrī Nārada said to Śrī Vasudeva: [324] [325] Thus, *rāgānugā* has been proven.
And she, Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone, is the primary one,
because that very fact has been demonstrated by such statements as, "The gopīs [loved him] out of desire" (BhP 7.1.29).
For it is observed that even among the Daityas, there is the attainment of absorption (āveśa) in that very [deity] through hatred as well,
and because they achieve supernatural powers (siddhi).
But it is not elsewhere, neither in any other part nor in any other possessor of parts.
Therefore it has been said: "Therefore, by whatever means possible, one should fix the mind upon Kṛṣṇa."

And so forth. Therefore, because he has obtained the means for such immediate immersion (*jhaṭity-āveśa*), he himself does not describe the worship according to the Vedic injunctions (*vaidhopāsanā*) within the eleventh [chapter], but rather [describes] only the four-armed form elsewhere. And in that regard:
Because pure *rāga* is seen only in Śrī-Gokula, the path of *rāgānugā* is preeminent there; for indeed,
even the Lord Himself sports among them in the form of their sons and so forth, according to such statements as, "In whatever way they surrender unto Me" (Gītā 4.11).
From such passages as "the thunderbolt for the Mallas" (BhP 10.43.14) and from "consisting of His own will" (BhP 10.14.2),
it follows that [this is not] performed by a devotee.
Even the desire to fondle him, characterized by feeding, bathing, fanning, and so forth, arises for him as something entirely natural.
Indeed, it is through the very presence of common devotion that [the Lord says]:
"Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water..."
"Therefore, I eat what is offered with devotion by one whose self is purified"—thus it was said.
And Śrī Śukadeva praised this very point out of longing:
"Some massaged the feet of that Great Soul."
"Others, their sins destroyed, fanned him with fans," and so forth.
By this, there is no loss of his sovereignty;
for even at that time, his sovereignty was manifest elsewhere as well.
Because it is a matter of form; and because the quality of being composed of the devotee's desire is itself a praiseworthy nature in the Lord.
Just as He brought about the liberation from the Yamalārjuna trees while bound by the will of Śrī Vrajeśvarī, even with such sovereignty, His subjection to Śrī Vrajeśvarī was praised by Śrī Śukadeva.
This has indeed been demonstrated by the verse beginning with "evaṃ sandarśitā hy aṅga" (BhP 10.9.19).
Therefore,

for those who even today are devoted to the path of *rāgānugā* (devotion following the path of passion) toward Him, [He is perceived] solely through attributes such as His being the son of the King of Vraja.
This is consistent with the practice of worship,
as stated by the Blessed Lord Himself in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa to the cowherds who were filled with wonder at His lifting of Mount Govardhana:

"If you have affection for me, and if I am worthy of your praise, then let your mind toward me be like that toward your own kinsmen. (ViP 5.13.11). Alternatively, there is a reading: "Therefore, O kinsmen, show me the same honor as you would toward a relative. Likewise—
"I am neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor a yakṣa, nor a dānava;
I have been born as your kinsman, so there is no need for you to think otherwise.
And regarding the statement, "You two have treated me with the affection due to a son" (BhP 10.3.36), here [the meaning is] Śrī...
Since Vasudeva and the others are characterized primarily by sovereignty and knowledge, the Lord’s sanction for them should be understood as being twofold;
even in their previous birth, their devotion was said to be characterized primarily by austerity and other such qualities.
Therefore, rather than praising the splendor seen from the face of the illustrious Queen of Vraja,
one should highly esteem her very mercy— which consists of maternal affection and is synonymous with *māyā*—
and likewise the fortune of the illustrious Lord of Vraja, whose childhood [was graced by such grace].
"O Brahmin, what did King Nanda do when his mind was exalted by the playful display of his son's nature?"— with these two verses beginning thus,
the venerable King of Sages [Śukadeva Gosvāmī] described that very same state of his.
He praised love itself with the words beginning, "Thus, my dear friend, was He revealed by Hari" (BhP 10.9.29).
Having thus observed Śrī Vasudeva and Devakī, Śrī Nārada spoke to practitioners as follows:
Regarding what was taught in the passage beginning with "by seeing, embracing, and conversing" (BhP 11.5.43), the commentary states:

"Just as the entirety of the Bhāgavata dharma is accomplished simply by the fondling of a son," and likewise: "Therefore, do not maintain the notion that Kṛṣṇa—the Lord of all lords—is merely your offspring" (BhP 11.5.45). This is the point.
Furthermore, this has been introduced in the *Ṭīkā* in a manner consistent with that [view]:
"Now, if affection for one's son were the cause of liberation, then everyone would be liberated; to this he says: 'the notion that [he is] one's offspring. This is what was intended.

The meaning is that even though he has attained the state of being his offspring and has come under the influence of such a disposition toward him, there exists a natural and superior supreme sovereignty;
or else, it is as explained previously.
The augment *aṭ* is archaic (ārṣa); however, the letter *a* here signifies negation or absence, according to the lexicon which states that *an-* means "not.
Therefore, because of this double negation, the meaning is: "Form the very idea of [my] progeny.
For this very reason, disregarding both knowledge and ignorance, the performance of the path solely following attachment (*rāgānugā*) is praised.
This is established by such passages as, "Whether they have known Me or not" (BhP 11.11.33),
and so forth; therefore, because it is pure, devotion characterized by *rāga* (intense attachment) alone is the most preeminent within Śrī Gokula itself, and thus it is excellent.
Thus it has been said.

Therefore, since this [devotion] cannot exist elsewhere, the great majesty of the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa—characterized by a love that follows from passion (*rāgānugā*), the vision of the Self, and the vision of the Lord’s full divinity—is established as truly immense. Furthermore, therein...
Of Him whose nature consists of the pastimes in Gokula; now, he begins the description of the majesty of merely worshipping Him,
as follows:
"O sages, I have been well questioned by you for the welfare of the world, since you have inquired about Kṛṣṇa, by whom the self becomes perfectly serene. (BhP 1.2.5).
In this regard, it should be stated that previously, the cause of the mind's serenity was asked.
By this, however, only the question regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa has been stated as its cause;
it is not, however, "that indeed is the supreme duty of men."

Just as in the immediately following section [of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa], beginning with the verse cited above (1.2.6), the process starting from the diligent dedication of one's actions up to the culmination in devotion is described as the cause for the worship that occurs after the Lord's manifestation, so too is it stated here.
For this very reason, he states that even the discourse concerning other incarnations has nothing but attachment to them as its fruit:
"The stories of Hari, whose prowess is wonderful, are the supreme auspiciousness for the world."
Tell me, O highly fortunate one, how [I may abide] within the Self of all.
"Having fixed my mind without attachment upon Kṛṣṇa, I shall cast off this body"—thus [he spoke]. "Of Hari," meaning of that which is his form as an incarnation;
"in Kṛṣṇa, the soul of all and the possessor of all parts," [referring to] Śrīmad Arjuna.
Friend!
(174) [326] Likewise, as it is at the end of the Śrīmad-Uddhava-saṃvāda; for although in that regard, according to the previous chapter—

Although the Blessed Lord has stated that the practice of the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*), when described as being completed, produces its own fruit only through association with devotion (*bhakti*), nevertheless, Śrī Uddhava— the supreme devotee who does not accept even a fraction of that practice of the yoga of knowledge— says:
I consider this practice of yoga to be very difficult to master for one who lacks self-control;
tell me directly, O Acyuta, how a person may achieve perfection with ease.
"O lotus-eyed one, for the most part, yogis who strive to fix the mind fail due to a lack of concentration, being exhausted by the effort of restraining the mind. (BhP 11.29.1–2).
Here, in his own statement, he indicates that because this [restraint of the mind] is difficult to achieve, it generally lacks a successful conclusion.
Because it has been so stated; and because devotion that is being cultivated is intended as both easy to perform and as that which necessarily culminates in its fruit,
his own intention is that devotion to Him alone is what must be practiced.

Thus it has been shown. Therefore, disregarding that very practice of the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga-caryā*), even those who perform devotion—such as those who practice devotion specifically to Your form as Śrī Kṛṣṇa alone—do so precisely by disregarding the fruits of the yoga of knowledge and the like; this He states again in four verses.
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Lord of all, may the swans take refuge in Your lotus feet, which yield bliss; for through the practice of yoga and ritual action, they shall surely attain happiness.
"O proud ones, we are deluded by Your Māyā.

For this reason, some indeed despair; however, those who are like swans (*haṃsa*), skillful in discerning the essential from the non-essential, perceive only Your lotus feet—which fulfill all bliss—as the certain source of happiness.
They should resort to and serve [the Lord] in such a way that there may be devotion to His lotus feet;
this devotion to the feet is for the purpose of manifesting Your own lotus feet as they are directly perceived.
Moreover, these pure devotees, though obstructed by the performance of ritualistic yoga and by Your illusory energy, do not suffer any interruption in their practice of devotion.
For those who possess pride do not truly become proud; rather,
in the accomplishment of the goals of human endeavor, it is the Lord’s unconditional compassion for the destitute alone that is the most effective means.

The meaning is that they do not consider it to be the result of their own effort, as yogis and others do. He says this because the fruit obtained by such a devotee through the yoga of knowledge and so forth is not merely that, but something else, indeed great: [327] For one who is thus devoted, the fruit of the yoga of knowledge and so forth is not merely that, but something else, indeed great; thus he says:
O Acyuta, O friend of all, what wonder is there in this that You have made Yourself one with Your servants who have no other refuge? He who, though the Lord of lords, chose to dwell among the deer.
His footstool is pressed by the crowns of the glorious [gods];
He is the sole kinsman to His servants who have no other refuge,
or rather, the kinsman of all beings down to the asuras.
O Lord, it is not at all surprising that You, who are a kinsman providing unconditioned benefit through the granting of liberation and other blessings,

manifest Your own essence within Your pure devotees— such as Bali and others— who have no other refuge and are indifferent to the practice of knowledge, yoga, or ritual action, for their very self is Yours.
The meaning is "dependence.

This has been stated in such passages as, "Yoga does not establish me" (BhP 11.12.1), and so forth. Furthermore, for You, toward those who have become thus, there is no regard for birth, qualities, and the like, within the internal pastimes (*antaraṅga-līlā*).
He says "is even seen" and then "he who," meaning that which is seen.
"With" (saha) signifies coexistence, the sense being friendship; [it refers to] with the deer wandering in Vṛndāvana.
But as for himself, though he possesses such characteristics as "of the lords" (*īśvarāṇām*) and so forth— where "lords" refers to Śrī Śiva, Brahmā, and others—
he is the supreme fruit of knowledge, yoga, and so on.
You bestow upon the Daityas that liberation which consists of forms;
however, regarding Your servants, You remain personally subject to them, just as You abide in friendship with the Pāṇḍavas and others, in the role of a messenger, or in the posture of the hero.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that devotion to You, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who are of such a nature, is the primary [path].
He states the conclusion: (page 175)
Who indeed would abandon You— the Lord who is the beloved of the soul of all, the bestower of every goal upon those who have taken refuge in Him, and the knower of one's own deeds?
Or who would worship another, which leads only to forgetfulness and not to true prosperity?
Or what could possibly fail to come to pass for us who take refuge in the dust of Your feet?

Thus, from the instruction of the venerable Lord Kapila— beginning with the words, "To You who are thus situated, whose lotus-face is serene and whose eyes are as reddish as the interior of a lotus"— [he spoke] out of his own realization of what he had done.

"One who recognizes the benefit you have bestowed upon him—characterized by the manifestation of beauty and other qualities—who indeed would cast it away? And even that hook of the mind he gradually detaches" (BhP 7.28.34).
Thus, as taught therein, is it not abandoned only by a specific qualified person?
The meaning is that no one [is such]. Therefore, the implication is that whoever abandons you is indeed ungrateful. In what manner are you? By your very nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

"Thus [he says], 'the Lord who is dear to all as their own self, more beloved than ten million lives,' and so forth. Likewise, in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*): who else apart from you would worship any other deity as a means for dharma, knowledge, and the like, for prosperity (*bhūti*), for sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), for the forgetting of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), or for liberation (*mokṣa*)? No one at all."
The meaning is as follows: "But for us, even those various fruits are included within devotion to You alone"—thus he says, "And what more?
By the word "or" (vā), a disregard for even that [attainment] is indicated.
As it has been said: "That which is attained through ritual acts, that which by austerity..."
And so forth. O Lord,
even with a lifespan as long as that of Brahmā, the wise, remembering Your deeds, do not find sufficient praise for You, their joy being fully realized.
O Lord, he who, by shaking off the impurities of embodied beings both within and without,
reveals his own state through the forms of the Teacher and the Caitya—
though the wise are omniscient and possess a lifespan equal to that of Brahmā, they too [do not perceive it] until the end of that time.
The meaning is: "even while serving you.

Having experienced increased joy—meaning having attained the supreme bliss of devotion to you—and remembering the favor done by you, they remember the repayment, that is to say, the counter-favor which constitutes the clearing of their debt.
They do not approach her; they see her.
Therefore, it was said that one should not release [the seed]. He says what has been done: he who...
You, by virtue of being the vessel for Your grace among certain embodied beings who possess all bodies—
appearing externally in the form of a teacher (*ācārya*) as a guru, and internally in the form of a shrine (*caitya*) as the manifestation of the mind— [are present].

Shaking off all that is impure—which stands in opposition to devotion to You—by means of the form of the object of meditation, he manifests his own goal, which is self-experience. Thus ends the section on Śrī Uddhava (verses 11.29, 326–329). [330]
In the same way, the Śrī Bhagavān also spoke immediately thereafter regarding the excellence of his own bhakti;

and having spoken with four verses beginning with "Alas, I shall tell you of my pure bhakti directed toward such as you" (BhP 11.29.8), he further addressed those of such a nature out of compassion concerning his own worship.
He reflected on another matter for the sake of instigation through four points:
because people for the most part are intent on rivalry and the like, even when they somehow turn inward, [they do not realize] your nature as the inner controller of all.

Considering them to be knowers who possess only a partial understanding, out of compassion— in order to swiftly remove their competitiveness and other such traits, and to turn them inward toward Himself— He manifests His own portion in the form of the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin), as described in passages such as: "By a single fraction of Myself, I stand supporting this entire world" (Gītā 10.42).
He instructed him on his own vessel within the place of vessels, as follows:
"One who is pure in heart should behold Me alone—unveiled both externally and internally—within all beings, and the Self within oneself, like the ether. [BhP 11.29.12]
And the commentary says: "With the three verses beginning with 'mām', he speaks of internal devotion;
this [devotion] consists in perceiving Me alone—the Self abiding as the Lord—within all beings and within oneself. (page 176)
Of what nature is that Lord?
The meaning is that He is full both outside and inside. Why is that? Because He is unveiled, meaning free from all obscuration.
And why is that?
The meaning is: because space, being without limbs and being all-pervasive.

In this context, it has been explained that by saying "me alone," one should perceive the very form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and not merely the form of the internal controller (antaryāmin); it is with this intention that he spoke of "internal devotion" (antaraṅgā bhakti). [331]
And therefore—
O you of great splendor— he who honors all beings with the thought that they are of my own nature,
and who considers them so, relies solely upon knowledge.
"A wise person is considered one who looks with equanimity upon a Brahmin, a Pukkasa, a thief, a devotee of Brahman, the sun, a spark of fire, the non-cruel, and the cruel.
Even though he has resorted solely to knowledge and the vision of the Inner Controller (antaryāmi), in the manner previously described, he regards all things...

A wise person is considered such when, regarding all beings as being characterized by my own nature—that is, perceiving them as qualified by the existence of my own Śrī Kṛṣṇa-form—he honors them; and from my perspective, he is one who possesses equal vision toward Brahmins and others, seeing them all as equal to me alone. [332]

And then, having stated the fruit of such a specific form of one's own worship— characterized by the immediate destruction of rivalry and so forth— with the verse beginning "tataś ca nareṣv abhīkṣṇam" (BhP 11.29.15),
and having taught the means for seeing Him in that way, namely, prostration to all, with the verse beginning "visṛjya" (BhP 11.29.16), up until...

Having stated the limit of such meditation through the passage beginning with *ity ādinā*, and having declared that in all respects there is a spontaneous self-manifestation (*svataḥ sva-sphūrti*), he says through the passage beginning with *sarvam*— namely,
that which is meditated upon in the heart by those who discourse on Brahman as this Brahman, O Knower, is not like the [conceptualized] Brahman of the Neo-Vedantins (*navya*).
"Those who have gone there do not become deluded, they do not grieve, and they do not rejoice.

Thus, in the words of the Blessed Lord addressed to the Pracetasas, and in its commentary (*ṭīkā*), it has been stated that Brahman is precisely the ever-fresh manifestation (*navya-sphūrti*) of that Blessed Lord at every step; and that very thing is the fruit of that realization.

Having said this— or rather, having explained how the Brahman-hood of another incarnation occurs, and that the manifestation of the Supreme Brahman in human form, known by the name "Brahman" as established in the *Gopālatāpanī*, is its fruit— he praises such worship as being superior even to all else.
For this, in my view, is the most effective of all methods:
the manifestation of my own nature within all beings through the activities of mind, speech, and body.
"Of all methods" means of all means; "the most effective" means the most appropriate.

"Mad-bhāva" is the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of me in my form as Śrī Kṛṣṇa. And this [contemplation] is superior even to the worship of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmī*) through the worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Śrī...
In accordance with the conclusion of the Gītā, it has been said:
"O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine."
Go to Him alone as your refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared to you by me;
having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.
(Verse 18, p. 177) Hear again from Me the supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.
Fix your mind on Me, be My devotee, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me;
thus you shall come to Me alone. I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me.
"Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (Gītā 18.66).
And here, the "secret" refers to the knowledge taught in the preceding chapter.

The knowledge of the Inner Controller (antaryāmin) is more secret; the worship of Him—characterized by the state of having Him as one's mind and so forth, and characterized by taking refuge in Him alone—is the most secret of all; thus it is the same [as the previous statement].
Thus, in the very ninth chapter of the Śrī Gītā:
"But this most secret knowledge, along with realized wisdom (vijñāna), I shall declare to you, who are free from carping; having known which, you will be liberated from evil" (Gītā 9.1).
Having praised the subject matter about to be explained in the passage beginning with "The royal science, the royal secret" (Gītā 9.2),
Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself censured those who lack faith in His own worship in the form of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, while praising those who possess such faith, as follows:
The deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human form,
not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
Futile their hopes, futile their actions, futile their knowledge, and devoid of discernment,
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and fiendish.
"But those of great soul, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings" (Gītā 9.13).
The meaning is that they know me alone, who have assumed a human form out of disregard [for my true status]. Therefore...

Since worship of Śrī Kṛṣṇa is established as superior even to the worship of all internal controllers (antaryāmis) by virtue of being "the most secret of all" immediately following that statement— and because the word "all" is used here— it is proven that worship of Him is the highest of all; consequently,
its superiority over the worship of His other incarnations is established all the more clearly.
Then he states that very point by way of a *kaimutya* (a fortiori) argument:
"Whatever quality is attributed to me, who am the Supreme, if it is for the sake of a fruitless result..."
"O best of beings, that exertion would be as useless as [the effort spent on] fear and the like;
for whatever dharma ordained by the Vedas has been performed by offering it unto Me— if it is rendered fruitless,
meaning it is conceived as being without result because it was not offered with the desire for the fruit— then in that case..."
In this context, "exertion" (*āyāsa*) refers to fatigue; it is not "without purpose" (*anirartha*), meaning it is not in vain.

The qualification "fruitless" (*niṣphalāya*) intends to emphasize the excellence of its non-meaninglessness by the absence of any obstacle to that devotion, such as the enjoyment of fruits and so forth.

In that regard, regarding the meaning of "not being so" (anirarthatva), by way of a *kaimutya* argument, there is the illustrative example "like fear and so forth," which manifests one's own unique status as the object of worship characterized as Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
just as [fear arises] toward Kaṃsa and others from Me...
The meaning is that even the exertion arising from fear and so forth is not in vain by virtue of the mere connection [to Kṛṣṇa], because it brings about liberation.
Now, regarding those who, like the illustrious Uddhava, are solely devoted to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, [this applies] both to their state as a means (*sādhana*) and to their state as the goal (*sādhya*).
He states that Śrī Kṛṣṇa Himself alone is the supreme object to be attained:
"O dear one, whatever purpose there is for men in knowledge, action, yoga, commerce, and the wielding of power— all that is You, my fourfold form" (BhP 11.29.33).
Whatever fourfold object exists in knowledge and so forth, characterized by dharma and the rest, all that is indeed myself alone. Among these, liberation resides in knowledge;
while virtue and desire reside in action.

It should be understood that there is a fourfold nature: in yoga, there are various characteristics of supernatural attainments (*siddhi*); in livelihood (*vārtā*), there is worldly wealth; and in the wielding of the rod of punishment (*daṇḍadhāraṇa*), there is likewise various worldly wealth.
Thus, the fourfold nature is to be known.

// 11.29 // The Blessed Lord // 330–334 // [335] Again, in this very manner, the illustrious Uddhava also requested: "Obeisances unto You, O Great Yogi; please instruct me, who have surrendered to You."
"So that there may be unswerving devotion to Your lotus feet.
And the commentary says: "Even though You have done much for me, nevertheless, he requests this much, saying: 'May there be obeisances...'"
"Instruct" means "teach.
He states the very necessity of instruction with the words "as follows": "This [discipline] does not depart even in liberation."
// 11.29 // The illustrious Uddhava // 335 // [336] For this very reason, with another intention, he said: "O lotus-eyed one, in whatever way You are, of whatever kind, and of whatever nature..."
"One who desires liberation should meditate upon this; you ought to tell me this meditation.
And the commentary says: "You ought to tell me—me, who am desirous of knowing—how one who seeks liberation should meditate upon You."
Furthermore, this very service to you is the supreme human goal;
there is no need for meditation.
Thus it was said by you: "The garlands and perfumes used [by You]," and so forth; this is the speech of the glorious Uddhava. // 11.14 // 336 // 337 //
Recalling that his supreme auspiciousness of nature remains unmanifest even amidst all his incarnations, he said: "Alas! Bakī [offered] this breast-poison..."
Even though that unchaste woman caused her to drink [poison] with the intent to kill her, she attained the destination appropriate for a nurse;
who else but Him should we go for refuge? [BhP 3.2.23]
She went by the very same path that is customary for a nurse.
// 3.2 // That very same [point].
// 337 // [338] Now, he describes the supreme distinctiveness of even Gokula, which consists of pastimes such as the *rāsa* dance together with the illustrious wives of Vraja:
Whoever, endowed with faith, hears or describes this playful pastime of Viṣṇu with the women of Vraja,
shall obtain supreme devotion for the Blessed One and fulfill their desires.
The wise man quickly dispels heart-disease before long;
by the word "ca" (and), it is implied that he removes other things as well. Or, the word "atha" may be used instead of "ca."
One should either hear it or describe it;
this is also an illustration for [the practice of] meditation and so forth.
Since there exists nowhere else a state higher than this supreme one, one quickly abandons even the heart-disease of desire and the like;
herein lies the supreme nature even in its general sense.
Even among those [attainments], it is established by its very nature that the worship of Him consisting of the pastimes associated with the supremely excellent Śrī Rādhā is indeed the most supreme;
however, the secret pastimes are [beyond] human [comprehension].
She is not to be worshipped through the senses as if she were a modification [of them], nor through the relationships of father, son, or servant, because that would contradict her own true nature.
Furthermore, her secret nature is revealed in some places only in small measure, while in others...
"It should be understood that this applies in every respect."—
Śrī Śuka. (338) [339] Therein, those paths of devotion have been shown.

And herein, whatever secret— whether pertaining to the means or the goal— that has been obtained through the grace of the venerable Guru or the Blessed Lord, and which constitutes one's very own all-in-all,
must not be disclosed to anyone. As it has been said:
"O Goddess, this must not be told to another by any means, even when asked;
for everything becomes successful when the secret of the gods is well-kept.
[BhP 8.17.20] "Becomes successful" means it becomes fruit-bearing.
// 8.17 // Śrī-Viṣṇu [to] Aditi // 339 // [340] Thus, devotion consisting of the means of accomplishment has been shown; therein, the sequence of attainment and Śrī-...

This is shown by the words, "of one who desires to hear with faith at the commencement of the Sūta's instruction" (BhP 1.2.16), and likewise in the speech of Śrī Nārada, "I existed in a past life" (BhP 1.5.23), and so forth; and as in the speech of Śrī Kapiladeva, "From association with the virtuous, there arises knowledge of My power... (BhP 3.25.21).

In such passages as these, the sequence should be understood through the following: first, by the verse beginning "In this regard, for one desiring liberation, a person becomes detached through devotion" (BhP 3.25.23); and then, by the verse beginning "In pure devotion, some do not even long for oneness with Me" (BhP 3.25.31).
Likewise, in the *Śrī-Prahlāda-kṛta-daitya-bālānuśāsana*, which deals with pure devotion alone, it is stated: "By service to the guru" (*BhP* 7.7.25) and so forth.
Having thus summarized that very sequence, he speaks of it along with an illustration:
Devotion to the Supreme Lord, the experience of Him, and detachment from everything else— these three occur simultaneously for one who takes refuge,
just as they occur in one who is eating.
Contentment and nourishment result from eating after one's hunger has been removed.
O King, for the devotee who thus worships the feet of Acyuta with constant devotion, devotion, detachment,
and the awakening to the Lord truly arise.
"Then he attains supreme peace directly.

And the commentary (*ṭīkā*) states: "For a person who approaches Hari—that is, one who worships Him—there is devotion characterized by love, which is the experience of the Supreme Lord; through that experience, there arises a manifestation of the form of the Blessed Lord, the object of that love, and for one who is satisfied by that..."

Consequently, detachment from other things such as the home and so forth occurs; this triad—[detachment, devotion, and contentment]—would exist at one and the same time, precisely at the time of devotion.
Just as for one who is eating, there is satisfaction, happiness, nourishment, and the filling of the stomach.
And there should be a cessation with every morsel;
this is an illustration so that it may likewise apply to every grain of rice.
In the same way, when any of the triad beginning with affection arises toward a single vessel, it should continue accordingly.
For one who worships, supreme love and other qualities arise, just as supreme satisfaction and so forth arise for one who eats a great quantity of food.
And from that, by the grace of the Blessed One, one becomes one who has accomplished his purpose; thus he says: "Thus [he attains] the foot of Acyuta"—this is the verse.
"Peace" means the state of having achieved one's purpose;
the meaning is that it is manifested directly, both internally and externally, as the supreme human goal, without any mediation.
The examples for devotion to the previous verses and so forth, as well as contentment and the rest, should be understood in their respective order;
this same sequence applies hereafter as well.

Because devotion and contentment are of the singular nature of happiness; because nourishment and experience are of the singular nature of self-sustenance; and because the removal of hunger and dispassion are of the singular nature of peace—although a lack of thirst for food arises even in one who has eaten, for the experiencer of the Lord, it arises only toward other sense objects.
This is the dissimilarity;
nevertheless, it is understood that the example refers only to the aspect of freedom from craving for other things.
// 11.2 // Śrīkavi [composed] the Nimim; // 340 //
Thus has this subject matter been explained;
herein, other specific details should also be investigated according to the views of the scriptures and the great authorities.
The teacher, the scripture, faith, inclination, following, and accomplishment— all these that belong to me shine as the lotus feet of those two.
May Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, whose pair of lotus-eyes are perpetually bathed by the honey of compassion, who have come for refuge, be my sole resort.

Thus, within the *Śrī Bhāgavata-sandarbha*, which contains the essence of the teachings of Śrī Rūpa and Sanātana— who were followers of the feet of the divine Lord Kṛṣṇa Caitanya (the incarnation whose purpose was to purify the Kali-yuga by distributing His own worship)— and who were honored by the assembly of all the kings of Vaiṣṇavas... [Śrī-] *Bhagavat-sandarbha*.
The fifth compendium, named Bhakti-sandarbha.
And thus this Śrī Bhakti-sandarbha is completed.
